lessons.title: The basic step on 1 (forward–back and side)

scenes.text: Kabir, 29, a software tester in Bengaluru, signs up for salsa after his sister's wedding sangeet — he wants to dance at the next one.
He keeps stepping with the wrong foot and bumping into his partner. His teacher draws a simple map on the floor with tape.
“Leaders: left foot forward on 1. Followers: right foot back on 1. Mirror each other.”
Two weeks later Kabir dances the basic with eyes up, smiling at his partner — not staring at his feet.

steps.title: Roles: leader and follower
steps.body:
Partner salsa has two roles: **leader** and **follower**. Anyone of any gender can dance either role; many dancers learn both. In this course 'leader' and 'follower' just describe who starts which foot.

In **On1** (often called LA style or 'linear on 1'), the **break step** — the step that changes direction — happens on **1**.

steps.title: Forward–back basic (leader)
steps.body:
Start with feet together, weight on the right foot.

- **1** – left foot steps forward (small step).
- **2** – shift weight back onto the right foot in place.
- **3** – left foot comes back next to the right.
- **(4)** – pause.
- **5** – right foot steps back.
- **6** – shift weight forward onto the left foot in place.
- **7** – right foot comes back next to the left.
- **(8)** – pause.

**Follower** does the exact mirror: right foot back on 1, left foot forward on 5.

steps.title: Side basic
steps.body:
Same rhythm, sideways:

- **1** left foot to the side, **2** replace weight on right, **3** left foot closes.
- **5** right foot to the side, **6** replace weight on left, **7** right foot closes.

The side basic is useful on a crowded floor and as a resting step between moves.

steps.title: Posture that makes you look like a dancer
steps.body:
- Stand tall: imagine a string lifting the top of your head.
- Knees **soft**, never locked.
- Weight over the **balls of the feet**, heels light but touching.
- Steps **small** — about the length of your own foot. Big steps make you late.
- Hips move because knees bend and straighten alternately with each weight change (often called Cuban motion) — don't push the hips sideways on purpose at first.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stepping on 4 and 8 (you drift ahead).
- Taking long steps and leaning back.
- Looking at your feet — it pulls your posture forward. Look at your partner's chest or a point in the mirror.
- Holding your breath. Breathe out on 1 to stay relaxed.

steps.title: Try this: 5-minute drill
steps.body: Without music, say the counts aloud and do 8 forward-back basics. Then 8 side basics. Then put on a slow salsa track and do 2 minutes of each. Record a 20-second phone video and check: are steps small? Are you pausing on 4 and 8?

activity.prompt: Put the leader's forward–back basic in order (On1).
items: 3: left foot closes next to right
7: right foot closes next to left

quiz.q: In On1 salsa, on which count does the leader's forward break step happen?
quiz.why: In On1 salsa, the leader's forward break step is on count 1. On2 would break on 2.

quiz.q: What does the follower do on count 1 of the forward–back basic?
quiz.why: The follower mirrors the leader, so on count 1 the follower steps back with the right foot while the leader steps forward with the left.

quiz.q: Why should steps be small?
options: Big steps make you late and off-balance
quiz.why: Salsa is fast, so big steps make you late and off-balance. Small steps keep you on time and in control.

quiz.q: Which posture cue is correct?
options: Soft knees, weight on balls of feet
quiz.why: Soft knees and weight on the balls of the feet let you move quickly and smoothly. Locked knees, leaning back and staring at your feet hurt balance.

lessons.title: Frame and connection: dancing with a partner safely

scenes.text: Meera, 35, a doctor in Kochi, dances alone beautifully. With a partner, her arms go floppy and she misses every lead.
Her partner Tom, a visiting teacher from Manchester, says: “Imagine holding a big beach ball. Arms soft, but not empty.”
Meera finds the middle — not stiff, not floppy. Suddenly she feels the gentle push and pull of his leads.
She also learns it is always fine to say “a little lighter, please” — comfort comes first.

steps.title: Open position (hand hold)
steps.body:
Partners face each other, about an arm's length apart.

- Leader's palms face **up**, follower's fingers rest on top, palms down (a light 'hook' with the fingers, no thumbs gripping).
- Elbows are **in front of the body**, slightly bent, at about waist height.
- Never grab or squeeze. Thumbs stay relaxed — gripping can hurt wrists in turns.

steps.title: Closed position
steps.body:
- Leader's right hand rests on the follower's **shoulder blade** (upper back), not the waist or lower back.
- Follower's left hand rests lightly on the leader's right shoulder or upper arm.
- Leader's left hand holds the follower's right hand at about shoulder height.
- Keep a small space between bodies — salsa closed position is not a hug.

steps.title: What 'connection' and 'tone' mean
steps.body:
**Tone** is a gentle, springy firmness in your arms — like holding a full cup of tea without spilling. With tone:

- When the leader moves back, the follower feels it and moves too.
- The arm acts like a spring, not a rope (too floppy) or a rod (too stiff).

Leads come mostly from the leader's **body and core**, transmitted through the arms — not yanking with the hands.

steps.title: Safety and consent on the social floor
steps.body:
- **Ask** for a dance politely; accept 'no, thank you' with a smile. Anyone may decline any dance without giving a reason.
- Adjust to your partner's level — no complicated moves on a beginner.
- No dips, lifts or drops on the social floor unless you both know them and agree.
- If any hold is uncomfortable, say so. If someone touches you inappropriately, you may stop dancing immediately and tell the organiser.

steps.title: Try this: the beach-ball drill
steps.body: With a partner, hold open position. Leader walks slowly forward 4 steps and back 4 steps without music; follower keeps the same distance. Then do the same with the basic step. If the distance keeps changing, adjust tone — firmer if you lose the lead, softer if it feels like pushing.

a.text: At a social night in Delhi, a stranger asks you to dance. During the first song he grips your hand tightly and tries a dip you don't know.

choices.label: Say calmly: “No dips please, and a lighter grip.”
choices.feedback: Clear, polite, and your right. Most dancers will adjust immediately.

choices.label: Stay silent and hope the song ends soon
choices.feedback: Understandable, but your body's safety matters more than politeness.

b.text: He apologises and dances gently. Next song, he asks again.

choices.label: Dance again if you feel comfortable
choices.feedback: Good — communication made the dance better.

choices.label: Say “Thank you, I'll rest now”
choices.feedback: Also perfect. You never owe anyone a dance.

c.text: He tries another dip and your wrist twists.

choices.label: Stop dancing, step back and say it hurt
choices.feedback: Right call. Stopping mid-song is completely acceptable for safety.

choices.label: Keep going
choices.feedback: Pain is a signal to stop. Keep yourself safe first.

end1.text: Social dancing works on respect: ask, listen, adjust. Speaking up is part of good partnership.

end2.text: You can always stop a dance. Tell the organiser if someone is unsafe or ignores your words. Rest the wrist and see a doctor if pain or swelling persists.

quiz.q: Where does the leader's right hand go in closed position?
quiz.why: In closed position, the leader's right hand rests on the follower's shoulder blade. It is a clear, respectful place to lead from.

quiz.q: What is 'tone' in partner dancing?
options: Gentle springy firmness in the arms
quiz.why: Tone is gentle, springy firmness in the arms. It lets the lead travel, and it sits between limp arms and gripping hard.

quiz.q: Is it acceptable to decline a dance?
quiz.why: Anyone can decline any dance, and a polite 'no, thank you' is enough. You don't owe a reason.

quiz.q: Leads come mainly from…
quiz.why: A lead comes from the leader's body and core moving, and the arms simply transmit it. Shouting or finger pushing is not leading.

lessons.title: Your first full song and a practice plan

scenes.text: Joseph, 52, a bank manager in Goa, wants to dance salsa with his wife at their 25th anniversary in three months.
He can't attend classes every day, so he makes a 15-minute home plan: counts, basics, one combination, one full song.
Week by week he records a short video and notices his steps getting smaller and his timing steadier.
At the party they dance an entire song. Nobody cares about fancy moves — they see two people enjoying the music together.

steps.title: Build a beginner combination
steps.body:
Link what you know into a 32-count sequence:

- 2 × forward–back basic (16 counts)
- 1 × side basic (8 counts)
- 1 × forward–back basic (8 counts)

Repeat this through a slow song. When it is easy, add a turn from the next course.

steps.title: The 15-minute plan
steps.body:
- **2 min** – warm-up: march on the spot, ankle circles, shoulder rolls.
- **3 min** – count a song aloud and clap the 1.
- **4 min** – basics without music, then with music.
- **4 min** – your combination with a full song.
- **2 min** – cool down: calf and hip-flexor stretches, slow breathing.

Do it 4–5 days a week. Short, frequent practice beats one long weekly session.

steps.title: Self-check with video
steps.body:
Record 30 seconds every week from the front at hip height. Check three things only:

- Am I pausing on 4 and 8?
- Are my steps small?
- Am I looking up and breathing?

Compare with last week — progress is easier to see on video than in the mirror.

steps.title: Look after your body
steps.body: Wear shoes that let you pivot (smooth sole, or suede dance shoes). Avoid sticky rubber soles on turns — they can twist knees. Stop if you feel sharp pain in knees, ankles or back; rest, and see a doctor or physiotherapist if it lasts more than a few days.

steps.title: Where salsa comes from
steps.body: Salsa grew in the 1960s–70s among Caribbean (especially Cuban and Puerto Rican) communities in New York, building on Cuban son and other Afro-Caribbean forms. Today there are many styles — LA (On1), New York (On2), Cuban (casino, also danced in circles called *rueda*), Colombian (Cali) — all fun, none 'wrong'.

activity.prompt: Your first week of salsa practice — tick off as you go.
items: Clap the 1 through a full salsa song
Do 8 forward–back basics without music, counting aloud
Dance the 32-count combination through one full song
Record a 30-second video and check pauses, step size and posture

quiz.q: Which practice pattern builds skill fastest for most beginners?
quiz.why: Short practice four to five days a week builds habits and timing better than one long weekly session. Watching videos without moving doesn't train the body.

quiz.q: Why are sticky rubber soles risky for salsa turns?
options: They stop the foot pivoting, twisting knees
quiz.why: Sticky rubber soles grip the floor, so the foot can't pivot in a turn. The twist then goes into the knee and can injure it.

quiz.q: Which style is commonly danced in a circle called rueda?
quiz.why: Rueda de casino is Cuban-style salsa danced in a circle with called moves. New York On2 and LA On1 are mostly danced in a line (slot).

quiz.q: What three things should you check in your weekly video?
options: Pauses on 4 & 8, small steps, posture & breathing
quiz.why: Checking pauses on 4 and 8, small steps, and posture and breathing covers the basics that matter most early on. Costume and spins can wait.

questions.q: In On1 salsa, which beats are pauses?
questions.why: In On1 salsa you step on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, so counts 4 and 8 are pauses. Counts 1 and 5 are steps.

questions.q: How many steps in one full basic (8 counts)?
questions.why: Steps happen on 1-2-3 and 5-6-7, giving six steps in the eight counts. The other two counts are pauses.

questions.q: The leader's first step in the forward–back basic is…
questions.why: The leader begins with the left foot forward on 1, and the follower mirrors with the right foot back. A right foot forward would be the wrong foot.

questions.q: What does 'break step' mean?
questions.why: The break step is where you change direction, which is count 1 in On1. It is not a rest or a mistake.

questions.q: Which hold is correct for open position?
options: Leader palms up, follower's fingers resting on top
questions.why: In open position, the leader's palm faces up and the follower's fingers rest lightly on top. Gripping with thumbs can hurt wrists.

questions.q: Your steps keep landing late. The most likely fix is…
questions.why: Smaller steps take less time, so you can land on the beat. Bigger steps make you later.

questions.q: A partner feels like a 'wet noodle'. What is missing?
questions.why: A partner without tone feels like a 'wet noodle', so the lead can't travel through the arms. Gentle springy firmness fixes it.

questions.q: Where should closed-position contact be for the leader's right hand?
questions.why: The leader's right hand goes on the shoulder blade, which is clear and respectful. The waist, hip or lower back can feel intrusive.

questions.q: The singer starts each line on your count of 5. What should you do?
options: Shift your count by four beats
questions.why: Lines usually start on count 1, so if they start on your 5, you are four counts off. Shift your count by four to match.

questions.q: Which is NOT okay on a social floor?
questions.why: Dipping a stranger without agreement is not okay because dips need both partners' consent and skill. Asking, adjusting to a beginner and declining politely are all fine.

questions.q: Hip motion in salsa is mainly produced by…
options: Alternate bending and straightening of the knees with weight changes
questions.why: Cuban motion comes from alternately bending and straightening the knees as weight changes. Pushing the hips sideways or twisting the shoulders is not the source.

questions.q: You feel sharp knee pain after a session that is still there four days later. Best action?
options: Rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist
questions.why: Sharp knee pain that lasts four days is more than normal soreness. Rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist; dancing through it can worsen the injury.

courses.title: Salsa turns and partner work
courses.summary: Spin without dizziness, lead and follow the right turn, cross-body lead and inside turn, and combine them into musical sequences.
outcomes: Learners can spot and turn on balance
Learners can lead or follow a right turn and a left (inside) turn
Learners can dance the cross-body lead in a slot
Learners can build 3 combinations and adapt them to a partner

lessons.title: Spinning without getting dizzy: spotting and balance

scenes.text: Zara, 16, from Mumbai, loves turns but always staggers out of them.
Her teacher Diego shows her 'spotting': keep the eyes on one point and whip the head around last.
He also tells her to pull her arms in close and turn on the ball of the foot, knees soft.
After a week of slow practice, Zara can do a clean single turn and stop facing her partner — calm and smiling.

steps.title: Spotting
steps.body:
Pick a spot at eye level (your partner's face, a light switch).

- As your body begins to turn, **keep your eyes on the spot** as long as you can.
- When your head cannot stay any longer, **whip it around quickly** and find the same spot again.
- Your eyes see the spot most of the time, so the brain stays oriented and dizziness drops.

steps.title: Turning technique
steps.body:
- Turn on the **ball of the foot**, heel slightly lifted.
- Keep feet close together, knees soft.
- Stack your body: head over chest over hips over feet.
- Arms close to the body (or the free arm framing the face) — arms out wide slow you down and pull you off balance.
- Engage your core gently, like zipping up a tight jacket.

steps.title: Solo right turn on 5–6–7
steps.body:
A common solo turn:

- **1-2-3**: a forward basic (prep).
- **5**: step forward with the right foot and pivot clockwise on it.
- **6**: continue the turn, stepping the left foot around.
- **7**: finish facing the front, feet together.
- **8**: pause and balance.

Practise at half speed until you can stop on 7 without a wobble.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Looking at the floor (instant dizziness).
- Leaning back or forward during the turn.
- Rushing — the turn has the same 3 counts as a basic, there is time.
- Practising on carpet or sticky floors — risky for knees.

steps.title: Try this: 10 quarter-turns
steps.body: Turn just 90° at a time, spotting four walls in order. Then half-turns. Then full turns. Ten slow, clean turns are worth more than fifty dizzy ones.

statements.s: Spotting means keeping your eyes on a point as long as possible, then whipping the head around.
statements.why: That is exactly the technique that reduces dizziness.

statements.s: You should turn on your flat heel for the best balance.
statements.why: Turn on the ball of the foot — heels create friction and strain knees.

statements.s: Arms held wide help you turn faster.
statements.why: Wide arms slow the turn and pull you off-balance; keep them close.

statements.s: Sticky rubber soles are ideal for turning.
statements.why: They grip too much and can twist the knee.

statements.s: A turn in salsa still fits into the 3 steps of a half-basic.
statements.why: Turns use counts 1-2-3 or 5-6-7 like any other step.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of spotting?
quiz.why: Spotting means keeping your eyes on one point as long as possible during a turn. It reduces dizziness and keeps you oriented.

quiz.q: Where should your weight be when turning?
quiz.why: Turn on the balls of your feet, which let you pivot smoothly. Heels or the outside edges make it clumsy and risky.

quiz.q: Which body alignment helps balance in a turn?
options: Head, chest, hips stacked over feet
quiz.why: Stacking head, chest and hips over your feet keeps you centred, so you stay balanced in a turn. Leaning or twisting pulls you off balance.

quiz.q: A safe way to learn turns is…
quiz.why: Learn turns gradually: quarter-turns, then half, then full. This builds control and balance before speed.

lessons.title: The cross-body lead

scenes.text: Arjun, 24, from Hyderabad, keeps colliding with his partner Chloe when they try the cross-body lead.
Teacher Lina draws an imaginary 'slot' — a straight line on the floor along which the follower travels.
“Leader, you open the door on 1-2-3, then the follower walks through on 5-6-7.”
Next attempt, Arjun steps out of the way and Chloe glides past. No collision.

steps.title: What the slot is
steps.body: LA and New York styles are **linear** or **slot** styles: the follower moves back and forth along an imaginary line, and the leader steps out of the line to let the follower pass. The **cross-body lead (CBL)** is the most important move in slot salsa — many other moves are built on it.

steps.title: Leader's cross-body lead (On1)
steps.body:
- **1** – left foot steps forward (break).
- **2** – replace weight on right.
- **3** – left foot steps back and slightly to the left, turning the body about 90° to open an 'L'. You are now out of the slot.
- **5** – right foot steps back (or in place) while gently guiding the follower across with the left hand.
- **6** – left foot turns another 90° so you complete the turn.
- **7** – right foot closes. You now face the opposite direction, follower in front of you.

Total rotation for the leader: about 180°.

steps.title: Follower's cross-body lead
steps.body:
- **1** – right foot back. **2** – replace weight on left. **3** – right foot forward (start walking).
- **5** – left foot forward, walking past the leader along the slot.
- **6** – right foot forward and pivot to turn about 180°.
- **7** – left foot back next to the right, now facing the leader again.

Followers: keep walking straight along the slot; don't anticipate or cut the corner.

steps.title: Leading it clearly
steps.body: Leaders: the lead starts from your **body** — when you turn your torso on 3, the hand naturally guides. On 5 your left hand moves the follower's right hand across at waist height, smoothly, no pulling. The right hand can rest on the follower's shoulder blade to help direct.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leader not opening the 'L' on 3 → follower crashes into you.
- Follower turning early on 5 instead of 6 → ends in the wrong spot.
- Yanking the hand → painful and unclear. Lead with the body.
- Big steps — the CBL needs only small steps.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do 8 CBLs in a row without music, counting aloud. Then add slow music. Swap roles once — leaders who know the follower's footwork lead more kindly, and vice versa.

activity.prompt: Match each count of the leader's cross-body lead to what happens.
pairs: Replace weight on the right foot
Step back-left, open the 'L' out of the slot
Guide the follower across the slot
Complete the turn and close, facing the other way

quiz.q: What is 'the slot'?
options: An imaginary line the follower travels along
quiz.why: The slot is an imaginary line the follower travels along in linear salsa. Staying in it keeps the dancers from colliding.

quiz.q: On which count does the leader open the 'L' out of the slot?
quiz.why: The leader opens the 'L' on count 3 to clear the path for the follower. Then the follower walks through.

quiz.q: A follower turns on 5 instead of 6 and ends up crooked. What went wrong?
quiz.why: The follower should walk through on 5 and turn on 6. Turning on 5 is too early, so she ends up crooked.

quiz.q: The best way for a leader to lead the CBL is…
options: Turn the torso and guide smoothly
quiz.why: Lead the cross-body lead by turning your torso and guiding smoothly. Pushing, pulling hard or just saying 'go' is not a body lead.

quiz.q: About how much does the leader rotate in a CBL?
quiz.why: In a cross-body lead the leader rotates about 180° and ends facing the opposite direction. A full 360° would bring them back to the start.

lessons.title: Right turn and inside (left) turn

scenes.text: Priya, 31, from Chennai, and Daniel, her partner from Nairobi, try a right turn. Priya's hand gets twisted.
Their teacher shows a 'halo' — the leader's hand draws a small circle above the follower's head, and the follower's fingers stay loose to rotate.
Then she adds the inside turn into the cross-body lead.
By the end of the night they link basic → right turn → CBL → CBL with inside turn. Their first real routine!

steps.title: Right turn (follower turns clockwise)
steps.body:
A **right turn** means the follower turns to their right — **clockwise** seen from above.

- **1-2-3**: leader does a forward basic and gently brings the follower's hand slightly to the leader's left on 3 (prep).
- **5-6-7**: the leader raises the joined hands and draws a small halo **clockwise** above the follower's head. The follower turns on 5-6-7 (as in the solo turn) while the leader does a back basic in place.
- **8**: hands come down, back to open position.

steps.title: Inside (left) turn on the cross-body lead
steps.body: In the CBL, on **5** the leader raises the follower's right hand and draws a halo **anticlockwise**. The follower walks forward on 5 and turns **left** (anticlockwise) on 6-7, finishing facing the leader. Prep happens on **3**: the leader's left hand moves slightly to their left and down to signal.

steps.title: Hands in turns: the golden rules
steps.body:
- Follower: **fingers loosely hooked**, never gripping — let your hand rotate inside the leader's.
- Leader: hand stays **above the follower's head** and draws a **small** circle — big circles drag the follower off balance.
- Leader: **never** force the turn; if the follower doesn't turn, just go back to basic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No prep → follower doesn't know a turn is coming.
- Leader's hand too low → follower must duck.
- Pushing the follower around instead of guiding.
- Follower anticipating — wait for the lead.

steps.title: A 32-count combination
steps.body:
- 8: forward–back basic
- 8: right turn (prep on 1-2-3, turn on 5-6-7)
- 8: cross-body lead
- 8: cross-body lead with inside turn

Repeat. This sequence alone can carry you through a whole beginner song.

activity.prompt: Sort each cue: right turn or inside (left) turn?

items.text: Halo drawn clockwise above follower's head
Done from the forward–back basic, turning on 5-6-7
Follower walks forward on 5 and turns left on 6-7

quiz.q: A right turn means the follower turns…
quiz.why: A right turn means the follower turns clockwise, toward her right, as seen from above. Anticlockwise is a left turn.

quiz.q: How should the follower's hand be during a turn?
options: Flat on the leader's palm with thumb wrapped
Loosely hooked so it can rotate
quiz.why: The follower's hand should be loosely hooked so it can rotate inside the leader's hand. Gripping can strain the wrist or fingers.

quiz.q: If a follower doesn't take a turn lead, the leader should…
quiz.why: If a turn lead isn't taken, don't force it. Go back to a basic and try again later.

quiz.q: Why is the 'prep' important?
options: It signals the coming turn so the follower is ready
quiz.why: The prep signals that a turn is coming so the follower is ready. Without it the follower may be surprised.

quiz.q: The leader's halo should be…
quiz.why: The leader's halo is a small circle of the hand above the follower's head. Small circles keep her centred and stop her ducking.

lessons.title: Musicality, social dancing and levelling up

scenes.text: Sana, 27, an architect in Lucknow, can do lots of moves but her dancing looks 'mechanical'.
Her mentor plays a song and points out the 'mambo' section where horns build up, and the quiet breaks.
Sana learns to simplify in soft parts, add styling during horn hits and freeze for a beat during breaks.
Her friends say her dancing now looks like the music, not like a list of moves.

steps.title: Musicality basics
steps.body:
Musicality means your dancing **matches the song**:

- **Quiet verse**: simpler moves, basics, gentle styling.
- **Build-up / mambo section** (horn riffs, energy rising): turns, shines, bigger moves.
- **Breaks / hits**: a sudden stop or accent in the music — try a pause or a sharp pose.
- **Phrases**: start new moves on 1 of a phrase so they feel 'right'.

steps.title: Shines (solo footwork)
steps.body: In many songs partners separate for **shines** — solo footwork patterns danced facing each other. Simple shines include the *suzie-q* and *cross-over* steps. Learn one shine and use it during instrumental sections.

steps.title: Adapting to a partner
steps.body:
- Start every dance with 16 counts of basic to feel each other's timing.
- Use moves your partner can do; a smooth simple dance is better than a failed complicated one.
- Smile, make eye contact, say thank you at the end.

steps.title: 4-week level-up plan
steps.body:
- **Week 1**: spotting drills daily, CBL ×20.
- **Week 2**: right turn and inside turn, both roles once.
- **Week 3**: learn one shine; dance 3 full songs per session.
- **Week 4**: go to a social night; dance with at least 3 different partners; journal what felt good.

steps.title: On2 and other styles
steps.body: In **New York On2**, the break happens on count **2** (and 6). Cuban **casino** is circular and often danced in **rueda**. Colombian **Cali** style has fast, intricate footwork. Learn one style well first, then explore.

activity.label: How energetic is this part of the song?

bands.text: Quiet verse — basics, gentle styling, connect with your partner.
Chorus — add a turn or a cross-body lead with inside turn.
Build-up — multiple turns, a shine, bigger movement.
Mambo section / big horns — your most exciting (but safe!) moves; hit the accents.

quiz.q: What is a 'shine' in salsa?
quiz.why: A shine is solo footwork danced apart from your partner, often in instrumental sections. It is not a lift or a light cue.

quiz.q: In New York On2, the break step is on…
quiz.why: In New York On2, the break steps are on counts 2 and 6. On1 breaks on 1 and 5.

quiz.q: A quiet verse is best matched by…
quiz.why: A quiet verse suits basics and gentle styling, matching the music's energy. Lifts, running and big turns fit louder moments.

quiz.q: Why start each social dance with 16 counts of basic?
options: To feel your partner's timing and connection
quiz.why: Starting with 16 counts of basic helps you feel your partner's timing and connection before trying moves. It is not a formal rule.

questions.q: What reduces dizziness in turns?
questions.why: Spotting keeps your eyes oriented on one point, which reduces dizziness. Closing your eyes makes dizziness worse.

questions.q: A right turn is…
questions.why: A right turn is clockwise for the follower, seen from above. A left turn is anticlockwise.

questions.q: The cross-body lead is danced along a…
questions.why: The cross-body lead is danced along the slot, a straight line. It isn't circular or square.

questions.q: When does the leader open the 'L' in a CBL?
questions.why: The leader opens the 'L' on count 3 to clear the follower's path. Counts 1, 6 and 8 are not the opening beat.

questions.q: Follower's hand in turns should be…
questions.why: A loosely hooked hand lets the follower's hand rotate safely in a turn. A tense or gripping hand strains the wrist.

questions.q: Where does the inside turn of a CBL happen?
questions.why: The leader preps on 3, and the follower turns during 5-6-7. Counts 4 and 8 are pauses.

questions.q: A follower keeps ducking under turns. Most likely cause?
questions.why: If the leader's hand is too low, the follower must duck under it to turn. Keeping it above her head lets her turn upright.

questions.q: What should a leader do when a turn lead fails?
questions.why: If a turn lead fails, calmly go back to a basic step. Forcing it or repeating faster can hurt or confuse your partner.

questions.q: A horn build-up in the music suggests…
options: Bigger, more energetic moves or shines
questions.why: A horn build-up signals rising energy, so bigger, more energetic moves or shines fit. Match the dancing to the music.

questions.q: Which statement about On2 is true?
options: It is only danced in circles
questions.why: On2 salsa breaks on counts 2 and 6. It isn't only for circles and still has pauses.

questions.q: Total leader rotation in a basic CBL is about…
questions.why: In a basic cross-body lead the leader rotates about 180°, ending facing the opposite way. A 360° would bring him back to the start.

questions.q: Which combination is correctly structured in 8-count units?
options: Basic (8) → right turn (8) → CBL (8) → CBL + inside turn (8)
questions.why: Each move fills one 8-count, so basic, right turn, CBL and CBL with inside turn are four 8-counts. The other combos use counts that don't fit the 8-beat structure.

courses.title: Bollywood and hip-hop: groove, expression, choreography
courses.summary: Find your groove, learn signature Bollywood expressions and hip-hop foundations, and learn a short routine for a sangeet, school show or party.
outcomes: Learners can bounce and rock on the beat (hip-hop groove)
Learners can use hand gestures, facial expression and storytelling in Bollywood dance
Learners can break a song into 8-counts and learn choreography in chunks
Learners can plan and rehearse a 1-minute group item for an event

lessons.title: Groove first: bounce, rock and the two-step

scenes.text: Rohan, 13, from Kolkata, wants to join his school's hip-hop crew but feels 'stiff like a robot'.
Crew captain Aisha tells him: “Forget moves. For a week, just bounce to every song you hear.”
He bounces in the kitchen and in his room. His knees start to feel the music on their own.
At the next practice he does a simple two-step — and it finally looks relaxed.

steps.title: The down bounce
steps.body:
Hip-hop grooves sit on the beat. The basic **down bounce**:

- Feet hip-width apart, knees soft.
- On every beat, bend the knees slightly so the body drops **down** on the beat, and rises between beats.
- Chest and head ride along — don't hold your upper body stiff.

The **up bounce** is the reverse: the body rises on the beat. Try both; each gives a different feeling.

steps.title: Rock and two-step
steps.body:
- **Rock**: shift weight forward and back (or side to side) on the beat, chest leading slightly.
- **Two-step**: step right foot to the side, bring the left to touch next to it; step left to the side, bring right to touch. Add the bounce and let your arms swing naturally.

These foundations make every later move look 'in the pocket' (in time with the groove).

steps.title: Where hip-hop dance comes from
steps.body: Hip-hop culture grew in the **Bronx, New York, in the 1970s** — with DJing, MCing (rap), graffiti and **breaking** (b-boying/b-girling). Related 'funk styles' such as **locking** and **popping** developed on the US West Coast in the same era. Breaking made its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Doing big moves without a groove underneath — it looks disconnected.
- Locked knees — the bounce lives in soft knees.
- Copying the shape but not the **timing**. Watch where the accent is: on the beat or on the 'and'.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Put on a mid-tempo hip-hop track. 1 minute down bounce, 1 minute up bounce, 1 minute rock, 1 minute two-step. Then freestyle 1 minute mixing all four. Use the rhythm game to test whether you can hit every beat.

items.back: Body drops on the beat by bending the knees; rises between beats.
Body rises on the beat; drops between beats.
Weight shifts forward/back or side to side, chest leading, on the beat.
Step to the side, touch the other foot in; repeat to the other side with a bounce.
Perfectly in time with the groove, relaxed rather than rushed.

quiz.q: In a down bounce, the body…
quiz.why: In a down bounce, you drop your body weight down on the beat. In an up bounce you rise on the beat.

quiz.q: Where did hip-hop culture begin?
quiz.why: Hip-hop culture began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s. It later spread worldwide.

quiz.q: Why learn grooves before big moves?
options: They keep moves connected to the music
quiz.why: Learning grooves first keeps your moves connected to the music's timing and feel. Big moves without groove look disconnected.

quiz.q: Which is a 'funk style' linked with hip-hop dance?
quiz.why: Locking and popping are funk styles linked with hip-hop dance from the West Coast. Waltz and tango are ballroom, and Kathak is classical Indian.

lessons.title: Bollywood: expression, hands and story

scenes.text: Nisha, 26, in Jaipur, is choreographing a family dance for her cousin's sangeet. Her uncles can't follow complicated steps.
She realises Bollywood dance is really about storytelling: faces, hands, a few strong signature moves.
She picks one move per line of the song and teaches with simple names: 'phone call', 'heart', 'thumka'.
On the night, the whole family performs. The crowd cheers loudest for the uncles' perfectly timed thumka.

steps.title: What makes Bollywood dance
steps.body: Hindi film dance mixes many sources: Indian classical (for example kathak gestures and spins), folk (bhangra, garba, lavani), and global styles (jazz, hip-hop, Latin). What ties it together is **expression and storytelling** — dancers act the lyrics with face and hands, and the dance follows the song's emotions.

steps.title: Signature moves to know
steps.body:
- **Thumka** – a sharp hip accent to one side on a beat.
- **Jhatka** – a sharp accent or 'jerk' of shoulders or hands.
- **Screw-the-bulb** – hands up, twisting as if changing a bulb (bhangra-style).
- **Shoulder bounce** – from bhangra: shoulders bounce up and down with the beat.
- **Lyric gestures** – miming the words: hand to heart, pointing, a 'telephone' hand, wiping tears.

Hold each move clearly for its count; sharp start, sharp finish.

steps.title: Faces sell the dance
steps.body: Decide the emotion of each section: playful, romantic, proud, cheeky. Practise in a mirror: eyes and eyebrows lead, smile with the eyes, look at the audience (or your partner) on key lyrics. A simple step with a confident face beats a complex step with a nervous face.

steps.title: Breaking the song into chunks
steps.body:
1. Listen and mark each **8-count** of the song.
2. Write the lyric line next to each 8-count.
3. Choose **one main move** per 8-count — often lyric-based.
4. Group 4 eight-counts into a 'chunk'. Teach and drill one chunk at a time.
5. Add **formations** last (lines, V shape, two rows).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Too many different moves — the audience remembers repetition.
- Ignoring the lyrics' meaning (a happy gesture on a sad line looks odd).
- Everyone facing each other instead of the audience.
- Not rehearsing entrances and exits — the first and last 10 seconds matter most.

activity.prompt: Match each Bollywood move to its description.
pairs: Sharp hip accent to the side
Sharp accent of shoulders or hands
Hands up, twisting as if changing a light bulb
Bhangra-style bouncing shoulders on the beat
Miming the words with hands and face

quiz.q: What ties Bollywood dance styles together?
quiz.why: Bollywood dance styles are tied together by expression and storytelling, using the face and hands to convey the song's emotion. It borrows from many dance forms.

quiz.q: A good way to choreograph for beginners is…
quiz.why: For beginners, one main move per 8-count that is repeated is easy to learn and remember. Changing the move every count is too hard.

quiz.q: Which move comes from bhangra?
quiz.why: Shoulder bounces are a classic bhangra move from Punjab. The moonwalk is pop, the cross-body lead is salsa, and the pirouette is ballet.

quiz.q: When should formations be added?
quiz.why: Add formations last, after the moves are learnt. Spacing makes sense only once everyone knows what they are doing.

quiz.q: Why do expressions matter so much?
options: They communicate the song's story and emotion
quiz.why: Expressions communicate the story and emotion of the song, which is central to Bollywood. They do much more than hide mistakes.

lessons.title: Learning choreography fast

scenes.text: Aisha's crew in Delhi has only two days to learn a new 1-minute piece for a college fest.
They film the choreographer slowly, then mirror the video and count every move.
Each dancer writes a 'count sheet' in their own words.
By day two, they can do it at full speed — and in sync.

steps.title: Counts are your map
steps.body:
Every piece of choreography is a series of **8-counts**. Number them: 1st eight, 2nd eight… Write a short note for each count or half-count. Example:

- 1st eight: 1-2 step-touch R, 3-4 step-touch L, 5 arms up, 6 down, 7-8 turn.

If you get lost, you can jump back in at the start of the next eight.

steps.title: The learn-it method
steps.body:
- **Watch** the whole section twice without moving.
- **Feet first**, then arms, then head and face.
- Learn at **half speed**, counting aloud.
- **Chain**: learn 8-count A, then B, then A+B, then C, then A+B+C.
- Speed up gradually with the music.

steps.title: Mirroring
steps.body: If a teacher faces you, their right is your left. Many teachers 'mirror' for students (they use their left when telling you 'right'). Agree on this at the start. When learning from video, use the mirror/flip option or turn your back to the screen.

steps.title: Staying in sync as a group
steps.body:
- Pick a **reference dancer** and match their timing.
- Clean section by section: angles of arms, height of jumps, which foot.
- Film the group from the audience's view and spot whoever is early or late.
- Rehearse with the actual stage size marked on the floor.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Choose a 32-count section from any song you love. Write a count sheet for it, then teach it to a friend or family member using only your count sheet.

activity.prompt: Put these steps for learning a routine in a good order.
items: Watch the whole section twice without moving
Learn the footwork at half speed, counting aloud
Add arms, then head and face
Chain 8-counts: A, B, A+B, C, A+B+C
Speed up gradually with the music
Film yourself and fix early/late moments

quiz.q: What is a count sheet?
options: Written notes of moves per count
quiz.why: A count sheet is a written list of which moves happen on which counts. It helps dancers remember and rehearse accurately.

quiz.q: When learning a new section, start with…
quiz.why: Start learning a new section with the feet, as they carry the timing and direction. Add arms and face afterwards.

quiz.q: What does 'chaining' mean?
options: Adding sections one at a time and repeating the joined sequence
quiz.why: Chaining means adding one section at a time and repeating the joined sequence: A, then A+B, then A+B+C. This builds memory.

quiz.q: A teacher facing you says 'right'. You should…
quiz.why: A teacher facing you may be mirroring, so clarify whether 'right' means their right or yours. Agreeing on this avoids confusion.

lessons.title: Putting on a show: sangeet, school or fest

scenes.text: Kamala, 70, in Madurai, wants to be in her granddaughter's wedding dance but has knee pain.
The choreographer gives her a seated part — hands, expressions and a grand entrance on a chair.
The rest of the family dances around her. She becomes the highlight of the item.
Good choreography includes everyone safely.

steps.title: Plan the item
steps.body:
- **Length**: 1–3 minutes is ideal for family or school events.
- **Music edit**: cut to the best parts, fade in/out cleanly, check the volume.
- **Structure**: strong entrance (8–16 counts) → 2–3 chunks → big finish pose.
- **Roles**: give simpler parts to beginners and seniors, and a 'feature' moment to each group.

steps.title: Inclusive choreography
steps.body:
- Seated or standing-only versions of the same move (hands and face do the same thing).
- Avoid deep squats, jumps or floor work for anyone with knee/back issues.
- Children: short, repetitive, playful moves; put them at the front.
- Wheelchair users: arm choreography, turns of the chair if they want, featured moments.

steps.title: Stage safety
steps.body:
- Check the stage floor for wet patches, wires, loose tiles.
- Rehearse in the costume and shoes you will wear — long lehengas, dupattas and heels change everything.
- Pin dupattas safely; avoid moves that can catch jewellery or fabric.
- Have water ready; warm up for 5 minutes before going on.

steps.title: A 2-week rehearsal plan
steps.body:
- Days 1–3: learn chunk 1 and 2.
- Days 4–6: chunk 3, finish pose, entrance.
- Days 7–9: formations and spacing on a marked floor.
- Days 10–12: full runs with costume; film and clean.
- Day 13: dress rehearsal at the venue if possible.
- Day 14: rest, light run-through, enjoy the show!

a.text: Your college fest item is in 3 days. One dancer keeps missing rehearsals and the group is upset.

choices.label: Talk privately: ask what's going on and agree a plan
choices.feedback: Good — you find out the problem before judging.

choices.label: Post an angry message in the group chat
choices.feedback: Public blame usually makes things worse.

b.text: She says she has a part-time job in the evenings. She can practise mornings.

choices.label: Schedule a short morning session and send her a practice video
choices.feedback: Flexible and fair — team problem solved.

choices.label: Remove her from the item without discussion
choices.feedback: Sometimes needed, but try solutions first.

c.text: She feels humiliated and says she'll quit. Two others take her side.

choices.label: Apologise and talk calmly with everyone
choices.feedback: Repairing quickly is a strong leadership move.

choices.label: Ignore it and keep rehearsing
choices.feedback: The conflict will show on stage.

end1.text: You kept the team together. Great shows come from good teamwork as much as good steps.

end2.text: The team is smaller and tense. Next time: private conversations, clear schedules, and kindness first.

quiz.q: A good length for a family or school dance item is…
quiz.why: One to three minutes suits a family or school dance item. It keeps energy high and is easy to learn.

quiz.q: Why rehearse in costume?
options: Costumes and shoes change how you move
quiz.why: Costumes and shoes change how you move; long skirts, dupattas and heels all need practice. Rehearsing in them avoids surprises on stage.

quiz.q: An elderly relative with knee pain wants to join. Best choice?
options: Give a seated or standing-only version
quiz.why: Inclusive choreography adapts the move, so a seated or standing-only version lets the relative join safely. Excluding or hiding them isn't respectful, and jumping risks the knee.

quiz.q: A dancer keeps missing rehearsal. First step?
quiz.why: First talk privately to understand why they miss rehearsal; there may be a reason you can help with. Public criticism or instant removal is unfair.

questions.q: In a down bounce the body drops…
questions.why: A down bounce means you drop on the beat. The beat is the moment your weight goes down.

questions.q: A thumka is…
questions.why: A thumka is a sharp hip accent, a classic Bollywood move. It isn't a bow, a jump or a spin.

questions.q: Hip-hop culture began in…
questions.why: Hip-hop culture began in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s. Cuba, Mumbai and Paris are not its origin.

questions.q: When learning choreography, learn first…
questions.why: Learn the feet first because they carry the timing and direction. Arms, face and bows follow.

questions.q: A count sheet helps you…
questions.why: A count sheet maps moves to counts, so it helps you remember what to do on each count. It isn't for finance or headcount.

questions.q: Which is part of Bollywood's mix of influences?
questions.why: Bollywood dance mixes influences including Kathak and bhangra, along with folk and global styles. It is not entirely new.

questions.q: A section feels messy as a group. Best fix?
options: Pick a reference dancer and clean angles/timing
questions.why: For a messy group section, choose a reference dancer and clean the angles and timing. Adding moves or speed makes it worse.

questions.q: Why should a dance repeat key moves?
options: Audiences remember repetition and beginners can learn it
questions.why: Repeating key moves helps audiences remember them and lets beginners learn the routine. It's clear design, not laziness.

questions.q: In 'chaining', after learning A and B you practise…
questions.why: In chaining, after learning A and B you practise A+B together before adding C. This joins sections as you go.

questions.q: Which is a stage safety check?
options: Wet patches and loose wires on the floor
questions.why: Wet patches and loose wires are physical hazards that can cause falls, so they are part of a stage safety check. Lighting colours, seat numbers and prices aren't safety issues.

questions.q: Breaking first appeared at the Olympics in…
questions.why: Breaking made its Olympic debut at Paris 2024. It was not part of London 2012 or Tokyo 2020.

questions.q: Your teacher faces you and lifts their left arm saying 'right arm'. They are probably…
questions.why: When a teacher faces you, they often mirror: lifting their left arm while saying 'right arm' so you can copy directly. It isn't a mistake.

courses.title: Bharatanatyam and Kathak foundations
courses.summary: Start two great Indian classical dance traditions correctly: Bharatanatyam's aramandi, adavus, hastas and abhinaya, and Kathak's tatkar, teentaal, chakkars and tihais.
outcomes: Learners can hold aramandi safely and do basic adavu patterns
Learners can name and form the first ten single-hand (asamyuta) hastas
Learners can explain nritta, nritya and natya and the nine rasas
Learners can recite and step basic Kathak tatkar in teentaal
Learners understand why guided training with a guru/teacher matters

lessons.title: Bharatanatyam: aramandi and the first adavus

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 9, starts Bharatanatyam at a dance school in Chennai. On day one, her knees ache.
Her teacher, Revathi akka, checks her posture: “Knees out over your toes, back straight, heels together. Don't force it.”
They practise the first tatta adavu slowly — striking the floor with flat feet to the syllables 'tai ya tai hi'.
In a few months, Lakshmi can hold aramandi through a whole set of adavus.

steps.title: What Bharatanatyam is
steps.body: Bharatanatyam is a classical dance from **Tamil Nadu**, with roots in temple and court traditions and in the ancient Sanskrit text **Natyashastra** (attributed to Bharata). It combines precise geometric footwork and lines with deep expressive storytelling.

steps.title: Aramandi (half-sitting)
steps.body:
Aramandi is the basic posture:

- Heels together, toes turned out to the sides.
- Knees bend **outward**, directly over the toes — making a diamond shape between the legs.
- Spine upright, chest open, shoulders down.
- Hands often on the waist while learning.

**Safety**: the turnout must come from the **hips**, not by twisting the knees. Go only as low as you can while keeping knees over toes.

steps.title: Adavus: the building blocks
steps.body:
**Adavus** are the basic units of movement, combining footwork, hand positions and body lines, done to rhythmic syllables (**sollukattu**). Each family of adavus has several numbered variations and is practised at different speeds.

Examples of adavu families: **tatta adavu** (striking flat feet), **natta adavu** (stretching a leg out and touching the heel), **visharu adavu** (sweeping arm movements).

steps.title: Worked example: tatta adavu, first variation
steps.body:
Sitting in aramandi, hands on waist:

- On 'tai' strike the floor with the **right** foot (flat).
- On 'ya' strike with the **left** foot.
- On 'tai' right, on 'hi' left… continuing evenly.

Practise at **first speed** (one strike per beat), then **second speed** (two per beat), then **third speed** (four per beat). Keep the height constant — no bobbing up and down.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Knees falling forward inside the toes → strain on knees. Keep knees over toes.
- Leaning forward or sticking the bottom out.
- Rising out of aramandi between strikes.
- Striking with the heel or toe only instead of the whole flat foot.
- Forcing depth too early. Strength and flexibility come with weeks of practice.

steps.title: Learn with a teacher
steps.body: Classical forms are traditionally learnt from a **guru or trained teacher** who corrects posture regularly. Use these lessons to understand and practise, but get regular feedback from a qualified teacher — online or in person. Syllables and adavu numbering differ a little between schools (banis), so follow your teacher's version.

statements.s: In aramandi the knees bend outward over the toes.
statements.why: This protects the knee and creates the classic diamond shape.

statements.s: It is fine to let the knees fall forward if you can't turn out.
statements.why: Go less deep instead; knees must stay over toes.

statements.s: Adavus are basic movement units practised at different speeds.
statements.why: They are the alphabet of Bharatanatyam.

statements.s: Bharatanatyam comes from Kerala.
statements.why: It comes from Tamil Nadu (Kerala's classical forms include Mohiniyattam and Kathakali).

statements.s: Sollukattu are the rhythmic syllables the adavus are danced to.
statements.why: Syllables like 'tai ya tai hi' guide the rhythm.

quiz.q: Bharatanatyam originates in…
quiz.why: Bharatanatyam comes from Tamil Nadu. Manipuri is from Manipur, Odissi from Odisha and bhangra from Punjab.

quiz.q: What is aramandi?
quiz.why: Aramandi is Bharatanatyam's half-sitting basic posture with the knees turned out. It is not a gesture, costume or spin.

quiz.q: Turnout should come from…
quiz.why: Turnout should come from rotating at the hips. Twisting the knees or ankles can injure them.

quiz.q: Tatta adavu involves…
options: Striking the floor with flat feet
quiz.why: Tatta adavu means striking the floor with flat feet to a rhythm. It's a basic foot-stamping pattern.

quiz.q: Second speed means…
options: Twice as many movements per beat
quiz.why: Second speed means twice as many movements per beat compared with the first speed. Each faster speed doubles the density.

lessons.title: Hastas, nritta–nritya–natya and the nine rasas

scenes.text: Farhan, 15, from Hyderabad, loves Bharatanatyam's speed but finds the 'acting part' embarrassing.
His teacher shows how a single hand shape — pataka, a flat hand — can mean a cloud, a forest, a river, a blessing.
He practises expressing nine emotions in the mirror, one by one.
In his first padam, the audience understands the story even without knowing the Tamil lyrics.

steps.title: Hastas: the hand alphabet
steps.body:
The text **Abhinaya Darpana** (attributed to Nandikeshvara) describes **asamyuta hastas** (single-hand gestures, traditionally 28) and **samyuta hastas** (double-hand gestures). The **first ten single-hand hastas** are:

1. **Pataka** – flag (all fingers together, straight)
2. **Tripataka** – ring finger bent
3. **Ardhapataka** – ring and little fingers bent
4. **Kartarimukha** – scissors (index and middle apart)
5. **Mayura** – peacock (ring finger touches thumb)
6. **Ardhachandra** – half moon (thumb stretched out from pataka)
7. **Arala** – index finger bent
8. **Shukatunda** – parrot's beak
9. **Mushti** – fist
10. **Shikhara** – fist with thumb up

steps.title: Nritta, nritya and natya
steps.body:
- **Nritta**: pure dance — rhythm, footwork and lines, no story (e.g. adavus, jatiswaram).
- **Nritya**: expressive dance — gesture and expression interpret lyrics and emotion (e.g. padam).
- **Natya**: drama — the full theatrical presentation of a story with characters.

steps.title: The nine rasas (navarasa)
steps.body:
Rasa is the 'flavour' of emotion the audience experiences. The nine traditionally listed are:

- **Shringara** – love/beauty
- **Hasya** – laughter/humour
- **Karuna** – compassion/sorrow
- **Raudra** – anger/fury
- **Veera** – heroism/courage
- **Bhayanaka** – fear
- **Bibhatsa** – disgust
- **Adbhuta** – wonder
- **Shanta** – peace

The Natyashastra describes eight; shanta was added later in the tradition.

steps.title: Worked example: one hasta, many meanings
steps.body: **Pataka** (flat hand) can show: the start of a dance, clouds, forest, river, a blessing, the night, a wave, a horse… The meaning comes from **context** — where the hand is placed, how it moves and the face's expression.

steps.title: Try this: navarasa in the mirror
steps.body: Spend 30 seconds on each rasa. Change only the face (eyes, eyebrows, mouth, breath) — no hands. Then add one hasta that fits. Notice how the **eyes** carry most of the expression.

cards.back: Flag — all fingers straight and together. Many meanings: cloud, river, forest, blessing.
Pataka with the ring finger bent.
Scissors' face — index and middle fingers apart.
Peacock — ring finger tip touches the thumb.
Half moon — pataka with the thumb stretched away.
Peak — fist with the thumb raised.

quiz.q: Nritta is…
quiz.why: Nritta is pure dance, with rhythm and movement but no story or meaning. Nritya adds expression and interpretation.

quiz.q: Which rasa means wonder?
quiz.why: Adbhuta is the rasa of wonder. Karuna is compassion or sorrow, Raudra is anger and Hasya is laughter.

quiz.q: Which hasta is a fist with the thumb raised?
quiz.why: Shikhara, meaning 'peak', is a fist with the thumb raised. Mushti is a plain fist, and pataka is a flat hand.

quiz.q: How does an audience know what pataka means at a moment?
options: From context: placement, movement and expression
quiz.why: A hasta's meaning depends on context: its placement, movement and the dancer's expression. The same hand shape can mean different things.

quiz.q: Which rasa was added later to the Natyashastra's eight?
quiz.why: The Natyashastra lists eight rasas, and shanta, peace, was added later as the ninth. Veera, shringara and bhayanaka were already among the eight.

lessons.title: Kathak: tatkar and teentaal

scenes.text: Ishaan, 12, in Lucknow, gets his first pair of ghungroo (ankle bells). They are loud — and every mistake is loud too.
His guruji plays teentaal on the tabla and recites: “Ta thei thei tat, aa thei thei tat.”
Ishaan learns to strike evenly with flat feet, keeping knees soft and the upper body still.
When he lands perfectly on sam with the tabla, guruji nods: “Shabash!”

steps.title: What Kathak is
steps.body: Kathak is a classical dance of **North India**. The name is linked with *katha* (story) — early Kathak artists were storytellers. It developed in temple traditions and later in Mughal and Rajput courts. Major schools (**gharanas**) include **Lucknow**, **Jaipur** and **Banaras**. It is known for fast rhythmic footwork, spins (**chakkars**) and expressive storytelling.

steps.title: Teentaal: the 16-beat cycle
steps.body:
**Teentaal** has **16 beats** (matras) in **4 sections (vibhags) of 4**: 4+4+4+4.

- Beat **1** = **sam** (marked X, clapped) — the most important beat; phrases often end here.
- Beat **5** = 2nd tali (clap).
- Beat **9** = **khali** (marked 0, a wave of the hand — 'empty').
- Beat **13** = 3rd tali (clap).

The tabla **theka** (basic pattern) is:

**Dha Dhin Dhin Dha | Dha Dhin Dhin Dha | Dha Tin Tin Ta | Ta Dhin Dhin Dha**

steps.title: Basic tatkar
steps.body:
Stand with feet slightly apart, knees soft, upper body still. Strike with the flat foot:

**Ta** (R) **thei** (L) **thei** (R) **tat** (L) | **Aa** (R) **thei** (L) **thei** (R) **tat** (L)

Four of these groups of four = one cycle of teentaal (16 beats). Practise at **thah** (single speed), then **dugun** (double), then **chaugun** (four times).

steps.title: Tihai: landing on sam
steps.body:
A **tihai** is a phrase played or danced **three times**, calculated so that the final syllable lands exactly on **sam** (beat 1). It creates a satisfying 'arrival'.

Example: a phrase of 5 beats with a gap of 1, repeated three times = 5+1+5+1+5 = **17 beats**. Start it on sam: the last syllable falls on beat 17, which is the next sam (16 + 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Striking with heels only → painful heels and dull sound.
- Uneven volume between feet — the weaker foot needs extra practice.
- Bouncing the upper body — the torso should stay calm.
- Practising on hard tiles or concrete for long periods; a wooden floor is kinder to joints.

activity.prompt: A tihai phrase is 5 beats long with a 1-beat gap between repeats: 5 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 5. How many beats does the whole tihai take?

quiz.q: How many beats in teentaal?
quiz.why: Teentaal has 16 beats, in four groups of four (4+4+4+4). It is the most common taal in Kathak.

quiz.q: Which beat is khali in teentaal?
quiz.why: In teentaal, beat 9 is khali, the 'empty' beat shown with a wave of the hand. Beat 1 is sam, and 5 and 13 are claps.

quiz.q: A tihai is…
options: A phrase repeated three times landing on sam
quiz.why: A tihai is a phrase repeated three times that ends exactly on sam, the first beat. It gives a strong rhythmic finish.

quiz.q: Which is a Kathak gharana?
quiz.why: Lucknow is a major Kathak gharana, along with Jaipur and Banaras. Kochi, Imphal and Chennai are linked to other traditions.

quiz.q: In tatkar the sound comes from…
quiz.why: In tatkar, the footwork sound is made by striking with the flat foot. It is not clapping or heels or toes only.

lessons.title: Kathak chakkars, safety and a daily riyaz

scenes.text: Aditi, 22, a Kathak student in Jaipur, dreams of doing many fast chakkars like her guru.
She tries 9 spins in a row, gets dizzy and nearly falls.
Her guru teaches her to spot, keep her body upright and build up from 3 spins.
Months of riyaz (daily practice) later, she lands 9 spins and ends cleanly on sam.

steps.title: Kathak chakkars
steps.body: Kathak spins are traditionally done on the **heel** of one foot, with the other foot pushing around in small steps, body upright, arms framing the body. Spinning with a **spot** (eyes on one point) is essential. Chakkars are often counted to land on **sam** — for example a set of spins as part of a tihai.

steps.title: Riyaz: a 30-minute daily plan
steps.body:
- **5 min** warm-up: ankles, knees, hips, neck rolls, light march.
- **10 min** tatkar in teentaal: thah, dugun, chaugun with a tabla app or metronome.
- **5 min** hand movements and hastas.
- **5 min** chakkars: build from 3 to 5 to 7, always spotting.
- **5 min** expression practice and cool-down stretches.

steps.title: Look after your joints
steps.body: Classical dance is athletic. Warm up before practice, stop with sharp pain, and see a doctor or physiotherapist for knee, ankle or heel pain that lasts more than a few days. Ghungroo practice on concrete can stress the heels — prefer wooden floors or a mat where possible.

steps.title: Indian classical dance family
steps.body: India has several recognised classical dance forms, including **Bharatanatyam** (Tamil Nadu), **Kathak** (North India), **Kathakali** and **Mohiniyattam** (Kerala), **Kuchipudi** (Andhra Pradesh), **Odissi** (Odisha), **Manipuri** (Manipur) and **Sattriya** (Assam). Each has its own technique, music and costume.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Keep a riyaz diary for two weeks: date, minutes, what you practised, one thing that improved, one thing to fix tomorrow.

activity.prompt: Match each classical dance form with its home state or region.

quiz.q: What helps most against dizziness in chakkars?
quiz.why: Spotting keeps you oriented in chakkars (spins) and reduces dizziness. Closing your eyes or looking at the floor makes it worse.

quiz.q: Riyaz means…
quiz.why: Riyaz means regular, disciplined practice, usually daily, in Indian classical arts. It is not a costume or a performance.

quiz.q: Sattriya is a classical dance from…
quiz.why: Sattriya is a classical dance of Assam. It grew out of the Vaishnavite monasteries.

quiz.q: Heel pain that lasts more than a few days should be…
options: Checked by a doctor or physiotherapist
quiz.why: Heel pain lasting more than a few days should be checked by a doctor or physiotherapist. Dancing through it can make the injury worse.

questions.q: Aramandi is…
questions.why: Aramandi is Bharatanatyam's half-sitting posture with the knees turned out. It is not a raga, a spin or a drum.

questions.q: Teentaal has how many beats?
questions.why: Teentaal has 16 beats, grouped 4+4+4+4. Eight beats would be a different taal such as kaharwa.

questions.q: Pataka is…
options: A flat hand with fingers together
questions.why: Pataka, meaning 'flag', is a flat hand with the fingers together. A fist is mushti and scissors is kartari.

questions.q: Kathak is associated with which region?
questions.why: Kathak is associated with North India. Kerala, Manipur and Tamil Nadu have other classical dances.

questions.q: In aramandi the knees should be…
questions.why: In aramandi the knees are over the toes and turned outward. Locked, forward-facing or touching knees put stress on the joints.

questions.q: Nritya means…
options: Expressive dance interpreting lyrics and emotion
questions.why: Nritya is expressive dance that interprets lyrics and emotion with gesture and face. Pure dance without meaning is nritta.

questions.q: Sam in teentaal is beat…
questions.why: Sam, the first beat of the cycle, is beat 1 in teentaal and is marked X. Beat 9 is khali.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the nine rasas?
questions.why: The nine rasas include adbhuta, karuna and hasya, but tandava is a vigorous style of dance, not a rasa.

questions.q: A tihai repeats a phrase…
questions.why: A tihai repeats a phrase three times, with the last repeat ending on sam. Twice or four times would not make a tihai.

questions.q: Second speed in an adavu means…
questions.why: Second speed in an adavu means two movements per beat, so the density doubles. It doesn't mean two dancers or half speed.

questions.q: Which hasta has the ring finger touching the thumb?
questions.why: Mayura, the peacock hasta, has the ring finger touching the thumb. The other hastas use different finger positions.

questions.q: A tihai of 5+1+5+1+5 beats started on sam of teentaal ends on…
questions.why: The tihai is 5+1+5+1+5 = 17 beats. Starting on beat 1 of a 16-beat cycle, 16 beats finish the cycle and the 17th beat lands on the next sam.

questions.q: Why should beginners learn classical dance with a qualified teacher?
options: Posture and technique need regular expert correction to be safe and correct
questions.why: Posture and technique need regular expert correction to be safe and accurate, which is central to classical training. Videos help but can't spot your errors.

courses.title: Contemporary dance and smart practice
courses.summary: Explore contemporary dance — weight, breath, floor work and improvisation — then learn how to warm up, prevent injury, practise efficiently and create your own one-minute piece.
outcomes: Learners can use breath, weight and release in movement
Learners can do safe beginner floor work
Learners can improvise using movement tasks
Learners can warm up, cool down and plan practice to avoid injury
Learners can choreograph and share a one-minute solo

lessons.title: Breath, weight and release

scenes.text: Tanvi, 19, a trained Kathak dancer in Bhopal, joins a contemporary workshop. Everything feels 'too loose'.
Teacher Marcus, from Berlin, asks the class to let the head fall forward, then the arms, then roll down the spine.
“Use gravity. Fall, then recover.” Tanvi discovers a softer, flowing quality she has never used.
Her Kathak spins later look even better, because her body is less tense.

steps.title: What contemporary dance is
steps.body: Contemporary dance is a broad, evolving style that grew from 20th-century **modern dance** and later experiments. It values **personal expression, natural movement, use of gravity and the floor**, and often blends techniques from ballet, modern, jazz, Indian and other traditions. In India, artists such as Chandralekha and Astad Deboo created influential work bridging Indian forms and contemporary ideas.

steps.title: Key ideas from modern dance
steps.body:
- **Contraction and release** (associated with Martha Graham): curving the spine from the core on an exhale, then lengthening.
- **Fall and recovery** (associated with Doris Humphrey): giving in to gravity and then rebounding.
- **Movement for its own sake** (associated with Merce Cunningham): dance need not tell a story; chance methods were sometimes used to order movements.
- **Release technique**: moving with minimal unnecessary tension, using momentum and breath.

steps.title: Worked example: the roll-down
steps.body:
1. Stand tall, feet hip-width, knees soft.
2. Exhale and let the chin drop to the chest.
3. Continue curling down one vertebra at a time, arms hanging heavy.
4. Hang at the bottom; breathe twice; let the head be heavy.
5. Inhale and roll up slowly, stacking the spine, head last.

Do 3 slow roll-downs at the start of every session.

steps.title: Playing with weight
steps.body: Try the same arm movement three ways: **heavy** (like it's filled with sand), **light** (like a feather), **sudden** (like touching something hot). Changing the quality of movement — not just the shape — is the heart of contemporary dance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing 'loose' with 'collapsed' — release still needs control and alignment.
- Holding the breath; let breath lead movement.
- Copying a teacher's flexibility. Move within your own range.

items.back: Spine curves from the core on an exhale, then lengthens — associated with Martha Graham.
Yielding to gravity and rebounding — associated with Doris Humphrey.
Moving with minimal unnecessary tension, using breath and momentum.
How a move is done — heavy, light, sudden, sustained — not just its shape.

quiz.q: Contemporary dance grew mainly out of…
quiz.why: Contemporary dance grew mainly out of 20th-century modern dance, whose pioneers rejected strict ballet rules. It is not mainly from salsa or breaking.

quiz.q: 'Fall and recovery' is associated with…
quiz.why: 'Fall and recovery' is Doris Humphrey's technique, using the pull of gravity and recovery from it. Martha Graham is known for contraction and release.

quiz.q: In a roll-down, the head comes up…
quiz.why: In a roll-down and roll-up, the head comes up last, after the spine has stacked up. This protects the neck and back.

quiz.q: 'Release' in contemporary dance means…
options: Moving without unnecessary tension, with control
quiz.why: Release means moving without unnecessary tension while staying in control. It is not collapsing or stopping.

lessons.title: Floor work basics (safely)

scenes.text: Rahul, 17, from Guwahati, does hip-hop. In contemporary class, he bangs his knees and elbows on the floor.
The teacher shows him how to go down through a spiral — using hands, side of the leg and hip, rolling not dropping.
They practise log rolls, shoulder rolls and getting up smoothly.
No more bruises. Rahul uses floor work in his next hip-hop freestyle.

steps.title: Why spirals and rolls
steps.body: Floor work is moving **into, on and out of the floor**. The secret is to **spread the impact over soft, padded surfaces** (outer thigh, hip, back muscles) and to **roll** rather than drop onto bony points (knees, elbows, spine bumps).

steps.title: Worked example: spiral down to the floor
steps.body:
1. Stand, step the right foot back behind the left.
2. Bend both knees and spiral the body to the right.
3. Lower through the **outside of the right leg** to sit on the right hip.
4. Place hands lightly as support, then roll onto your back.

Reverse it to come up: roll to the side, onto the hip, push through the feet and spiral up.

steps.title: Log roll and shoulder roll
steps.body:
- **Log roll**: lie on your back, arms overhead, body long; roll sideways like a log, keeping the body in one line.
- **Shoulder roll** (backward): from sitting, roll back over **one shoulder** (never straight over the neck), with the head turned to the other side.

steps.title: Safety rules
steps.body:
- Never put weight directly on the neck or head.
- Use a clean, smooth floor or mat.
- Kneepads are fine while learning.
- Learn new floor moves slowly with a teacher; stop with any pain.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise 5 spiral downs and up each side, then 5 log rolls each direction. Move slowly enough that you make almost no sound — quiet floor work usually means safe floor work.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a safe spiral down to the floor.
items: Step the right foot back behind the left
Bend both knees and spiral to the right
Lower through the outside of the right leg
Use hands lightly and roll onto the back

quiz.q: Floor work should land on…
options: Soft, padded surfaces like the outer thigh and hip
quiz.why: Floor work should land on soft, padded parts like the outer thigh and hip. Bony places like knees, elbows, spine and head take impact badly and can be hurt.

quiz.q: In a backward shoulder roll you roll over…
quiz.why: In a backward shoulder roll you roll diagonally over one shoulder, never straight over the neck. The padded shoulder takes the weight and protects the spine.

quiz.q: Quiet floor work usually means…
quiz.why: Quiet floor work shows control, because a loud landing means high impact. A soft, controlled landing protects joints and bones.

quiz.q: Is it okay to wear kneepads while learning?
quiz.why: Yes. Kneepads are a sensible protection while you learn floor work, because they cushion bony knees until your technique is safe.

lessons.title: Improvisation tasks and making a 1-minute piece

scenes.text: Mei, 23, a student from Singapore studying in Pune, has a choreography assignment: a 1-minute solo.
She chooses the theme 'monsoon' and improvises: drizzle (light fingers), storm (sudden, heavy), puddles (jumps), stillness after rain.
She films her improvisations and picks the best 8 phrases.
Her final piece has a clear beginning, build, climax and calm ending. The class is moved.

steps.title: Improvisation with tasks
steps.body:
Improvisation is easier with a **task** (a rule to follow). Examples:

- Move only one body part at a time, passing movement from part to part.
- Draw your name in the air with your elbow, then your knee, then your head.
- Move as if the air is honey; then as if it's ice-cold water.
- 'Mirror' a partner: one leads, the other copies, then switch without stopping.

steps.title: Building a solo from improvisation
steps.body:
1. Pick a **theme** (monsoon, a memory, a city, a word).
2. Improvise for 3 minutes per idea; **film** everything.
3. Choose 6–8 favourite moments; learn them as fixed phrases.
4. Order them: **beginning → development → climax → ending**.
5. Vary **levels** (high/middle/floor), **speed**, **direction** and **dynamics**.
6. Add music last, or try silence.

steps.title: Tools choreographers use
steps.body:
- **Repetition** with changes (bigger, smaller, faster, backwards).
- **Canon**: dancers do the same phrase starting at different times.
- **Unison**: everyone moves together.
- **Stillness**: a pause can be the strongest moment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Too many ideas — pick one theme and dig deep.
- Staying at one level and one speed.
- Ending weakly; plan the last 10 seconds carefully.

activity.prompt: Pick a theme for your 1-minute piece. Write 4 movement ideas for it (one each for beginning, development, climax and ending).
activity.hint: Example — 'Train journey': beginning = swaying while seated; development = walking against the motion; climax = fast spins like wheels; ending = slow stop and look out of a window.

quiz.q: An improvisation 'task' is…
options: A rule or prompt that guides movement
quiz.why: An improvisation task is a rule or prompt, like 'lead with your elbow', that guides your movement. Tasks spark ideas by giving you structure.

quiz.q: 'Canon' in choreography means…
options: Same phrase started at different times
quiz.why: In canon the same phrase starts at different times for different dancers, like a round in singing. In unison everyone moves together.

quiz.q: Why film your improvisations?
options: To find and keep the best moments
quiz.why: You cannot remember everything you improvise, so filming helps you find and keep the best moments to develop later.

quiz.q: A solo with variety uses changes in…
quiz.why: Variety in a solo comes from changing levels, speed, direction and dynamics. These changes keep the audience interested.

lessons.title: Warm-up, cool-down and injury-smart practice

scenes.text: Coach Neha runs a dance studio in Indore. She has a rule: nobody dances before a 10-minute warm-up.
A new student, Vikram, skips it once, tries a high kick and strains a hamstring.
Neha helps him rest, applies a cold pack wrapped in cloth, and advises him to see a physiotherapist.
Vikram returns three weeks later and never skips the warm-up again.

steps.title: A good dance warm-up (8–10 minutes)
steps.body:
- **Pulse raiser** (3 min): march, jog on the spot, step-touches.
- **Mobility** (3 min): neck, shoulder rolls, spine curls, hip circles, ankle circles.
- **Dynamic stretches** (2 min): leg swings, lunges with a twist, arm swings.
- **Rehearse** (2 min): gentle versions of today's moves.

Save long held (static) stretches for after dancing — that's when muscles are warm.

steps.title: Cool-down
steps.body: 5 minutes: slow walking, then static stretches held about 20–30 seconds each (calves, hamstrings, quads, hip flexors, chest), and slow breathing. This helps you relax and recover.

steps.title: Practise smarter
steps.body:
- **Short and frequent** beats long and rare.
- Mix **technique**, **choreography** and **free dance** each week.
- Rest days matter; muscles adapt while resting.
- Sleep, water and food are part of training.
- Track progress with video and a practice diary.

steps.title: When to stop and see a professional
steps.body: Stop dancing and get checked by a doctor or physiotherapist for: sharp or sudden pain, swelling, a joint that feels unstable, numbness or tingling, or pain that lasts more than a few days. For an emergency in India, call **112**. This is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write your personal 8-minute warm-up on a card and stick it where you practise. Use it every time for a month.

activity.prompt: Warm-up or cool-down?

items.text: Holding a hamstring stretch for 30 seconds
Calf stretch against a wall, held

quiz.q: Long held static stretches are best done…
quiz.why: Long held static stretches are best done in the cool-down, when muscles are warm. Stretching cold muscles or during jumps raises the injury risk.

quiz.q: A pulse raiser is…
options: Activity that gently raises heart rate
quiz.why: A pulse raiser is an activity that gently raises your heart rate, such as light jogging. It warms the body before harder movement.

quiz.q: Which needs a professional check?
options: Swelling and a joint that feels unstable
quiz.why: Swelling and a joint that feels unstable can mean a real injury, so they need professional assessment. Sweating, mild tiredness and happiness are normal.

quiz.q: India's all-emergency number is…
quiz.why: 112 is India's single emergency number. 100 is police, 1098 is child help and 14416 is Tele-MANAS mental health support.

quiz.q: Why do rest days matter?
options: Muscles adapt and repair during rest
quiz.why: Muscles adapt, repair and grow stronger during rest, so rest days are part of training. Skipping them can lead to overuse injuries.

questions.q: Contemporary dance often uses…
questions.why: Contemporary dance often works with gravity, breath and the floor, using weight rather than fighting it. It is not limited to partner work or straight lines.

questions.q: A warm-up should come…
questions.why: A warm-up comes before dancing to raise body temperature and prepare muscles. Doing it after or never raises injury risk.

questions.q: 'Contraction and release' is associated with…
questions.why: Contraction and release, using breath and the spine, is Martha Graham's technique. Doris Humphrey is known for fall and recovery.

questions.q: In floor work, you should avoid landing on…
questions.why: Avoid landing on bony points like the knees, and never roll over the neck. Padded areas such as the outer thigh, hip and back muscles absorb impact.

questions.q: What makes an improvisation easier?
questions.why: A clear task gives you structure and a starting idea, which makes improvising easier. Loud music or a mirror does not.

questions.q: 'Unison' means…
questions.why: Unison means dancers do the same move at the same time. Canon is the version where they start at different times.

questions.q: Which is a good structure for a 1-minute solo?
questions.why: A clear arc of beginning, development, climax and ending helps the audience follow even a one-minute solo. Random order feels confusing.

questions.q: Static stretches in a cool-down are usually held about…
questions.why: Static stretches in a cool-down are usually held about 20 to 30 seconds. Two seconds is too short and ten minutes is too long.

questions.q: You land floor work loudly. What does it suggest?
options: High impact — slow down and roll more
