questions.why: A loud landing means high impact, so slow down and roll more through padded areas. Quiet, controlled floor work is the goal.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason to stop and seek professional advice?
questions.why: Mild muscle tiredness is a normal result of dancing. Swelling, numbness or tingling and an unstable joint are warning signs for professional advice.

questions.q: Changing the same arm move from 'heavy' to 'sudden' changes its…
questions.why: Changing 'heavy' to 'sudden' changes the quality or dynamics of the movement, meaning how it is done. The direction, count and shape stay the same.

questions.q: Why roll over one shoulder instead of straight over the head?
options: To keep weight off the neck
questions.why: Rolling over one shoulder keeps your weight off the neck. Rolling straight over the head puts dangerous pressure on the neck.

arts-music-advanced.title: Music for working musicians
arts-music-advanced.description: Harmony and voice leading, modes, jazz chords and reharmonisation, rhythm and polyrhythm, ear training, songwriting and arranging, production and mixing, deeper raga theory, and the business of royalties and a music career.

courses.title: Harmony, voice leading and modes
courses.summary: Go beyond chord shapes: understand chord function, move voices smoothly, use secondary dominants and borrowed chords, and write in the modes.
outcomes: Learners can label diatonic chords with Roman numerals and functions
Learners can apply core four-part voice-leading rules
Learners can write and resolve secondary dominants
Learners can use modal interchange (borrowed chords) deliberately
Learners can identify and compose with the seven modes

lessons.title: Diatonic harmony and chord function

scenes.text: Vikram, 27, a session guitarist in Mumbai, can play any chord chart — but when a producer asks “why does this progression feel stuck?”, he has no answer.
His friend Ines, a Portuguese film composer, writes the chords as Roman numerals: I – iii – I – iii.
“Both chords are tonic-function. Nothing is moving. Try I – IV – V – I.”
The producer smiles at the new version. Vikram starts thinking in functions, not shapes.

steps.title: Roman numerals in a major key
steps.body:
Build triads on each scale degree of a major key using only the key's notes:

**I – ii – iii – IV – V – vi – vii°**

Upper case = major, lower case = minor, ° = diminished. In C major: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°. With sevenths: **Imaj7, ii7, iii7, IVmaj7, V7, vi7, viiø7** (Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7, Bm7♭5).

steps.title: Three functions
steps.body:
- **Tonic (T)** – home, rest: **I**, and substitutes **vi** and **iii**.
- **Predominant / subdominant (PD)** – moving away, preparing: **IV**, **ii**.
- **Dominant (D)** – tension that wants home: **V**, **vii°**.

The classic cycle is **T → PD → D → T** (e.g. I – IV – V – I, or I – ii – V – I). The dominant's pull comes from the **leading tone** (B in C) rising to the tonic and the tritone (B–F in G7) resolving inward to C–E.

steps.title: Worked example: analysing a progression
steps.body:
Key of G major: **G – Em – C – D – G**

- G = I (T)
- Em = vi (T substitute)
- C = IV (PD)
- D = V (D)
- G = I (T)

Function flow: T → T → PD → D → T. A smooth, satisfying arc. Replace C with Am (ii) — still PD, a slightly softer colour.

steps.title: Root movement tendencies
steps.body: Strong progressions often move roots **down by fifths** (or up by fourths): vi → ii → V → I (Am → Dm → G → C in C). Roots moving down by thirds (I → vi → IV) share two common tones and sound smooth. Roots moving by step (IV → V) need careful voice leading (next lesson).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'minor chord = sad chord': vi in a major key is still part of a major-key story.
- Ending phrases on V and wondering why it feels unfinished — that's a **half cadence** (useful, but intentional).
- V → IV in classical style feels weak (a 'retrogression'); in rock and blues it is common and fine. Know the style.

activity.prompt: Sort the chords in C major by function.

quiz.q: In C major, which chord is ii?
quiz.why: In C major, chord ii is built on D using only C-major notes: D, F, A. That makes it D minor, not D major.

quiz.q: Which chords share tonic function in a major key?
quiz.why: I, vi and iii share two notes with the tonic chord, so they have tonic function. IV and ii are predominant, and V and vii° are dominant.

quiz.q: The seventh chord on V in a major key is…
quiz.why: The seventh chord on V is a major triad plus a minor seventh, which is a dominant 7. In C major it is G B D F.

quiz.q: I – ii – V – I follows which function cycle?
quiz.why: ii is predominant (PD) and V is dominant (D), so I–ii–V–I is tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic. Order matters, and the dominant leads back to tonic.

quiz.q: A phrase ending on V is called a…
quiz.why: A phrase ending on V is a half cadence, which sounds unfinished. An authentic cadence is V–I, plagal is IV–I and deceptive is V–vi.

lessons.title: Four-part voice leading that sounds professional

scenes.text: Anjali, 34, arranges carols for a college choir in Bengaluru. Her chords are right, but the parts jump around and the singers struggle.
Her old teacher, Mr. Pinto, circles three things in red: parallel fifths, a leading tone that falls, and a tenor leaping a seventh.
She rewrites using common tones and stepwise motion.
The choir sight-reads it beautifully. “It sings itself now,” says the alto section leader.

steps.title: Four voices and their spacing
steps.body:
Classic four-part (SATB) writing — soprano, alto, tenor, bass. Typical comfortable ranges:

- Soprano ≈ C4–G5 · Alto ≈ G3–C5 · Tenor ≈ C3–G4 · Bass ≈ E2–C4

**Spacing rule**: keep adjacent upper voices (S–A and A–T) within an **octave**; tenor–bass may be wider. Don't let voices cross.

steps.title: The core rules
steps.body:
1. **Keep common tones** in the same voice when chords share notes.
2. Move other voices by the **smallest step** possible.
3. Avoid **parallel perfect fifths and octaves** between any two voices (they weaken independence).
4. The **leading tone** resolves **up** to the tonic (especially in the soprano or bass).
5. A chordal **seventh** resolves **down by step**.
6. In root-position triads, usually **double the root**; never double the leading tone.
7. Prefer **contrary motion** between bass and soprano.

steps.title: Worked example: V7 → I in C
steps.body:
G7 voiced (bass to soprano): **G – F – B – D**

Resolve to C:

- Bass G → C (root to root)
- Tenor F (the 7th) → **E** (down by step)
- Alto B (leading tone) → **C** (up by step)
- Soprano D → **C** (down by step)

Result: C – E – C – C. An incomplete tonic chord (no G) with a tripled root is the normal result when V7 resolves strictly in root position — perfectly correct.

steps.title: Voice leading for keyboard and guitar players
steps.body:
The same ideas make comping smoother:

- Keep the hand in one area; move to the **nearest inversion** of the next chord.
- C → Am → F → G in close voicings: C-E-G → C-E-A → C-F-A → B-D-G. Only one or two notes move each time.
- Listen to the **top note** — it forms an inner melody.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Parallel fifths hiding in inner voices (check every pair: S–A, S–T, S–B, A–T, A–B, T–B).
- Big leaps in inner voices — singers hate them.
- Applying classical rules to every style. Rock power chords are parallel fifths by design. Rules are tools for a style, not laws of nature.

statements.s: In common-practice style, the leading tone normally resolves up to the tonic.
statements.why: Its half-step pull upward is the heart of the dominant.

statements.s: A chordal seventh usually resolves up by step.
statements.why: It resolves down by step (F → E in G7 → C).

statements.s: Parallel octaves between bass and soprano are encouraged.
statements.why: They reduce independence of voices in classical style.

statements.s: Adjacent upper voices should usually stay within an octave of each other.
statements.why: Wider gaps between S–A or A–T make the texture hollow.

statements.s: Doubling the leading tone in a V chord is a good idea.
statements.why: Both copies would need to resolve up, causing parallel octaves.

quiz.q: What should you do first when connecting two chords that share notes?
options: Keep the common tones in the same voices
quiz.why: Keep common tones in the same voice when chords share notes. This makes the connection smooth, and the other voices move by the smallest steps.

quiz.q: In G7 → C, the note F typically moves to…
quiz.why: The chordal seventh F in G7 normally resolves down by step to E in C. Staying on F or leaping would leave the dissonance unresolved.

quiz.q: Which interval motion is avoided in strict four-part writing?
quiz.why: Parallel perfect fifths (and octaves) are avoided in strict four-part writing because they reduce the independence of the voices.

quiz.q: Which pair can be more than an octave apart?
quiz.why: Tenor and bass may be more than an octave apart, but adjacent upper voices should stay within an octave.

quiz.q: In root-position triads, which note is usually doubled?
quiz.why: In root-position triads the root is normally doubled, as it is the most stable choice. The leading tone should not be doubled.

lessons.title: Secondary dominants and borrowed chords

scenes.text: Rehana, 30, scores short films in Hyderabad. Her director says a scene of a grandmother's memory “needs a lump in the throat”.
She takes her plain C – F – G – C and swaps F for F minor on the last phrase.
The borrowed minor iv adds a bittersweet ache. Then she adds an E7 before Am for a surprising lift.
The director replays it three times. “That's the feeling.”

steps.title: Secondary dominants
steps.body:
Any major or minor diatonic chord can be 'tonicised' by placing **its own dominant** before it. Written **V/x** ('five of x').

In C major:

- **V/V** = D7 → G
- **V/vi** = E7 → Am
- **V/ii** = A7 → Dm
- **V/IV** = C7 → F
- **V/iii** = B7 → Em

(vii° can't be tonicised — it's diminished.) Each secondary dominant brings a note from outside the key (F♯ in D7, G♯ in E7) — that's the 'lift'.

steps.title: Worked example: 'Twinkle'-style melody
steps.body:
Original: C – F – C – G – C.

With secondary dominants: **C – C7 – F – D7 – G7 – C**

- C7 is V/IV, pulling to F.
- D7 is V/V, pulling to G7.

Resolve the new leading tones: B♭ in C7 falls to A in F; F♯ in D7 rises to G.

steps.title: Modal interchange (borrowed chords)
steps.body:
Borrow chords from the **parallel minor** (C minor when in C major):

- **iv** (Fm) – bittersweet, nostalgic
- **♭VI** (A♭) – warm, cinematic
- **♭VII** (B♭) – rock/anthemic
- **♭III** (E♭) – bold
- **iiø7** (Dm7♭5) – dark predominant

Classic move: **IV → iv → I** (F → Fm → C): the A falls to A♭ then to G — a beautiful chromatic line.

steps.title: Where you hear these
steps.body: Film and pop writers use iv and ♭VI for emotional peaks; rock uses ♭VII → I ('Mixolydian cadence'); gospel and jazz chain secondary dominants (e.g. E7 → A7 → D7 → G7 → C, each a V of the next). Many Hindi film songs colour a major-key melody with a borrowed minor chord at emotional lines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to resolve: a secondary dominant that doesn't go to its target sounds like a mistake (unless you're deliberately using a deceptive resolution).
- Clashing with the melody: if the tune sings A over a borrowed Fm (which has A♭), it will clash — adjust one or the other.
- Overuse — one surprise per phrase is plenty.

activity.prompt: In C major, match each secondary dominant to its target chord.

quiz.q: V/V in G major is…
quiz.why: V/V is the dominant of the dominant. In G major, V is D, so V/V is A7, the dominant seventh of D.

quiz.q: Which note makes E7 sound 'outside' C major?
quiz.why: E7 contains G♯, which is not in C major. G♯ is the leading tone of A, so it sounds 'outside' the key.

quiz.q: Fm in the key of C major is…
options: A borrowed iv from C minor
quiz.why: Fm in C major is the iv chord borrowed from C minor, the parallel minor. It is not diatonic to C major.

quiz.q: The line A → A♭ → G appears in…
quiz.why: The inner line A → A♭ → G fits F (contains A), then Fm (contains A♭), then C (contains G): IV → iv → I.

quiz.q: Why can't vii° be tonicised?
options: A diminished chord can't act as a stable temporary tonic
quiz.why: Only major or minor chords can be a temporary tonic. A diminished chord is too unstable to act as a tonic, so vii° isn't tonicised.

lessons.title: The seven modes and modal writing

scenes.text: Sam, 22, a guitarist from Shillong, plays the same pentatonic licks over every song. His band says his solos 'sound the same'.
A jazz bassist, Ruth, plays a D minor vamp and asks him to emphasise B natural instead of B♭.
Suddenly the solo glows with a Dorian colour.
Sam starts learning each mode's 'character note' — and his solos start telling stories.

steps.title: Modes as rotations of the major scale
steps.body:
Play the C major scale starting on each note:

- **Ionian** C–C (major)
- **Dorian** D–D
- **Phrygian** E–E
- **Lydian** F–F
- **Mixolydian** G–G
- **Aeolian** A–A (natural minor)
- **Locrian** B–B

Same notes, different home — so each has a different sound.

steps.title: Parallel view and character notes
steps.body:
Compare each mode to major or minor **on the same root**:

- **Lydian** = major with **♯4** (dreamy, floating)
- **Mixolydian** = major with **♭7** (bluesy, rock)
- **Dorian** = minor with **♮6** (soulful, funky)
- **Phrygian** = minor with **♭2** (dark, Spanish/flamenco flavour)
- **Aeolian** = natural minor (♭3 ♭6 ♭7)
- **Locrian** = minor with **♭2 and ♭5** (unstable, rare as a home)

The **character note** is what you emphasise to make the mode audible.

steps.title: Worked example: build E♭ Lydian
steps.body:
E♭ major = E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C D. Raise the 4th: A♭ → **A**.

E♭ Lydian = **E♭ F G A B♭ C D**. (It's the B♭ major scale starting on E♭.)

steps.title: Making a mode sound like itself
steps.body:
- Use a **drone or vamp** on the root (e.g. D–Dm7–Em7 for Dorian, keeping D in the bass).
- Put the character note on **strong beats** or long notes.
- Avoid V7 → I cadences, which pull everything back to plain major/minor.
- Characteristic chord pairs: Dorian i–IV (Dm–G), Mixolydian I–♭VII (G–F), Lydian I–II (F–G), Phrygian i–♭II (Em–F).

steps.title: Modes meet thaats
steps.body: Indian musicians already know these colours: **Kafi ≈ Dorian**, **Khamaj ≈ Mixolydian**, **Kalyan ≈ Lydian**, **Bhairavi (thaat) ≈ Phrygian**, **Asavari ≈ Aeolian**, **Bilawal ≈ Ionian**. In jazz, Miles Davis's *So What* is a famous Dorian vamp.

activity.prompt: Match each mode to its character note (compared with major or minor on the same root).

quiz.q: D Dorian uses the notes of…
quiz.why: D Dorian is the second mode of C major, so it uses the same notes as C major, starting on D. It has a natural 6th, unlike natural minor.

quiz.q: Which mode has a raised 4th?
quiz.why: Lydian has a raised 4th (♯4) compared with the major scale. Dorian has ♭3 and ♭7, Mixolydian ♭7 and Phrygian ♭2.

quiz.q: G Mixolydian contains…
quiz.why: G Mixolydian is G A B C D E F, with a natural F (♭7 relative to G major). It has no F♯ or B♭.

quiz.q: Kafi thaat corresponds most closely to…
quiz.why: Kafi thaat has komal Ga and komal Ni with the other notes shuddha, which matches Dorian. Bilawal would be Ionian.

quiz.q: To keep a modal sound, it's best to avoid…
quiz.why: Strong V7–I cadences pull the ear back to ordinary major or minor, weakening the modal sound. Drones, vamps and the character note help keep it modal.

questions.q: In C major, the vi chord is…
questions.why: In C major, vi is built on A using key notes: A, C, E, an A minor chord. A major would need C♯.

questions.q: Which function does V belong to?
questions.why: V is the dominant chord, which creates tension that wants to resolve to the tonic. Predominant chords include ii and IV.

questions.q: A chordal seventh normally resolves…
questions.why: A chordal seventh normally resolves down by step. For example, F in G7 falls to E.

questions.q: Which mode is the natural minor scale?
questions.why: Aeolian, the sixth mode of the major scale, is the natural minor scale. Dorian, Phrygian and Locrian have different altered notes.

questions.q: V/V in C major is…
questions.why: V/V is the dominant of G, the dominant in C major. That is D7, which resolves to G.

questions.q: Which is a borrowed chord in C major?
questions.why: A♭ is ♭VI borrowed from C minor, since A♭ is not in C major. G, Dm and Em are all diatonic.

questions.q: Adjacent upper voices should normally be within…
questions.why: Adjacent upper voices (soprano–alto, alto–tenor) should normally be within an octave. Only tenor–bass may be wider.

questions.q: The character note of Phrygian is…
questions.why: The character note of Phrygian is its lowered 2nd (♭2), which sets it apart from the natural minor scale.

questions.q: In strict style, G7 → C resolution in root position often produces…
options: A complete C chord with doubled third
An incomplete C chord with tripled root
questions.why: In strict style, G7 to C in root position leads to a C chord with root tripled and no fifth, C–E–C–C. It is incomplete but avoids parallel fifths.

questions.q: E7 → Am in C major is analysed as…
questions.why: E7 is the dominant seventh of A, and Am is vi in C major. So E7 → Am is V/vi → vi, a secondary dominant.

questions.q: F → Fm → C creates which inner line?
questions.why: F → Fm → C contains the inner line A → A♭ → G, a chromatic descent from the chord third of F to the fourth of... G in C.

questions.q: E♭ Lydian contains which note not in E♭ major?
questions.why: E♭ Lydian has a raised 4th, which is A natural instead of A♭. That is the note not found in E♭ major.

questions.q: Why are parallel fifths fine in a rock power-chord riff but avoided in a chorale?
options: Rules belong to styles; chorale style values independent voices
questions.why: Voice-leading rules belong to styles. A rock power-chord riff values parallel fifths for their thickness, but chorale style prizes independent voices.

courses.title: Jazz chords, extensions and reharmonisation
courses.summary: Master seventh chords and extensions, the ii–V–I with guide tones, professional voicings, and the reharmonisation tools working players use every night.
outcomes: Learners can spell all common seventh chords and add correct extensions
Learners can play ii–V–I in major and minor with guide-tone voice leading
Learners can use shell, rootless and drop-2 voicings
Learners can apply tritone, backdoor, related-ii and diminished substitutions
Learners can reharmonise a simple melody while respecting it

lessons.title: Seventh chords and extensions

scenes.text: Kenji, 25, a Japanese pianist working in a Goa hotel band, gets a chart: Cmaj9, F13, Dm11, G7♭9.
He plays every extension stacked on top and it sounds muddy, especially an F natural on top of Cmaj7.
The bandleader, Lourdes, explains 'avoid notes' and which extensions each chord loves.
That night his chords sound lush, not muddy.

steps.title: The five core seventh chords
steps.body:
Using C as the root:

- **Cmaj7** = C E G B (1 3 5 7)
- **C7** (dominant) = C E G B♭ (1 3 5 ♭7)
- **Cm7** = C E♭ G B♭ (1 ♭3 5 ♭7)
- **Cm7♭5** (half-diminished, Cø7) = C E♭ G♭ B♭
- **Cdim7** (C°7) = C E♭ G♭ B𝄫 (sounds as A)

Also common: **Cm(maj7)** = C E♭ G B, and **C7sus4** = C F G B♭.

steps.title: Extensions: 9, 11, 13
steps.body:
Keep stacking thirds above the 7th: **9** (= 2nd), **11** (= 4th), **13** (= 6th).

- On **maj7**: 9 and 13 sound great; natural 11 clashes with the 3rd (a ♭9 interval above it) — use **♯11** instead (Lydian sound).
- On **m7**: 9 and 11 are lovely; 13 depends on context (Dorian ♮13 is common on ii chords).
- On **dominant 7**: 9 and 13 natural; natural 11 is usually avoided (unless it's a sus chord). **Altered** tensions — ♭9, ♯9, ♯11, ♭13 — add bite, especially when resolving to a minor chord.

steps.title: Worked example: spelling G13 and G7♭9
steps.body:
- **G13** = G B D F + A (9) + E (13). Typical voicing drops the 5th and often the root: **F – B – E** (7 3 13), with A added if desired.
- **G7♭9** = G B D F + A♭. Rootless: **B – D – F – A♭** — that's a diminished-seventh shape!

steps.title: What to leave out
steps.body: The **3rd and 7th** define a chord's quality — keep them. The **5th** is usually the first note dropped (unless it's altered). The **root** can be left to the bass player. This frees fingers for colour tones.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Natural 11 over a major or dominant chord (clashes with the 3rd).
- Stacking every extension in a low register — keep extensions above about middle C to avoid mud.
- Confusing m7♭5 (half-diminished, ♭7) with dim7 (double-flat 7).

cards.front: Which extension clashes on maj7 and dominant 7?
Which two notes define a chord's quality?

quiz.q: Dm7 is spelled…
quiz.why: Dm7 is built 1, ♭3, ♭5... exactly: root D, minor third F, fifth A, minor seventh C, giving D F A C.

quiz.q: Which tension is usually avoided on Cmaj7?
quiz.why: A natural 11 (F) against the major third (E) of Cmaj7 creates a harsh ♭9 clash, so it is usually avoided. ♯11 sounds fine.

quiz.q: Which note is usually dropped first in a voicing?
quiz.why: The 5th adds little colour, so players drop it first and keep the 3rd and 7th, which define the chord's quality.

quiz.q: Bm7♭5 is spelled…
quiz.why: Bm7♭5 is half-diminished: 1, ♭3, ♭5, ♭7, so B D F A. The F is natural (a diminished fifth above B).

quiz.q: Rootless G7♭9 (B D F A♭) has the shape of a…
quiz.why: B D F A♭ is a stack of minor thirds, which is the shape of a diminished seventh chord. It is the rootless G7♭9.

lessons.title: ii–V–I and guide-tone lines

scenes.text: Meenakshi, 29, a Carnatic-trained violinist in Chennai, joins a jazz jam. The tunes fly by with endless chord changes.
A saxophonist tells her: “Most of these tunes are ii–V–Is in different keys. Learn that and you've learned half of jazz.”
She practises connecting just the 3rds and 7ths of each chord — the guide tones.
Next jam, her lines outline the changes beautifully, even with only two notes per chord.

steps.title: The ii–V–I
steps.body:
In major: **iim7 – V7 – Imaj7**. In C: **Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7**.
In minor: **iiø7 – V7(♭9) – i** (often im6 or im(maj7)). In C minor: **Dm7♭5 – G7♭9 – Cm6**.

Roots fall by fifths (D → G → C) — the strongest root motion in tonal harmony.

steps.title: Guide tones: 3rds and 7ths
steps.body:
- **Dm7**: 3rd = F, 7th = C
- **G7**: 3rd = B, 7th = F
- **Cmaj7**: 3rd = E, 7th = B

Connect them by step or common tone:

- Line 1: **C → B → B** (7th of Dm7 → 3rd of G7 → 7th of Cmaj7)
- Line 2: **F → F → E** (3rd of Dm7 → 7th of G7 → 3rd of Cmaj7)

The 7th of each chord falls a half step to the 3rd of the next — a smooth, inevitable sound.

steps.title: Shell, rootless and drop-2 voicings
steps.body:
- **Shell**: root + 3 + 7 (or root + 7 + 3). Dm7 = D–F–C, G7 = G–F–B, Cmaj7 = C–E–B. Great left-hand or guitar voicings.
- **Rootless (piano)**: 3-5-7-9 or 7-9-3-5 (or with 13 on dominants). Dm9 = F A C E → G13 = F A B E → Cmaj9 = E G B D. Only one or two notes move each time.
- **Drop 2**: take a close four-note voicing and drop the second-highest note an octave. Cmaj7 close C–E–G–B → drop 2 = G–C–E–B. Popular on guitar.

steps.title: Try this: ii–V–I around the keys
steps.body: Play Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 with guide tones only, then move the whole progression down a whole step (Cm7–F7–B♭maj7), and again (B♭m7–E♭7–A♭maj7)… covering six keys. Then start on E♭m7 to cover the other six.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Practising ii–V–I only in C and F.
- Jumping between root-position chords — use guide-tone movement instead.
- Ignoring the minor ii–V; it appears constantly in standards.

activity.prompt: Guide tones in C: fill the missing notes (3rd of G7, then 3rd of Cmaj7).

quiz.q: ii–V–I in B♭ major is…
quiz.why: In B♭ major, ii is Cm7 and V is F7, resolving to B♭maj7. So the ii–V–I is Cm7 – F7 – B♭maj7.

quiz.q: Guide tones are the chord's…
quiz.why: Guide tones are the 3rd and 7th of a chord, because they define its quality and voice-lead smoothly to the next chord.

quiz.q: In Dm7 → G7, the note C moves to…
quiz.why: The 7th of Dm7 (C) falls by step to B, the 3rd of G7. This guide-tone motion is a hallmark of ii–V.

quiz.q: Minor ii–V–I in A minor is…
quiz.why: A minor ii–V–I uses the half-diminished ii, an altered dominant and a minor tonic: Bm7♭5 – E7♭9 – Am6.

quiz.q: A drop-2 voicing is made by…
options: Dropping the top note an octave
Dropping the second-highest note an octave
quiz.why: A drop-2 voicing takes a close-position chord and drops the second-highest note down an octave. It spreads the chord for guitar and piano.

lessons.title: Substitutions: tritone, backdoor, related ii and diminished

scenes.text: Rahul's wedding band in Delhi plays the same evergreen songs every season. The keyboardist, Farah, wants to keep them fresh without confusing the singer.
She swaps one G7 for a D♭7 before C — the bass slides down by half step.
The melody still fits, and the audience gets a subtle new colour.
The singer says, “Same song, but somehow classier.”

steps.title: Tritone substitution
steps.body:
Replace a dominant 7 with the dominant 7 a **tritone** away: **G7 → D♭7**.

Why it works: G7's guide tones are **B and F**; D♭7's are **F and C♭ (= B)** — the same tritone! Both resolve to C. The bass now moves **D♭ → C** by half step.

ii–V–I becomes **Dm7 – D♭7 – Cmaj7** (chromatic bass).

steps.title: Backdoor dominant and related ii
steps.body:
- **Backdoor**: approach I from **♭VII7** (B♭7 → C), often with its ii: **Fm7 – B♭7 – Cmaj7**. Borrowed from the parallel minor; warm and soulful.
- **Related ii**: put the ii chord before any dominant, including secondary dominants: D7 → G becomes **Am7 – D7 → G**. This turns a single chord into a mini ii–V.

steps.title: Passing diminished chords
steps.body:
A **dim7** a half step below the next chord creates a chromatic bass line:

- **Cmaj7 – C♯°7 – Dm7** (bass C → C♯ → D)
- **Fmaj7 – F♯°7 – C/G** (bass F → F♯ → G)

The °7 acts like a rootless V7♭9 of the target (C♯°7 ≈ A7♭9 → Dm7).

steps.title: Worked example: reharmonising a turnaround
steps.body:
Plain: | Cmaj7 | Am7 | Dm7 | G7 |

1. Make Am7 a dominant (V/ii): | Cmaj7 | **A7** | Dm7 | G7 |
2. Tritone-sub the G7: | Cmaj7 | A7 | Dm7 | **D♭7** |
3. Tritone-sub the A7: | Cmaj7 | **E♭7** | Dm7 | D♭7 |

Result bass line: C – E♭ – D – D♭ → C. Smooth, chromatic, very 'jazz'.

steps.title: Check the melody
steps.body: A substitution must **fit the melody note** at that moment. If the melody holds G over the G7 bar, D♭7 makes it a ♯11 (fine, colourful). If the melody holds D (the 5th of G7), over D♭7 it becomes a major 7th against the root — a clash. Always test against the tune.

a.text: You're reharmonising bar 7–8 of a ballad: | Dm7 | G7 | Cmaj7 |. The melody holds G throughout the G7 bar.

choices.label: Use the tritone sub D♭7
choices.feedback: G over D♭7 is a ♯11 — a lovely colour. Good choice.

choices.label: Use B♭7 (backdoor) instead
choices.feedback: Possible: G over B♭7 is the 13th. Also works!

choices.label: Use E♭maj7 just because it sounds fancy
choices.feedback: G is the 3rd of E♭maj7 — it fits the melody, but the chord doesn't lead to C as a dominant. It may feel random.

b.text: The singer loves it. Now the band leader asks for a chromatic bass line into bar 5 (Fmaj7 → ? → C/G).

choices.label: Insert F♯°7
choices.feedback: F → F♯ → G in the bass, F♯°7 acting like D7♭9 (V/V). Perfect.

choices.label: Insert F♯maj7
choices.feedback: F♯maj7 clashes with the key and doesn't resolve well.

c.text: The backdoor sounds warm. Add its related ii?

choices.label: Yes: Fm7 – B♭7 – Cmaj7
choices.feedback: Classic backdoor ii–V.

d.text: The band sounds lost at the resolution.

choices.label: Go back to a dominant-function substitute
choices.feedback: Function first, colour second.

end1.text: Your reharm respects the melody and keeps the harmonic function — that's professional reharmonisation.

end2.text: Try again with a chord that leads by half step or shares the target's dominant tritone.

quiz.q: The tritone sub of A7 is…
quiz.why: A tritone sub replaces a dominant with the dominant a tritone away. A tritone from A is E♭, so the sub is E♭7.

quiz.q: Why does D♭7 substitute for G7?
options: They share the same tritone (B/C♭ and F)
quiz.why: D♭7 and G7 share the same tritone (B and F, enharmonically C♭ and F), the 3rd and 7th. This is why one can replace the other.

quiz.q: The backdoor dominant in C is…
quiz.why: The backdoor dominant is ♭VII7, which in C is B♭7. It often resolves to C.

quiz.q: C♯°7 between Cmaj7 and Dm7 functions like…
quiz.why: C♯°7 is an A7♭9 without its root (C♯ E G B♭). So between Cmaj7 and Dm7 it works as V/ii.

quiz.q: Before using a substitution you must check…
options: That it fits the melody note
quiz.why: Always check that a substitution fits the melody note, since a clash with the tune ruins it. Melody comes first.

lessons.title: Reharmonising a melody, step by step

scenes.text: Deepa, 36, a jazz pianist in Pune, wants to play a gentle jazz version of a lullaby her mother sang.
She writes the melody, marks the important notes on strong beats, and lists possible chords for each.
She keeps the melody untouched and changes only what's underneath.
At her mother's 60th birthday, the family recognises the tune instantly — and hears it as never before.

steps.title: A 5-step reharm method
steps.body:
1. **Write the melody** and its original chords.
2. **Mark target notes** — long notes and notes on strong beats.
3. For each target note, **list chords** where it is a chord tone or a good tension (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 13, ♯11).
4. **Choose by bass line and function** — aim for smooth or purposeful bass movement and a clear cadence at phrase ends.
5. **Play and listen**; simplify anything that fights the melody.

steps.title: Worked example: melody note E in C major
steps.body:
E can be: the **3rd** of Cmaj7, the **root** of Em7, the **5th** of Am7, the **7th** of Fmaj7, the **9th** of Dm9, the **13th** of G13, the **♯11** of B♭maj7♯11, the **♭9** of E♭7 (tense!).

So a long E at a phrase start could sit on Cmaj7 (plain), Am9 (soft), Fmaj7 (dreamy) or B♭maj7♯11 (surprising).

steps.title: Taste rules
steps.body:
- Keep **cadences clear** at phrase ends so the listener knows where home is.
- Change **harmonic rhythm** deliberately (one chord per bar vs two) — a reharm can speed up before a cadence.
- Use **pedal points** (same bass note under changing chords) for calm.
- Less is more: one or two surprises per 8 bars.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take 'Twinkle Twinkle' or a simple bhajan. Reharmonise the first 8 bars twice: once 'warm' (diatonic 7ths, ii–Vs), once 'adventurous' (tritone subs, borrowed chords). Record both and ask a friend which they prefer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the melody to fit your chords — the melody is sacred.
- Constant chromaticism that loses the key.
- Ignoring the singer's comfort: in live work, tell the singer before trying new changes.

activity.prompt: The melody note is E. Match each chord to what E becomes in it.

quiz.q: In reharmonisation, what should normally stay unchanged?
quiz.why: In reharmonisation you keep the melody and change the chords beneath it. Changing the melody would make it a different tune.

quiz.q: Melody note A over a G7 chord is the…
quiz.why: Over G7, the note A is a 9th (G to A is a ninth when taken above the octave). It's a colourful but consonant extension.

quiz.q: A pedal point is…
options: A sustained bass note under changing chords
quiz.why: A pedal point is a sustained bass note held under changing chords. It creates tension and then release.

quiz.q: Target notes for reharmonisation are mainly…
options: Long notes and notes on strong beats
quiz.why: Reharmonise the important notes: long ones and those on strong beats. Short passing notes and grace notes matter less to the harmony.

questions.q: C7 is spelled…
questions.why: C7 is a dominant seventh: root C, major third E, fifth G, minor seventh B♭, so C E G B♭.

questions.q: ii–V–I in C is…
questions.why: In C, ii is Dm7, V is G7 and I is Cmaj7. The ii–V–I is the basic jazz cadence.

questions.q: Guide tones are…
questions.why: Guide tones are the 3rd and 7th. They define the chord's quality and move smoothly between chords.

questions.q: Which extension is normally avoided on a dominant 7 (non-sus)?
questions.why: A natural 11 clashes with the major 3rd on a dominant chord, creating a ♭9 interval, so it is normally avoided. ♭9, 9 and 13 are usable.

questions.q: Tritone sub of G7?
questions.why: The tritone sub of G7 is D♭7, since D♭ is a tritone from G. They share the same 3rd and 7th.

questions.q: Cm7♭5 is spelled…
questions.why: Cm7♭5 is half-diminished: C, E♭, G♭, B♭. It has a minor third, diminished fifth and minor seventh.

questions.q: In Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7, F becomes…
options: The 7th of G7, then falls to E
questions.why: F is the 7th of Dm7... actually it is the 3rd of Dm7 and then becomes the 7th of G7, falling to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7. This forms the guide-tone line F–F–E.

questions.q: Rootless G13 in an A/B voicing set is often…
questions.why: A rootless G13 (7, 9, 3, 13) is F A B E: 7th = F, 9th = A, 3rd = B, 13th = E. The other options don't match those degrees.

questions.q: Backdoor ii–V in C is…
questions.why: The backdoor ii–V in C uses iv7 and ♭VII7, which are Fm7 and B♭7. B♭7 then resolves to C.

questions.q: F♯°7 between Fmaj7 and C/G functions like…
questions.why: F♯°7 (F♯ A C E♭) is a rootless D7♭9, the dominant of G. So it functions as V/V between Fmaj7 and C/G.

questions.q: Drop-2 of close Cmaj7 (C E G B) is…
questions.why: Drop-2 takes the second-highest note of the close voicing (G in C E G B) and drops it an octave, giving G C E B from bottom to top.

questions.q: Melody holds D over G7; you try D♭7. What happens?
options: D becomes a major 7th against D♭ — a clash
questions.why: Over D♭7, the melody D is a major seventh against D♭ (C♭... D vs D♭ is a semitone-type clash), which sounds like a clash. Always test substitutions against the melody.

questions.q: Why is ♭9 often used on V7 resolving to a minor chord?
options: ♭9 is in the minor key (e.g. A♭ in C minor)
questions.why: The ♭9 on V7 resolving to a minor chord comes from the minor key (for example, A♭ in C minor) and the harmonic minor scale. It adds fitting colour.

courses.title: Rhythm, polyrhythm and ear training
courses.summary: Tighten your time feel, play polyrhythms and odd meters (including Indian talas), and train your ear to recognise intervals and chords and transcribe what you hear.
outcomes: Learners can subdivide, syncopate and swing accurately
Learners can play 3:2 and 4:3 polyrhythms using a grid
Learners can count odd meters and Hindustani/Carnatic talas
Learners can identify intervals and chord qualities by ear
Learners can follow a transcription method

lessons.title: Subdivision, syncopation and groove

scenes.text: Aditya, 24, plays bass in a Bengaluru indie band. Recordings reveal he rushes in every chorus.
Their producer, Grace, sets a metronome to click only on beats 2 and 4, then only on beat 4.
Aditya learns to feel subdivisions internally rather than chase the click.
The next session, the band locks in so tightly that the producer barely needs to edit.

steps.title: Subdivision is your internal ruler
steps.body:
Divide each beat into smaller equal parts:

- **2 per beat** (eighths): 1 & 2 &
- **3 per beat** (triplets): 1-trip-let 2-trip-let
- **4 per beat** (sixteenths): 1 e & a

The more precisely you feel the small parts, the steadier your big beats. Indian musicians say the same with **dugun/tigun/chaugun** (2×, 3×, 4×).

steps.title: Syncopation
steps.body: **Syncopation** = accents on weak beats or off-beats (the '&' or 'e/a'). Example in 4/4: accent on the '&' of 2 and the '&' of 4. Syncopation feels exciting only if the underlying pulse is rock-solid.

steps.title: Swing feel
steps.body: In swing, pairs of eighth notes are played **long–short**, roughly like the first and third notes of a triplet. The exact ratio changes with tempo and style — faster tempos tend to straighter eighths. Learn swing by **listening** to recordings and imitating, not by maths alone.

steps.title: Worked example: delay maths for a groove
steps.body: At **120 BPM**, one beat = 60 000 ÷ 120 = **500 ms**. An eighth note = 250 ms, a sixteenth = 125 ms, a triplet eighth ≈ 167 ms. Producers use this to set delays that sit in the groove.

steps.title: Try this: the shrinking click
steps.body:
1. Metronome at 80 BPM on every beat — play a groove for 2 minutes.
2. Set the click to 40 BPM and treat it as beats **2 and 4** only.
3. Then 20 BPM: one click per bar on beat 4.

If you're still with the click after 8 bars, your internal time is improving. Test yourself with the rhythm game too.

activity.prompt: At 90 BPM, how long is one beat (quarter note) in milliseconds? (60 000 ÷ BPM)

quiz.q: Sixteenth notes are counted…
quiz.why: Sixteenth notes are counted 1 e & a, which divides each beat into four parts. Eighths are counted 1 &.

quiz.q: Syncopation means…
options: Accents on weak beats or off-beats
quiz.why: Syncopation puts accents on weak beats or off-beats, displacing the expected strong-beat stress. It isn't about tempo or loudness.

quiz.q: In swing, eighth-note pairs are usually…
quiz.why: Swing eighths are played long–short, roughly like the first and third notes of a triplet. They are not equal.

quiz.q: At 120 BPM, an eighth note lasts…
quiz.why: At 120 BPM a beat is 500 ms, and an eighth note is half a beat, so 250 ms.

lessons.title: Polyrhythm, hemiola and clave

scenes.text: Kofi, 31, a percussionist from Accra, teaches a workshop in Kochi. He asks everyone to clap 2 with the left hand and 3 with the right at the same time.
Chaos — everyone laughs.
He draws a grid of 6 boxes and shows where each hand hits.
Ten minutes later, the room is clapping a clean 3:2, grinning.

steps.title: The grid method
steps.body:
To play **A against B**, use a grid of **A × B** pulses (the lowest common multiple).

**3:2** → 6 pulses:

- 3-side hits on pulses **1, 3, 5**
- 2-side hits on pulses **1, 4**

Combined pattern: 1 (both) · 2 (–) · 3 (three) · 4 (two) · 5 (three) · 6 (–).

steps.title: 4:3 on a grid of 12
steps.body:
- 4-side hits on pulses **1, 4, 7, 10**
- 3-side hits on pulses **1, 5, 9**

Count 1–12 slowly, tapping each hand at its pulses. Then speed up until the grid disappears and you feel two flowing streams.

steps.title: Hemiola
steps.body: A **hemiola** regroups three beats of two into two beats of three (or vice versa): two bars of 3/4 (1 2 3 | 1 2 3) felt as three groups of two (1 2 | 3 1 | 2 3). Common at cadences in Baroque music and constant in many African, Latin and Indian rhythms.

steps.title: Clave
steps.body:
In Afro-Cuban music, the **clave** is a two-bar pattern everyone aligns to. **Son clave (3-2)** in 4/4, counting eighth notes:

- Bar 1: hits on **1**, **the & of 2**, **4**
- Bar 2: hits on **2**, **3**

**Rumba clave** moves the third hit of the '3' side half a beat later (to the & of 4). A **2-3** clave starts with the second bar.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying polyrhythms fast before the grid is automatic.
- Letting one hand 'win' and flatten the other into its pattern.
- Playing against the clave in salsa/son — the band and dancers will feel it.

activity.prompt: Order the combined 3:2 pattern across the 6-pulse grid.

quiz.q: What grid size do you use for 3:2?
quiz.why: For 3:2 use the least common multiple of 3 and 2, which is 6. On a 6-pulse grid, the 3-side hits every 2 and the 2-side every 3.

quiz.q: In 4:3 on a 12-grid, the 3-side hits pulses…
quiz.why: On a 12-grid, 4:3 means the 3-side hits every 4 pulses: 1, 5, 9. The 4-side hits every 3: 1, 4, 7, 10.

quiz.q: A hemiola in 3/4 regroups two bars into…
quiz.why: A hemiola regroups two bars of 3/4 (six beats) as three groups of two. It creates a feeling of 3/2 against 3/4.

quiz.q: Son clave 3-2, bar 2 hits on…
quiz.why: In 3-2 son clave, the second bar is the '2' side and hits on beats 2 and 3.

quiz.q: Rumba clave differs from son clave by…
options: Moving the third hit of the 3-side half a beat later
quiz.why: Rumba clave moves the third hit of the 3-side half a beat later, to the & of 4 instead of beat 4. Otherwise it matches son clave.

lessons.title: Odd meters and Indian talas

scenes.text: Hamza, 28, a violinist in Lucknow, joins a fusion band whose drummer plays in 7/8 and whose tabla player plays Rupak.
In rehearsal, Hamza keeps losing the 'one'.
The tabla player explains: “Rupak is 3+2+2, and sam is on a khali. 7/8 here is 2+2+3 — same seven, different grouping.”
Hamza counts groupings, not numbers. By the gig he floats over the seven.

steps.title: Odd meters are groupings of 2s and 3s
steps.body:
- **5/4** = 3+2 or 2+3 (Dave Brubeck Quartet's *Take Five* is a famous 5/4 tune).
- **7/8** = 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2.
- **9/8** can be 3+3+3 (compound triple) or 2+2+2+3 (common in Balkan and Turkish music).

Count with syllables: 2 = 'ta-ka', 3 = 'ta-ki-ta'. 7/8 as 2+2+3 = ta-ka ta-ka ta-ki-ta.

steps.title: Hindustani talas beyond teentaal
steps.body:
- **Rupak** – 7 beats (3+2+2). Unusually, **sam is on khali** (beat 1 shown with a wave). Theka: Tin Tin Na | Dhi Na | Dhi Na.
- **Jhaptaal** – 10 beats (2+3+2+3). Khali on beat 6. Theka: Dhi Na | Dhi Dhi Na | Ti Na | Dhi Dhi Na.
- **Ektaal** – 12 beats (2+2+2+2+2+2). Khali on beats 3 and 7.
- **Dadra** 6 (3+3), **Keherwa** 8 (4+4), **Teentaal** 16 (4+4+4+4).

steps.title: A Carnatic window
steps.body: Carnatic music measures talas in **aksharas**. **Adi tala** = 8 aksharas (a laghu of 4 + two drutams of 2: **4+2+2**), shown with a clap, finger counts, clap-wave, clap-wave. **Misra chapu** = 7 (often felt as 3+4). **Khanda chapu** = 5 (2+3). Konnakol (spoken rhythm syllables) is a superb way to practise any odd grouping.

steps.title: Worked example: phrasing across the cycle
steps.body: In Rupak (7), a 3-beat phrase repeated: 3+3+3+3+3+3+3 = 21 = 3 cycles of 7. The phrase starts on sam and lands back on sam after three cycles — a natural 'cycle-crossing' pattern used in tihais and fusion grooves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting 1–7 flatly instead of feeling the groups.
- Assuming 7/8 always means 2+2+3 — ask the band or listen for the accents.
- Forgetting Rupak's sam is a wave, not a clap.

activity.prompt: Match each tala or meter to its grouping.

quiz.q: Which tala has sam on khali?
quiz.why: Rupak tala's first beat is khali (shown with a wave), so sam falls on a khali beat. Rupak has 7 beats.

quiz.q: Jhaptaal has how many beats?
quiz.why: Jhaptaal has 10 beats, grouped 2+3+2+3.

quiz.q: Adi tala has…
quiz.why: Adi tala has 8 aksharas, in the grouping 4+2+2. It is the most common Carnatic tala.

quiz.q: A 3-beat phrase repeated in Rupak returns to sam after…
quiz.why: A 3-beat phrase against Rupak's 7 beats realigns at the least common multiple of 3 and 7, which is 21 beats, or 3 cycles.

quiz.q: 7/8 is best felt as…
quiz.why: 7/8 is felt as groups of 2s and 3s, such as 2+2+3 or 3+2+2. The beats are not seven equal unrelated pulses.

lessons.title: Ear training and transcription

scenes.text: Leena, 20, a music student in Shillong, wants to play songs by ear but always reaches for chord websites — which are often wrong.
Her teacher gives her 10 minutes of interval drills a day plus one song to transcribe each week.
She starts with the bass line, then the melody, then the chords.
Six months later she transcribes a whole song in an evening, more accurately than the websites.

steps.title: Interval reference songs
steps.body:
Link each interval to a tune you know (ascending):

- **Minor 2nd** – the *Jaws* theme
- **Major 2nd** – *Happy Birthday* ('Hap-py **birth**')
- **Major 3rd** – *When the Saints Go Marching In* ('Oh **when**')
- **Perfect 4th** – *Here Comes the Bride*
- **Perfect 5th** – *Twinkle Twinkle* ('twin-kle **twin**-kle')
- **Major 6th** – *My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean* ('My **Bon**')
- **Octave** – *Somewhere Over the Rainbow* ('Some-**where**')

In sargam: Sa→Ga = major 3rd, Sa→komal Ga = minor 3rd, Sa→Ma = perfect 4th, Sa→Pa = perfect 5th.

steps.title: Hearing chord qualities
steps.body:
- **Major** – bright, stable
- **Minor** – darker, softer
- **Diminished** – tense, unstable
- **Augmented** – dreamy, suspended, 'question mark'
- **Dominant 7** – bluesy, wants to move
- **Major 7** – soft, jazzy, wistful
- **Minor 7** – mellow, smooth

Practise with an app or a friend playing random chords; name the quality before the root.

steps.title: A transcription method
steps.body:
1. Pick a short section (8 bars). Loop it; slow it down (many players keep pitch while slowing).
2. Find the **key**: hum the note that feels like home; match it on your instrument.
3. Transcribe the **bass line** first — it usually gives chord roots.
4. Sing then play the **melody**.
5. Work out **chord qualities** over each bass note.
6. Write it down and play along with the recording to check.

steps.title: A 10-minute daily ear routine
steps.body:
- 3 min: intervals (sing them, then identify them)
- 3 min: chord qualities
- 4 min: transcribe or sing back a short phrase from a song

Consistency matters more than duration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Only identifying intervals, never singing them — singing builds the inner ear.
- Starting transcription with dense piano chords instead of the bass.
- Trusting a chord website blindly.

activity.prompt: Match each interval to a reference tune (ascending).

quiz.q: Sa to Pa is a…
quiz.why: Sa to Pa spans 7 semitones, which is a perfect 5th. Sa to Ma is a perfect 4th.

quiz.q: When transcribing, a good first layer is…
quiz.why: Start transcribing with the bass line, because it gives the chord roots and foundation. Add melody and other layers afterwards.

quiz.q: Which chord quality sounds tense and unstable?
quiz.why: A diminished chord is built from stacked minor thirds, which makes it tense and unstable. Major, minor and major 7 sound more stable.

quiz.q: Why sing intervals, not just name them?
quiz.why: Singing intervals connects hearing and producing pitch, building the inner ear. Naming alone doesn't train it.

questions.q: Triplets divide a beat into…
questions.why: Triplets divide a beat into three equal parts. Duplets divide it into two, and sixteenths into four.

questions.q: At 60 BPM, one beat lasts…
questions.why: At 60 BPM there are 60 beats a minute, so each beat is 60,000 ms ÷ 60 = 1000 ms.

questions.q: Sa to Ma is a…
questions.why: Sa to Ma spans 5 semitones, a perfect 4th. Sa to Pa is 7 semitones, a perfect 5th.

questions.q: Grid size for 4:3?
questions.why: The grid for 4:3 is the product (least common multiple) of 4 and 3, which is 12.

questions.q: Jhaptaal grouping is…
questions.why: Jhaptaal has 10 beats grouped 2+3+2+3. A 4+4 grouping would be 8 beats.

questions.q: Swing eighths are typically…
questions.why: Swing eighths are long–short, roughly triplet-based, rather than equal.

questions.q: Son clave 3-2 bar 1 hits on…
questions.why: In son clave 3-2, bar 1 is the '3' side and hits on beat 1, the & of 2, and beat 4.

questions.q: Rupak has how many beats?
questions.why: Rupak has 7 beats, grouped 3+2+2.

questions.q: In 3:2 on a 6-grid, the 2-side hits pulses…
questions.why: In 3:2 on a 6-grid, the 2-side hits every 3 pulses, which is pulses 1 and 4. The 3-side hits 1, 3, 5.

questions.q: Ektaal khali beats are…
questions.why: Ektaal has 12 beats, with khali on beats 3 and 7 in the usual pattern, as the X 0 2 0 3 4 structure shows.

questions.q: At 100 BPM, a sixteenth note lasts…
questions.why: At 100 BPM a beat is 600 ms, so a sixteenth note, a quarter of a beat, is 600 ÷ 4 = 150 ms.

questions.q: A 3-beat motif over 4/4 realigns with beat 1 after how many beats?
questions.why: A 3-beat motif over 4/4 realigns after the least common multiple of 3 and 4, which is 12 beats.

questions.q: Best order for transcribing a song?
questions.why: Build transcription from the foundation up: bass first, then melody, then chord qualities, then check the whole. Drums alone or lyrics alone aren't enough.

courses.title: Songwriting and arranging
courses.summary: Write songs with strong form, hooks and singable melodies whose words sit naturally on the rhythm, then arrange them for a band or ensemble with clear roles, registers and textures.
outcomes: Learners can choose and use common song forms (verse–chorus, AABA, mukhda–antara)
Learners can write a hook and a melody with good contour
Learners can set lyrics with natural prosody
Learners can arrange with clear roles, registers and dynamics
Learners can write correctly for transposing instruments

lessons.title: Song form and the hook

scenes.text: Nikhil, 23, a singer-songwriter in Pune, has 30 song ideas — none finished. Each is a long verse that never 'arrives'.
A mentor, Aaliyah, maps a hit song on paper: verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse, pre, chorus, bridge, chorus.
“Your song needs a destination — a hook people can sing after one listen.”
Nikhil writes a chorus around a 4-word hook. His friends are singing it by the end of the evening.

steps.title: Common forms
steps.body:
- **Verse–chorus**: V – C – V – C – Bridge – C. Verses tell the story; the chorus repeats the main message.
- **Verse–pre-chorus–chorus**: the pre-chorus builds tension into the chorus.
- **AABA (32-bar)**: four 8-bar sections; the B is a contrasting 'bridge' (classic standards).
- **Mukhda–antara** (Hindi film/ghazal tradition): the **mukhda** is the opening refrain that returns; **antaras** are the verses that explore, each returning to the mukhda.

steps.title: What makes a hook
steps.body:
A **hook** is the short, memorable idea people remember — a lyric phrase, a melodic figure, or an instrumental riff. Good hooks are:

- **Short** (2–6 words or a 1–2 bar motif)
- **Repeated** (often several times in the chorus)
- **Placed** on strong beats and often at the start or end of the chorus
- **Contrasting** — higher, more rhythmic or more open-voweled than the verse

steps.title: Worked example: contrast between sections
steps.body:
Verse: low register, more words, stepwise melody, chords I–vi–IV–V.
Chorus: melody jumps up a 4th or 5th to start, fewer and longer notes, hook on bar 1 and bar 5, chords IV–V–I–vi.

Contrast in **register, rhythm density and harmony** makes the chorus feel like arrival.

steps.title: Finish songs
steps.body:
- Write the chorus first if you're stuck — it's the song's thesis.
- Set a deadline: a full rough draft in one sitting, polish later.
- Record voice memos of every idea; review weekly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Verse and chorus in the same register and rhythm — no lift.
- Hook buried in the middle of a long line.
- Taking too long to reach the first chorus; many popular songs reach it within about a minute.

activity.prompt: Order a typical verse–pre-chorus–chorus pop song form.

quiz.q: In Hindi film songs, the returning opening refrain is the…
quiz.why: The mukhda is the returning opening refrain of a Hindi film song, while the antaras are the verses that explore. Alap and tihai are other concepts.

quiz.q: AABA form is often…
quiz.why: Classic AABA form is 32 bars, made of four 8-bar sections. The B section is the bridge.

quiz.q: A good hook is usually…
quiz.why: A good hook is short, repeated and well placed, so it is easily remembered. Long, complex or hidden ideas don't stick.

quiz.q: What creates lift into a chorus?
options: Contrast in register, rhythm and harmony
quiz.why: Contrast in register, rhythm and harmony signals the chorus's arrival and creates lift. Staying the same would feel flat.

lessons.title: Melody and lyrics that fit (prosody)

scenes.text: Ritika, 26, a copywriter in Delhi, writes beautiful lyrics, but when she sings them the words sound awkward.
A producer points out: “You've put 'to-DAY' as 'TO-day'. The stress is on the wrong beat.”
She speaks each line aloud, marks the natural stresses, and moves them to strong beats.
The song suddenly sounds natural — like talking, but sung.

steps.title: Prosody: stresses on strong beats
steps.body:
**Prosody** = the fit between words and music. Spoken words have natural stresses: *to-DAY*, *TO-mor-row*, *ba-NA-na*. Put **stressed syllables on strong beats** (or long notes) and unstressed ones on weak beats.

In Hindi/Urdu, take care with long and short vowels (e.g. **दिल** vs **दील**) and with the natural meter of the line — many traditions (ghazal *behr*) have precise metrical patterns.

steps.title: Melodic contour
steps.body:
Strong melodies usually:

- Have a clear **shape** (arch, rise, fall) and one **high point** per phrase or section.
- Mix **steps** with occasional **leaps**, and often move back by step after a leap (gap-fill).
- Use **repetition with variation** — repeat a motif, then change its ending.
- Sit in the singer's best range, saving the top notes for the chorus or climax.

steps.title: Worked example: fixing a line
steps.body:
Line: *“I never knew tomorrow would come”*. Natural stresses: i **NE**-ver **KNEW** to-**MOR**-row would **COME**.

In 4/4, put NE on beat 1, KNEW on beat 2, MOR on beat 3, COME on beat 1 of the next bar (held). Weak syllables ('i', 'ver', 'to', 'row would') fall between.

steps.title: Lyrics craft
steps.body:
- **Show, don't tell**: concrete images ('cold chai on the window sill') beat abstract words ('I'm sad').
- **Rhyme types**: perfect (*rain/pain*), near/slant (*home/alone*). Near rhymes sound modern and natural.
- Keep one **point of view** and one **tense** unless changing deliberately.
- Make every chorus line support the title/hook.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stretching words unnaturally to fit a pre-written melody.
- Rhyming at the cost of meaning.
- Melodies that sit on one note for too long without rhythmic interest.

statements.s: Stressed syllables should usually land on strong beats or long notes.
statements.why: That's good prosody.

statements.s: A melody should leap constantly to stay interesting.
statements.why: Mix steps and leaps; return by step after a leap.

statements.s: Near (slant) rhymes like home/alone are acceptable in modern songwriting.
statements.why: They often sound more natural.

statements.s: Concrete images usually communicate feelings better than abstract words.
statements.why: Show, don't tell.

statements.s: The highest note of a song is best placed in the first line of verse 1.
statements.why: Save the peak for the chorus or climax.

quiz.q: Prosody means…
options: The fit between words and music
quiz.why: Prosody is how well the words and music agree, for example natural word stress landing on strong beats. It isn't key, tempo or rhyme scheme.

quiz.q: In 'to-DAY', the stress should fall on…
quiz.why: In 'to-DAY' the natural stress is on the second syllable, so DAY should land on a strong beat. This keeps words and music in agreement.

quiz.q: 'Gap-fill' in melody means…
options: Moving back by step after a leap
quiz.why: Gap-fill means moving back by step in the opposite direction after a leap. It balances the leap and sounds natural.

quiz.q: Which is a concrete image?
quiz.why: 'Two cups, one still full' paints a specific scene you can see, which is a concrete image. 'Life is hard' and 'I feel lonely' are abstract.

lessons.title: Arranging: roles, registers and texture

scenes.text: A college band in Kolkata has two guitars, keys, bass and drums — and everything sounds like a wall of mud.
Their arranger friend, Tomás, maps every instrument's register on a whiteboard. Guitars, keys and vocals are all crammed around middle C.
He moves keys up an octave, gives one guitar a high riff, makes the other play sparse chords, and lets the bass and kick lock together.
Same notes, same song — but now you can hear everything.

steps.title: Four roles in any arrangement
steps.body:
1. **Melody** – the lead (voice or instrument).
2. **Counter-melody** – a secondary line that answers or complements, often in gaps of the melody.
3. **Harmony / pad** – chords, sustained or rhythmic.
4. **Bass + rhythm** – foundation and groove.

Give each instrument a **clear job** in each section. Two instruments doing the same job in the same register fight each other.

steps.title: Register and frequency space
steps.body:
Spread parts across **low, mid and high** registers. Keep close-voiced chords out of the very low register (below about C3) — they turn muddy. Leave the vocal's range relatively clear during lines; fill in gaps between phrases.

**Density**: start sparse, add layers as the song builds, and strip back for contrast (e.g. a breakdown before the last chorus).

steps.title: Transposing instruments
steps.body:
Some instruments sound different from written pitch:

- **B♭ trumpet, B♭ clarinet**: sound a **major 2nd lower** than written (write a major 2nd higher).
- **B♭ tenor sax**: sounds a **major 9th lower**.
- **E♭ alto sax**: sounds a **major 6th lower**.
- **F horn**: sounds a **perfect 5th lower**.
- **Guitar and bass guitar**: sound an **octave lower** than written.

Concert C on trumpet is written as D.

steps.title: Worked example: building a chorus
steps.body:
Verse 2 → chorus build:

- Bass: from whole notes to an eighth-note pulse locked with the kick.
- Guitar 1: from muted strums to open chords.
- Guitar 2: enters with a high 2-bar riff in the gaps of the vocal hook.
- Keys: pad moves up an octave; adds a counter-melody in the last 4 bars.
- Drums: hi-hat to ride/crash; add tambourine on 2 and 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Everyone playing all the time.
- Counter-melodies that compete with the lead instead of answering in gaps.
- Forgetting to transpose parts for B♭/E♭/F instruments.

activity.prompt: Match each instrument to how it sounds compared with written pitch.

quiz.q: To get concert C from a B♭ trumpet, you write…
quiz.why: A B♭ trumpet sounds a major 2nd lower than written. So to sound concert C, write D, a major 2nd higher.

quiz.q: Close-voiced chords in a very low register tend to sound…
quiz.why: Close-voiced chords in a very low register crowd small intervals together, so they sound muddy. Spread them out for clarity.

quiz.q: A counter-melody works best when it…
options: Answers in the gaps of the melody
quiz.why: A counter-melody works best when it answers in the gaps of the main melody. It complements rather than competes with it.

quiz.q: A good way to make a final chorus hit harder is…
options: Strip back just before it, then add layers
Keep everything at the same density
quiz.why: Strip back just before the final chorus, then add layers, so contrast makes it hit harder. Same density all the time lacks impact.

lessons.title: Co-writing and the songwriter's workflow

story.title: Two writers, one song, one argument

scenes.text: Sneha (lyrics) and Daniel (music), who met online, co-write a song between Mumbai and Toronto.
It becomes a hit on social media — and they suddenly argue over who wrote what and how to split earnings.
A friend asks: “Did you make a split sheet on the day you wrote it?” They hadn't.
They agree a split, sign it, and promise to do it at every session from now on.

steps.title: A practical workflow
steps.body:
1. **Capture** ideas instantly (voice memo, notes).
2. **Sketch**: hook + chorus + chords in one sitting.
3. **Draft** the full form with placeholder lyrics.
4. **Rewrite**: prosody, imagery, melody high points.
5. **Demo**: simple recording to test the song.
6. **Feedback** from 2–3 trusted listeners; rewrite again.
7. **Arrange/produce**.

steps.title: Co-writing etiquette
steps.body:
- Agree roles loosely, but welcome ideas from everyone.
- 'Yes, and…' first — critique later. No idea is stupid in the first hour.
- At the end of every session, write a **split sheet**: song title, date, all writers' names and contact details, and agreed percentage shares of the composition (music and lyrics), signed by all.

steps.title: Why split sheets matter
steps.body: Without written agreement, disputes about authorship and shares are common when a song earns money. Many collecting societies and publishers ask for agreed splits when a work is registered. You'll learn more in the career & royalties course.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a complete song draft in 90 minutes: 10 minutes hook, 20 chorus, 30 verses, 15 bridge, 15 rough voice-memo demo. Don't polish — finish.

activity.prompt: Song-session checklist
items: Recorded every idea on a voice memo
Wrote the hook and chorus first
Checked lyric stresses against strong beats
Filled in and signed a split sheet with all co-writers
Saved files with date and version number

quiz.q: A split sheet records…
options: Song title, writers and agreed ownership shares
quiz.why: A split sheet records the song title, the writers and their agreed ownership shares. It documents authorship.

quiz.q: When is the best time to make a split sheet?
options: At the end of the writing session
quiz.why: Make the split sheet at the end of the writing session, while memories are fresh and no money is yet involved. Waiting causes disputes.

quiz.q: In early co-writing, a good approach is…
quiz.why: In early co-writing, say 'Yes, and…': build on ideas first and critique later. It builds trust and keeps ideas flowing.

quiz.q: Why make a rough demo?
options: To test the song before investing in production
quiz.why: A rough demo lets you test whether the song works before spending on production. It doesn't replace writing or need releasing.

questions.q: The returning refrain of a Hindi film song is the…
questions.why: The mukhda is the returning refrain of a Hindi film song. Antara is the verse, and gat and tihai belong to instrumental and rhythmic forms.

questions.q: A hook is…
questions.why: A hook is a short, memorable musical idea. It is not a bridge, drum fill or guitar strap.

questions.q: Prosody is about…
options: Fitting word stress to musical stress
questions.why: Prosody fits word stress to musical stress, so stressed syllables fall on strong beats or long notes. It isn't about volume or tuning.

questions.q: Which instrument sounds an octave lower than written?
questions.why: Guitar sounds an octave lower than written. Alto sax and trumpet are transposing instruments with other intervals, and flute sounds as written.

questions.q: AABA contains how many contrasting B sections?
questions.why: AABA has one contrasting B section, the bridge. The A sections repeat.

questions.q: Concert pitch F for an E♭ alto sax is written as…
questions.why: An E♭ alto sax sounds a major 6th lower than written. To sound concert F, write a major 6th higher, which is D.

questions.q: Two instruments in the same register doing the same job often…
questions.why: Two instruments in the same register doing the same job tend to fight each other and blur the sound. Give each its own role.

questions.q: After a big melodic leap, melodies often…
questions.why: After a big leap, melodies often move back by step in the opposite direction. This gap-fill feels balanced.

questions.q: For 'to-MOR-row', the stressed syllable should land…
options: On a strong beat or long note
questions.why: The stressed syllable 'MOR' should land on a strong beat or long note so the music supports natural speech stress. A weak beat would sound wrong.

questions.q: Which change most increases a chorus's sense of arrival?
options: Higher register, longer notes and fuller arrangement
questions.why: A higher register, longer notes and a fuller arrangement give the chorus contrast with the verse, so it feels like arrival. Staying the same lacks lift.

questions.q: B♭ tenor sax sounds…
questions.why: A B♭ tenor sax sounds a major 9th lower than written, which is an octave plus a major 2nd.

questions.q: Why record split sheets at each session?
options: To prevent later authorship and share disputes
questions.why: Split sheets recorded at each session document who wrote what and what share each gets, preventing later disputes. They don't replace copyright.

courses.title: Music production and mixing basics
courses.summary: Record clean audio, set gain properly, and use EQ, compression, reverb and delay to make a balanced mix — then check loudness and prepare a master for streaming.
outcomes: Learners can set recording levels with safe headroom
Learners can use EQ to remove problems and shape tone
Learners can set a compressor's threshold, ratio, attack and release
Learners can add depth with reverb and tempo-synced delay
Learners can reference mixes and understand LUFS loudness

lessons.title: Recording and gain staging

scenes.text: Ayaan, 19, records his first song in his bedroom in Jaipur. In the loud chorus the vocal crackles.
The meter was hitting red — the signal clipped. The take is ruined.
His cousin, a sound engineer, shows him: set the level so the loudest parts peak well below 0 dBFS.
The new take is clean, with room to spare. “Record clean, mix later,” she says.

steps.title: Sound, level and dBFS
steps.body: Digital level is measured in **dBFS** (decibels relative to full scale). **0 dBFS is the maximum**; anything above it **clips** (flat-topped waves → harsh distortion that can't be undone). Recording at **24-bit** gives plenty of dynamic range, so there's no need to record hot. A common target is **peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS**, leaving headroom. Use the sound-waves lab to see how amplitude relates to loudness.

steps.title: Mic basics
steps.body:
- **Dynamic mics** – rugged, handle loud sources (guitar amps, drums, live vocals).
- **Condenser mics** – more detailed, sensitive; need **phantom power (+48 V)**; common for studio vocals and acoustic instruments.
- **Proximity effect**: directional mics boost bass as you get closer.
- Use a **pop filter** for vocals; record in a soft-furnished space to reduce room reflections.

steps.title: Gain staging
steps.body: Set healthy levels at **every stage**: mic preamp → recorded track → plugins → channel fader → mix bus. A sensible habit: aim for tracks and plugin outputs averaging somewhere around −18 dBFS (often equated with 0 VU on analogue-modelled plugins), so plugins behave as designed and the mix bus doesn't clip.

steps.title: Worked example: setting a vocal level
steps.body:
1. Ask the singer to perform the **loudest** part of the song.
2. Raise preamp gain until peaks reach about −10 dBFS.
3. Check the quietest verse is still well above the noise floor.
4. Record a test take and listen for clipping, plosives ('p', 'b' pops) and room echo.
5. Adjust mic distance (about a hand-span is a common start) rather than shouting into it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recording as loud as possible 'for quality' — risks clipping with no benefit at 24-bit.
- Fixing problems later that could be fixed with mic placement now.
- Monitoring too loud for hours — protect your hearing; take breaks and keep listening levels moderate.

bands.text: Quite low — fine in 24-bit if the noise floor is low, but you could raise the gain a little.
Healthy — good headroom for unexpected loud moments.
Hot — risky; a louder note may clip.
Clipping! Above 0 dBFS the waveform is flattened and distorted. Lower the gain and re-record.

quiz.q: What happens above 0 dBFS?
quiz.why: 0 dBFS is the digital maximum, and a signal above it clips, which causes harsh distortion. Digital audio cannot go higher.

quiz.q: Condenser microphones usually need…
quiz.why: Most condenser microphones need +48 V phantom power from the interface or mixer. Dynamic mics do not.

quiz.q: Proximity effect means…
quiz.why: The proximity effect gives directional mics more bass when the source is close. Moving away reduces the low end.

quiz.q: A sensible recording peak target in 24-bit is about…
quiz.why: Peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS leave headroom, and in 24-bit there is plenty of resolution. Recording at 0 dBFS risks clipping.

lessons.title: EQ: carve space for every sound

scenes.text: Mira, 22, produces EDM in Bengaluru. Her kick and bass blur into one boomy mess.
Her mentor shows her the spectrum analyser: both peak in the same low frequencies.
She high-passes the guitars and pads, cuts a little low-mid mud, and gives kick and bass slightly different low-end focus.
The drop now punches on her phone, her car and the club system.

steps.title: The frequency map
steps.body:
Human hearing is roughly **20 Hz – 20 kHz** (the top end falls with age).

- **Sub** 20–60 Hz – felt more than heard
- **Bass** 60–250 Hz – warmth, weight
- **Low mids** 250–500 Hz – body; too much = 'mud'
- **Mids** 500 Hz–2 kHz – presence of most instruments
- **Upper mids** 2–5 kHz – clarity, attack; too much = harsh
- **Highs/air** 5–20 kHz – sparkle, breath, sibilance

These ranges are approximate guides, not hard borders.

steps.title: EQ tools
steps.body:
- **High-pass filter (HPF)** – removes lows below a cutoff. Use on vocals, guitars, keys, overheads to clear rumble and make room for kick and bass.
- **Bell (peaking)** – boost/cut around a frequency; **Q** sets width (high Q = narrow).
- **Shelf** – boost/cut everything above or below a point.
- **Cut narrow, boost wide**: find problems with a narrow cut; enhance tone with gentle wide boosts.

steps.title: Worked example: cleaning a vocal
steps.body:
1. HPF around 80–100 Hz (lower for deep voices) to remove rumble.
2. If boxy, try a small cut in the 250–500 Hz area (e.g. −2 to −3 dB).
3. For clarity, a gentle wide boost around 3–5 kHz.
4. For 'air', a high shelf around 10 kHz (+1 to +2 dB).
5. If 's' sounds are harsh, use a de-esser rather than cutting all highs.

Always compare with EQ bypassed at matched loudness — louder often fools us into thinking 'better'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- EQing in solo for ages — judge sounds **in the mix**.
- Boosting everything — if everything is boosted, nothing stands out; cut first.
- Over-high-passing until a track sounds thin.
- Trusting one pair of speakers or headphones; check on several systems.

activity.prompt: Which frequency area is most associated with each description?

items.text: Snare crack and guitar pick attack

quiz.q: A high-pass filter removes…
quiz.why: A high-pass filter lets highs pass and removes lows below the cutoff, such as rumble. A low-pass does the opposite.

quiz.q: Muddiness often lives in…
quiz.why: Muddiness usually sits in the low mids, around 250 to 500 Hz, where instruments crowd. Cutting there clears the mix.

quiz.q: A high Q value means…
quiz.why: A high Q means a narrow band, affecting only frequencies close to the centre. A low Q is wide.

quiz.q: Why match loudness when comparing EQ on/off?
options: Louder usually sounds 'better' and misleads you
quiz.why: Louder usually sounds 'better', which misleads you. Matching loudness lets you judge the EQ itself.

lessons.title: Compression: control and punch

scenes.text: Ishita, 28, mixes a podcast-style acoustic song in Kochi. Some words are too loud; others vanish.
She adds a compressor but squashes it so hard the vocal sounds lifeless and pumping.
A mixing tutor helps her set threshold, ratio, attack and release step by step, aiming for a few dB of gain reduction.
Now every word is audible and the vocal still breathes.

steps.title: What a compressor does
steps.body: A compressor **reduces the level of sounds that go above a threshold**, making the dynamic range smaller. Then **make-up gain** raises the whole signal back up. Result: quieter parts feel louder relative to peaks; the track sits steadily in the mix.

steps.title: The controls
steps.body:
- **Threshold** – level above which compression starts.
- **Ratio** – how much: at **4:1**, a signal 8 dB over threshold comes out only 2 dB over.
- **Attack** – how quickly it clamps down. **Slower** attack lets transients (the initial 'hit') through → punch. **Faster** attack tames peaks → smoother.
- **Release** – how quickly it lets go. Too fast → distortion/flutter; too slow → stays squashed, 'pumping'.
- **Knee** – soft (gradual) or hard (abrupt) onset.
- **Make-up gain** – restores level.

steps.title: Worked example: ratio maths
steps.body:
Threshold −20 dBFS, ratio 4:1. A vocal peak hits −8 dBFS (12 dB over threshold).

Output over threshold = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 dB → peak comes out at **−17 dBFS**. Gain reduction = **9 dB** (quite a lot for a vocal; try a higher threshold for 3–6 dB).

steps.title: Starting points (then use your ears)
steps.body:
- **Vocal**: ratio 3:1–4:1, medium attack, medium release, 3–6 dB gain reduction on loud phrases.
- **Bass**: 4:1, medium attack, for steady level.
- **Drum bus**: 2:1–4:1, slower attack for punch, 2–4 dB reduction.
- **Parallel compression**: blend a heavily compressed copy with the dry signal for density without losing dynamics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Compressing everything heavily 'because pros do' — it flattens life.
- Judging compression with make-up gain louder than bypass (loudness bias again).
- Very fast attack on drums, killing the transient punch.

activity.prompt: Threshold −24 dBFS, ratio 3:1. A snare peak reaches −12 dBFS. How many dB of gain reduction does the compressor apply? (Over = 12 dB → output over = 12 ÷ 3.)

quiz.q: A compressor mainly…
quiz.why: A compressor reduces the level of signal above a threshold, which controls dynamic range. It doesn't add reverb or change pitch.

quiz.q: Slower attack on drums usually…
quiz.why: A slower attack lets the initial transient through before compression starts, keeping the drum punchy. A fast attack clamps the hit.

quiz.q: At 4:1, a signal 8 dB over threshold comes out…
quiz.why: At 4:1, every 4 dB over the threshold becomes 1 dB over. So 8 dB over becomes 8 ÷ 4 = 2 dB over.

quiz.q: Parallel compression means…
options: Blending a heavily compressed copy with the dry signal
quiz.why: Parallel compression blends a heavily compressed copy with the dry signal. It adds density while keeping natural dynamics.

lessons.title: Space, balance, loudness and mastering

scenes.text: Arjun and Leah, a duo from Goa, master their single super loud so it 'competes'. On streaming it sounds squashed and no louder than others.
An engineer explains loudness normalisation and LUFS: streaming services turn very loud tracks down.
They remaster with more dynamics and a true-peak ceiling, checking against reference tracks.
Now the chorus actually hits harder than the verse — and it sounds great next to their favourite songs.

steps.title: Reverb and delay: depth
steps.body:
- **Reverb** simulates a space. Key controls: **decay/RT** (length), **pre-delay** (gap before the reverb starts — keeps vocals upfront), **size**, **damping** (darker tails).
- **Delay** repeats the sound. Sync to tempo: quarter note = **60 000 ÷ BPM** ms (500 ms at 120 BPM).
- Use **send/return (aux) buses** so many tracks share one reverb — more cohesive and CPU-friendly.
- EQ the reverb return (high-pass around 200–400 Hz) to stop low-end wash.

steps.title: Balance and panning
steps.body:
Start every mix with **faders and panning only**:

- Keep **kick, bass, snare and lead vocal centred**.
- Pan doubles, guitars, keys, backing vocals left/right to open the middle.
- Check the mix in **mono** — if parts vanish, there may be phase issues.
- Compare with a **reference track** in the same genre, at matched loudness.

steps.title: Loudness: LUFS and true peak
steps.body:
**LUFS** (Loudness Units relative to Full Scale) measures perceived loudness over time. Many streaming platforms **normalise** playback — several major services use around **−14 LUFS integrated** as a reference, others differ (some around −16). Overly loud masters are simply turned down, losing punch for nothing.

Mastering engineers commonly keep **true peak at or below about −1 dBTP** to avoid distortion after lossy encoding. Check each platform's current published guidance.

steps.title: Worked example: a simple mastering chain
steps.body:
1. Gentle **EQ** for overall balance (small moves).
2. Light **bus compression** (1–2 dB) to glue.
3. **Limiter** with ceiling around −1 dBTP; raise input until integrated loudness is in your target range without audible squashing.
4. Compare A/B with references at matched loudness.
5. Export at the delivery spec (often 24-bit WAV at the project sample rate, e.g. 44.1 or 48 kHz).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Smothering vocals in reverb with no pre-delay.
- Mastering for maximum loudness instead of the best sound.
- Mixing at very high volume for hours — ear fatigue causes bad decisions and hearing damage. Take breaks.

activity.prompt: Your song is 96 BPM. What delay time in milliseconds gives one quarter note? (60 000 ÷ BPM)

quiz.q: Pre-delay on a vocal reverb helps…
options: Keep the vocal upfront and clear
quiz.why: Pre-delay gives a gap before the reverb starts, so the dry vocal attack stays upfront and clear. Without it the vocal can get pushed back.

quiz.q: Which elements are usually panned centre?
options: Kick, bass, snare and lead vocal
quiz.why: Kick, bass, snare and lead vocal are typically panned centre to anchor the mix. Doubles and hi-hats are often panned wide.

quiz.q: LUFS measures…
quiz.why: LUFS measures perceived loudness over time, not just peaks. It is used for platform loudness targets.

quiz.q: If a master is much louder than a platform's normalisation target, it will usually be…
quiz.why: Platforms with loudness normalisation turn down masters that are louder than their target. Extra loudness gives no advantage.

quiz.q: A common true-peak ceiling in mastering is about…
quiz.why: A true-peak ceiling of about −1 dBTP leaves room for overshoots during encoding to lossy formats. 0 or +3 can clip after conversion.

questions.q: 0 dBFS is…
questions.why: 0 dBFS is the digital maximum level. Above it, the signal clips.

questions.q: A high-pass filter on a vocal removes…
questions.why: A high-pass filter on a vocal removes low rumble, such as stand thumps and air-conditioning noise. It doesn't touch sibilance or reverb.

questions.q: Quarter-note delay at 120 BPM is…
questions.why: At 120 BPM a quarter note lasts 60,000 ÷ 120 = 500 ms, so that is the delay time.

questions.q: Which mic usually needs phantom power?
questions.why: Condenser microphones usually need phantom power. Dynamic mics don't, and ribbon mics can be damaged by it.

questions.q: Muddiness is commonly addressed by cutting around…
questions.why: Muddiness commonly sits at 250–500 Hz, so you cut around there. Higher ranges affect brightness or air.

questions.q: Ratio 2:1 with a signal 6 dB over threshold gives output…
questions.why: At 2:1, the amount over the threshold is halved: 6 dB ÷ 2 = 3 dB over.

questions.q: Fast attack on a drum compressor tends to…
questions.why: A fast attack clamps the initial hit, reducing transient punch. A slower attack lets the punch through.

questions.q: Why use reverb on an aux send?
options: Shared cohesive space and less CPU
questions.why: Using reverb on an aux send lets many tracks share one space, giving a cohesive sound with less CPU than a reverb on each track.

questions.q: Checking a mix in mono reveals…
questions.why: Checking a mix in mono reveals phase problems and balance issues, because out-of-phase elements cancel. It doesn't show key or tempo.

questions.q: Why compare processed vs bypassed at matched loudness?
questions.why: Louder usually sounds better, which biases judgement. Matching loudness lets you hear the real effect of the processing.

questions.q: Threshold −18, ratio 4:1, peak at −6. Output peak?
