questions.why: The peak is 12 dB over the −18 threshold. At 4:1, that becomes 12 ÷ 4 = 3 dB over, so the output peak is −18 + 3 = −15 dBFS.

questions.q: A master at −7 LUFS on a platform normalising to −14 LUFS will…
options: Be turned down about 7 dB, keeping its squashed dynamics
questions.why: A −7 LUFS master on a platform normalising to −14 LUFS is turned down about 7 dB. It keeps its squashed dynamics, so loudness gives no benefit.

questions.q: Best way to protect hearing during long mixes?
questions.why: Mix at moderate levels and take regular breaks. This reduces ear fatigue and protects hearing, while very loud monitoring causes damage.

courses.title: Raga theory in depth
courses.summary: Go beyond thaats: understand raga grammar (aroha–avaroha, vadi–samvadi, pakad and chalan), time and mood, the architecture of a performance, and how Hindustani ragas relate to Carnatic melakartas.
outcomes: Learners can describe a raga using jati, aroha/avaroha, vadi/samvadi and chalan
Learners can explain why ragas with the same notes sound different
Learners can describe samay (time theory) and rasa associations
Learners can outline a khayal and an instrumental performance
Learners can map common ragas to Carnatic melakartas

lessons.title: Raga grammar: jati, aroha–avaroha, vadi–samvadi, chalan

scenes.text: Kavya, 24, a trained singer in Pune, sings Bhupali beautifully. Her guru asks her to sing Deshkar next — and she sings the same thing.
“Both use Sa Re Ga Pa Dha,” she protests.
Her guru explains: Bhupali lives in the lower half and stresses Ga; Deshkar lives in the upper half, stresses Dha and avoids lingering on Re.
Kavya realises a raga is a personality, not a scale.

steps.title: What defines a raga
steps.body:
A raga is a melodic framework with rules and a recognisable character. Traditional principles include:

- At least **five** notes; **Sa** is always present.
- **Ma and Pa are not both omitted** (a widely taught rule).
- A specific **aroha** (ascent) and **avaroha** (descent), which may differ.
- Important notes (**vadi**, **samvadi**), characteristic phrases (**pakad**), and typical movement (**chalan**).
- Often an associated **time** and **mood**.

steps.title: Jati: counting notes
steps.body:
- **Audav** = 5 notes · **Shadav** = 6 · **Sampurna** = 7

Ascent and descent can differ: **audav–sampurna** = 5 up, 7 down. Example: **Bhupali** is audav–audav (S R G P D in both directions). **Malkauns** is audav (S g M d n — komal Ga, Dha, Ni).

steps.title: Vadi, samvadi, anuvadi, vivadi
steps.body:
- **Vadi** – the most important note (the 'king').
- **Samvadi** – the second most important, usually a 4th or 5th from the vadi.
- **Anuvadi** – other notes used.
- **Vivadi** – a note foreign to the raga, used only rarely and skilfully.

Examples (as commonly taught): **Yaman** – vadi Ga, samvadi Ni. **Bhupali** – vadi Ga, samvadi Dha. **Malkauns** – vadi Ma, samvadi Sa.

steps.title: Worked example: Bhupali vs Deshkar
steps.body:
Both use **S R G P D** (no Ma, no Ni) — the same pentatonic set.

- **Bhupali**: focus in the **purvang** (lower half: Sa–Pa); Ga is the vadi; Re and Ga are prominent; peaceful, devotional evening feel.
- **Deshkar**: focus in the **uttarang** (upper half: Pa–Sa'); Dha is prominent; Re is weak and not dwelt upon; brighter, typically a morning raga.

Same notes, different emphasis and movement → different ragas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a raga as just its scale.
- Playing aroha/avaroha as straight lines; many ragas use **vakra** (zig-zag) movement.
- Learning rules from charts only — ragas are learnt by listening to masters and from a guru. Details of chalan vary across gharanas.

items.back: 5 notes.
6 notes.
All 7 notes.
The most important note of a raga.
The second most important note, usually a 4th or 5th from the vadi.
The characteristic way a raga moves — its typical melodic behaviour.
Zig-zag (non-linear) movement in ascent or descent.

quiz.q: Bhupali's jati is…
quiz.why: Bhupali uses five notes (S R G P D) in both ascent and descent, so its jati is audav–audav.

quiz.q: The vadi of Yaman (as commonly taught) is…
quiz.why: In Yaman, as commonly taught, the vadi is Ga and the samvadi is Ni.

quiz.q: Bhupali and Deshkar differ mainly in…
quiz.why: Bhupali and Deshkar use the same notes but differ in emphasis, register focus and chalan. A raga is more than its scale.

quiz.q: Which rule is widely taught about Ma and Pa?
quiz.why: A widely taught rule is that Ma and Pa are not both omitted from a raga's scale; at least one of them stays.

quiz.q: Malkauns uses…
quiz.why: Malkauns is S g M d n: komal Ga, Dha and Ni with shuddha Ma, and it omits Re and Pa.

lessons.title: Samay and rasa: time and mood of ragas

scenes.text: At a dawn concert by the Ganga in Varanasi, a flautist plays Bhairav as the sky turns pink.
Retired professor Dr. Mishra explains to visiting student Anna from Vienna why Bhairav is a morning raga.
“Komal Re and komal Dha with slow oscillation — it feels like awakening, devotion.”
Anna writes in her notebook: 'Time is part of a raga's meaning.'

steps.title: Time theory (samay)
steps.body:
Hindustani tradition associates many ragas with a time of day, dividing the day into **eight prahars** of about three hours. Examples commonly cited:

- **Early morning**: Bhairav, Lalit, Todi
- **Late morning/afternoon**: Bhimpalasi, Multani
- **Sunset/dusk**: Marwa, Poorvi, Shree
- **Evening/first part of night**: Yaman, Bhupali
- **Late night**: Malkauns, Darbari Kanada

In concerts today the rule is often relaxed, but many musicians still honour it.

steps.title: Sandhi prakash ragas
steps.body: Ragas sung at the **junctions of day and night** (dawn and dusk) are called **sandhi prakash** ragas. Many of them use **komal Re** — for example Bhairav (dawn) and Marwa and Poorvi (dusk) — which gives them a poignant, transitional feel.

steps.title: Seasonal ragas
steps.body: Some ragas are linked to seasons: the **Malhar** family (e.g. Miyan ki Malhar, Megh) with the **monsoon**; **Basant** and **Bahar** with **spring**. These associations come from tradition and poetry rather than physics — they work because generations of listeners share them.

steps.title: Rasa: emotional flavour
steps.body: The **rasa** idea (from the Natyashastra) is used to describe a raga's emotional colour: Bhairav — devotional, serious; Yaman — serene, romantic; Malkauns — deep, meditative; Bhairavi — tender, often used to close concerts. These are interpretive traditions; individual performances can bring out different shades.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating time theory as a scientific rule — it is an aesthetic tradition.
- Assuming every source agrees: some ragas have different time associations in different books and gharanas.

activity.prompt: Sort the ragas by their commonly cited time of performance.

quiz.q: How many prahars divide the day in time theory?
quiz.why: Time theory divides the day and night into eight prahars of about three hours each.

quiz.q: Sandhi prakash ragas are sung at…
quiz.why: Sandhi prakash ragas are sung at the junctions of day and night, which are dawn and dusk.

quiz.q: The Malhar family is associated with…
quiz.why: The Malhar family of ragas is associated with the monsoon and rain.

quiz.q: Bhairavi is often used to…
quiz.why: Bhairavi is traditionally used to close a concert, as a concluding raga. It is not used to tune the tanpura.

lessons.title: Architecture of a performance: alap to tihai

scenes.text: Sarah, 30, a cellist from London studying sitar in Kolkata, attends her first full concert.
For 20 minutes the sitarist plays without the tabla. Sarah wonders if the drummer is late.
Then the gat begins, the tabla enters, and the music gradually speeds to a dazzling jhala.
Afterwards her teacher explains the architecture — and Sarah hears the whole concert differently.

steps.title: Instrumental form
steps.body:
A typical full instrumental raga performance:

1. **Alap** – slow, unmetered, no tabla; the raga is unfolded note by note from the lower register upward.
2. **Jor (jod)** – a steady pulse appears, still without tabla; rhythmic patterns grow.
3. **Jhala** – fast, using the instrument's rhythmic (chikari) strings; a climax of the unmetered section.
4. **Gat** – a composed piece in a taal with **tabla**; may be **vilambit** (slow) then **drut** (fast), with improvised variations, taans and **tihais**.

steps.title: Vocal khayal form
steps.body:
1. A short **aochar/alap** to establish the raga.
2. **Bada khayal** – a **vilambit** (slow) bandish, often in vilambit ektaal, jhoomra or tilwada; slow, detailed elaboration (**badhat**), bol-alap, then taans as it moves.
3. **Chhota khayal** – a **drut** bandish, often in teentaal or ektaal; faster taans, sargam, bol-taans.
4. Possibly a **tarana** (fast, with syllables like *ta na dere na*).

**Dhrupad**, the older form, uses an extended alap with syllables like *nom-tom* and is accompanied by the **pakhawaj**, commonly in **chautaal** (12 beats).

steps.title: Bandish: sthayi and antara
steps.body: A **bandish** (composition) has a **sthayi** (first part, mostly in lower and middle registers) and an **antara** (second part, rising to the upper register). The **mukhda** — the opening phrase of the sthayi leading to sam — returns again and again as a home base during improvisation.

steps.title: Worked example: designing a tihai
steps.body:
Teentaal (16). You want a tihai that starts on beat 1 and ends on the next sam (beat 1 of the next cycle, = 17 beats total).

Try phrase length **p** and gap **g**: 3p + 2g = 17.

- p = 5, g = 1 → 15 + 2 = 17 ✓
- p = 3, g = 4 → 9 + 8 = 17 ✓

To start elsewhere, count backwards from the next sam.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rushing the alap — it establishes the raga's identity.
- Losing sam during long improvisations; always know where the mukhda will land.
- Thinking speed is the goal; musicality and raga purity come first.

activity.prompt: Order the sections of a full instrumental raga performance.
items: Drut gat with tabla, taans and tihais

quiz.q: Which section has no tabla and no fixed pulse?
quiz.why: Alap is the slow, unmetered opening, with no tabla and no fixed pulse. Khayal, tarana and gat have rhythm.

quiz.q: Bada khayal is sung in…
quiz.why: Bada khayal is the slow, elaborate composition, sung in vilambit laya (slow tempo). Chhota khayal is faster.

quiz.q: The antara of a bandish usually…
quiz.why: The antara is the second part of a bandish and usually rises towards the upper register, exploring higher notes. The sthayi stays lower.

quiz.q: Dhrupad is traditionally accompanied by…
quiz.why: Dhrupad is traditionally accompanied by the pakhawaj, a barrel-shaped drum. Tabla accompanies khayal.

quiz.q: For a tihai of 17 beats with gap 1, the phrase length is…
quiz.why: A tihai repeats a phrase three times with two gaps: 3p + 2g = 17. With gap 1, 3p = 15, so p = 5.

lessons.title: Hindustani meets Carnatic: melakartas and janya ragas

scenes.text: Aravind, a Carnatic violinist from Chennai, and Shabnam, a Hindustani sitarist from Lucknow, plan a jugalbandi.
They map ragas: Kalyani and Yaman share a scale; Mohanam and Bhupali share a scale; Mayamalavagowla matches Bhairav's notes.
They also learn how differently each tradition ornaments the same notes.
The concert in Bengaluru is a dialogue of cousins — familiar yet different.

steps.title: The 72 melakartas
steps.body: Carnatic music organises parent scales into **72 melakarta ragas** (a system associated with Venkatamakhi and later standardised). Every melakarta is **sampurna** (all seven notes in order, up and down). Ragas derived from them are **janya ragas** (they may omit notes or use zig-zag movement).

steps.title: Common bridges
steps.body:
Scale matches (melodic treatment differs!):

- **Shankarabharanam** (mela 29) ≈ Bilawal thaat / major scale
- **Kalyani** (mela 65) ≈ Kalyan thaat (Yaman's scale)
- **Kharaharapriya** (mela 22) ≈ Kafi thaat
- **Natabhairavi** (mela 20) ≈ Asavari thaat / natural minor
- **Hanumatodi** (mela 8) ≈ Bhairavi thaat
- **Mayamalavagowla** (mela 15) ≈ Bhairav thaat
- **Mohanam** (janya) ≈ Bhupali's notes (S R G P D)

Note the trap: Carnatic **Todi** (Hanumatodi) has the *scale* of Hindustani **Bhairavi thaat**, while Hindustani **Todi** is a different scale.

steps.title: Gamakas and ornamentation
steps.body: Carnatic music relies heavily on **gamakas** — oscillations, slides and inflections that are part of a raga's identity; the same written note may be sung with a characteristic movement. Hindustani music uses **meend** (glide), **andolan** (slow oscillation, e.g. komal Re and Dha in Bhairav), **kan** (grace notes), **murki** and **gamak** too. Notation alone never captures a raga — listening is essential.

steps.title: Collaborating across traditions
steps.body:
- Agree on Sa and the shared scale, then discuss which phrases are essential to each raga.
- Match tala structures: Adi tala (8) and teentaal (16) align easily (two Adi cycles = one teentaal cycle in count).
- Respect each tradition's ornaments rather than flattening them.

activity.prompt: Match each Carnatic raga to its Hindustani scale cousin.

quiz.q: How many melakartas are there?
quiz.why: There are 72 melakartas, the parent scales of the Carnatic system. Each has all seven notes.

quiz.q: All melakartas are…
quiz.why: All melakartas are sampurna, with all seven notes in order in both ascent and descent.

quiz.q: Carnatic Hanumatodi shares its scale with…
quiz.why: Hanumatodi has komal Re, Ga, Dha and Ni, which matches Hindustani Bhairavi thaat, not Todi thaat. The names can mislead.

quiz.q: Andolan means…
quiz.why: Andolan is a slow oscillation of a note, as with komal Re in raga Bhairav. It isn't a fast taan or a drum stroke.

quiz.q: Mela 29 is…
quiz.why: Melakarta number 29 is Dheerashankarabharanam, usually called Shankarabharanam, which matches the major scale.

questions.q: Audav means…
questions.why: Audav means five notes. Shadav means six and sampurna means seven.

questions.q: The vadi is…
questions.why: The vadi is the most important note of a raga, often called its 'king'. It is not a drum or a rhythm.

questions.q: Alap is…
questions.why: Alap is the slow, unmetered introduction that unfolds the raga without tabla. It is not a composition or a tala.

questions.q: Which raga is commonly cited as a morning raga?
questions.why: Bhairav is commonly cited as a morning raga. Malkauns and Darbari are late-night ragas, and Yaman is an evening raga.

questions.q: Kalyani corresponds to which thaat?
questions.why: Carnatic Kalyani corresponds to Kalyan thaat in Hindustani music, with tivra Ma and other notes shuddha.

questions.q: Bandish's second part is…
questions.why: The second part of a bandish is the antara. The first part is the sthayi, or mukhda.

questions.q: Bhupali and Deshkar share…
questions.why: Bhupali and Deshkar share the same notes, S R G P D, but differ in emphasis, vadi and time.

questions.q: Sandhi prakash ragas often feature…
questions.why: Komal Re is common in sandhi prakash ragas, such as Bhairav and Marwa, sung at dawn or dusk.

questions.q: Dhrupad is commonly performed in which 12-beat tala?
questions.why: Dhrupad is commonly performed in Chautaal, a 12-beat tala. Teentaal has 16 beats and Rupak 7.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes chalan?
options: The typical way the raga moves
questions.why: Chalan is the typical way a raga moves, meaning its characteristic phrases and melodic behaviour. It is not a dance or tuning.

questions.q: Carnatic Todi's scale matches Hindustani…
questions.why: Carnatic Todi (Hanumatodi) has the same notes as Hindustani Bhairavi thaat, so the names are a classic trap. It does not match Todi thaat.

questions.q: A 17-beat tihai with gap 4 has phrase length…
questions.why: A 17-beat tihai with gap 4: 3p + 2×4 = 17, so 3p = 9 and p = 3.

questions.q: Why can't a raga be fully learnt from a written scale chart?
options: Ornaments, emphasis and chalan define it and must be heard
questions.why: A raga is defined by its ornaments, emphasis and chalan, which must be heard, not just by its notes. It is a personality, not only a scale.

courses.title: Music career and royalties basics
courses.summary: Understand the two copyrights in every song, the main royalty streams, how collecting societies work in India and abroad, what to check in a contract, and how working musicians build sustainable careers.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish the composition copyright from the sound recording
Learners can name performance, mechanical, sync and neighbouring/performer royalties
Learners can name India's main music collecting bodies and what they collect for
Learners can spot key terms and red flags in music contracts
Learners can plan a multi-income music career

lessons.title: Two copyrights in every song

scenes.text: Ria writes the lyrics, Kabir writes the music, and an independent label pays for the recording of their song 'Monsoon Letters'.
The song gets radio play and a web-series sync offer. Everyone asks: who gets paid what?
A music-business teacher explains: there are two separate copyrights — the song (composition) and the recording (master).
Ria and Kabir realise they own a share of the composition even though the label owns the master.

steps.title: The composition and the sound recording
steps.body:
- **Musical work + literary work (the 'song')**: the melody/music and the lyrics. Owned by the **composer(s) and lyricist(s)**, often administered by a **publisher**.
- **Sound recording (the 'master')**: the specific recorded performance. Usually owned by whoever made/paid for the recording — often a **label**, or the artist if independent.

One recorded song therefore has at least two sets of rights holders, plus **performers' rights** for singers and musicians on the recording.

steps.title: Main royalty streams
steps.body:
- **Performance royalties** – when the song is publicly performed or communicated: radio, TV, live venues, restaurants, streaming.
- **Mechanical royalties** – when the song is reproduced (copies, downloads, and in many countries streams).
- **Synchronisation (sync) fees** – when music is paired with visuals: films, ads, games, web series. Usually needs permission from **both** the composition and master owners.
- **Neighbouring rights / performers' rights** – for public performance of sound recordings, paid to labels and performers in many countries.

steps.title: India: copyright duration
steps.body: Under India's **Copyright Act, 1957**, literary and musical works are generally protected for the **author's lifetime + 60 years**; sound recordings for **60 years** from the year after publication. Copyright exists automatically when a work is created and fixed; registration with the Copyright Office is optional but can help as evidence.

steps.title: Common misunderstandings
steps.body:
- 'I uploaded it first, so I own it.' Upload date is weak evidence; keep drafts, dated files and split sheets.
- 'Covering a song on YouTube is free.' Covers involve the composition rights; platforms may have licences, but monetisation and distribution rules vary.
- 'The label owns everything.' Depends on your contracts — read them.

This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Which copyright does each item belong to?

items.text: The final studio mix of a specific performance
A live recording released by a label
Chord progression and tune written by the composer
The recording owned by the label that paid for it

quiz.q: How many core copyrights does a released recorded song usually involve?
quiz.why: A released recorded song usually involves two copyrights: the composition (music and lyrics) and the sound recording (the master).

quiz.q: A sync licence is needed when…
options: Pairing music with visuals like films or ads
quiz.why: A sync (synchronisation) licence is needed when music is paired with visuals like films, ads or videos. Practising or private listening doesn't need it.

quiz.q: In India, musical works are generally protected for…
quiz.why: In India, musical works are generally protected for the author's life plus 60 years under the Copyright Act, 1957.

quiz.q: Is copyright registration required for protection in India?
options: No, protection is automatic; registration is optional evidence
quiz.why: Protection is automatic on creation. Registration is optional, but it provides useful evidence.

lessons.title: Collecting societies and getting paid

scenes.text: Farhan, 32, an indie composer in Mumbai, hears his song in a café and on FM radio — but never sees a rupee for it.
An older composer asks: “Are you a member of a collecting society? Are your works registered with correct splits?”
He joins, registers his catalogue with metadata and splits, and checks his distributor details.
A year later, royalty statements start arriving.

steps.title: What collecting societies do
steps.body: Collecting societies (also called CMOs or PROs) **license** music users (broadcasters, venues, platforms), **collect** fees, and **distribute** royalties to members based on usage data. Writers and publishers join for the composition side; labels and performers have their own bodies for the recording side.

steps.title: Key bodies in India
steps.body:
- **IPRS** (Indian Performing Right Society) – registered copyright society for **authors, composers and publishers** of musical and literary works.
- **PPL India** (Phonographic Performance Ltd) – licenses public performance of **sound recordings** on behalf of record labels/owners.
- **ISAMRA** (Indian Singers' and Musicians' Rights Association) – for **performers' rights** of singers and musicians.

Internationally, examples include PRS for Music (UK) and ASCAP/BMI (US) for writers. Societies have reciprocal agreements so royalties can flow across borders.

steps.title: The 2012 amendment in India
steps.body: The **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 2012** strengthened lyricists' and composers' rights: authors of underlying works (such as lyrics and music in a film or sound recording) are entitled to an equal share of royalties for certain uses beyond the film in a cinema hall, and this right cannot be waived or assigned except to legal heirs or a copyright society. Check current rules with a qualified professional.

steps.title: Worked example: metadata that gets you paid
steps.body:
For each song, keep a sheet with:

- Title (and alternate titles)
- All writers with legal names, roles and **% splits** (adding to 100%)
- Publisher (if any)
- **ISRC** (identifies a recording) and **ISWC** (identifies a musical work), where assigned
- Performers on the recording
- Release date and distributor

Missing or mismatched data is a major reason royalties go unpaid.

steps.title: Closing note
steps.body: Rules, rates and society procedures change. Read each society's current membership rules, and consult a music lawyer or accountant before signing anything important. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Match each organisation or code to what it represents.

quiz.q: A lyricist in India would typically join…
quiz.why: IPRS, the Indian Performing Right Society, represents authors, composers and publishers. A lyricist would join IPRS. PPL India covers sound recordings.

quiz.q: An ISRC identifies…
quiz.why: An ISRC identifies a specific sound recording. A musical work has an ISWC.

quiz.q: Why do royalties often go unpaid?
options: Missing or mismatched metadata and registrations
quiz.why: Royalties often go unpaid because of missing or mismatched metadata and registrations. Societies pay out based on correct data.

quiz.q: The 2012 amendment in India strengthened the rights of…
options: Lyricists and composers of underlying works
quiz.why: The 2012 amendment to India's Copyright Act strengthened the royalty rights of lyricists and composers of the underlying works.

lessons.title: Contracts: what to read before you sign

scenes.text: Sanya, 21, a singer from Chandigarh, is offered a deal by a small label: “It's standard — just sign today.”
Her aunt, a lawyer, reads it: all rights forever, worldwide, all future songs, and recoupable costs with no cap.
Sanya asks for changes: a fixed term, limited territory, rights reverting if unreleased, and clear royalty splits.
The label agrees to some changes. Sanya signs a fairer deal — and learns never to sign under pressure.

steps.title: Key terms to find in any music contract
steps.body:
- **Rights granted**: which rights (composition? master? name and likeness?) — assignment (ownership transfer) or licence (permission)?
- **Term**: how long? **Territory**: where?
- **Exclusivity**: can you work with others?
- **Royalties/splits**: percentages, on what (gross or net?), how often paid, statements and audit rights.
- **Advances and recoupment**: is the advance recovered from your royalties? Which costs are recoupable?
- **Reversion**: do rights come back if the work isn't released or after a period?
- **Termination**: how can either side exit?

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body:
- Pressure to sign immediately.
- 'All rights, worldwide, in perpetuity' for little or no payment.
- Rights to **all future works** with no end date.
- No statements or audit rights.
- Uncapped recoupable expenses.
- Vague terms like 'reasonable share'.

steps.title: Work-for-hire and session work
steps.body: Session musicians are often paid a **one-time fee** for recording, with no ongoing royalty from the master. That's normal — but agree it in writing, including credit, and check whether performers' rights or other entitlements apply in your country.

steps.title: Closing note
steps.body: Get independent advice from a music lawyer before signing significant agreements. Keep copies of everything, and get changes in writing. This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: A producer offers to record your song free — but the contract gives them 50% of the composition and full master ownership, forever.

choices.label: Sign quickly — free recording is a great deal
choices.feedback: Free studio time can cost you a lot over the song's lifetime.

choices.label: Ask to discuss terms and take the contract to a lawyer
choices.feedback: Smart — never sign under pressure.

b.text: The song becomes popular. You realise you've given away half your writing share forever.

choices.label: Learn from it and get advice before every future deal
choices.feedback: Painful, but valuable.

c.text: Your lawyer suggests: producer gets a producer royalty on the master, no composition share unless they actually co-wrote, a fixed term and a reversion clause.

choices.label: Propose these changes politely
choices.feedback: Fair, standard-minded counter-offer.

choices.label: Walk away immediately without discussing
choices.feedback: Sometimes right, but negotiation often works.

end1.text: The producer accepts most changes. Clear, fair terms protect the relationship too.

end2.text: Many artists learn this the hard way. Read, ask, and get advice before signing.

end3.text: You keep your rights, but lose a possible collaboration. Next time, try a counter-offer first.

quiz.q: 'Recoupment' means…
options: Recovering an advance or costs from your royalties
quiz.why: Recoupment means the label recovers an advance or costs from your royalties before you are paid more.

quiz.q: A reversion clause…
options: Returns rights to you under certain conditions
quiz.why: A reversion clause returns rights to you under certain conditions, such as the work not being released. It protects the artist.

quiz.q: Which is a red flag?
options: Rights to all your future works forever
quiz.why: A grant of rights to all your future works forever is overbroad and unlimited, so it is a red flag. Clear percentages, fixed terms and audit rights are good.

quiz.q: Before signing a major deal you should…
options: Sign fast to keep the offer
quiz.why: Before signing a major deal, get independent legal advice. Signing fast or ignoring the small print can cost you your rights.

lessons.title: Building a sustainable music career

scenes.text: Maya, 34, a keyboardist in Bengaluru, used to rely only on wedding gigs — and had nothing during the off-season.
She builds five income streams: live gigs, online teaching, session work, a small music library catalogue, and corporate workshops.
She tracks income monthly and invests in her skills each quarter.
Now she earns steadily all year and has time to write her own album.

steps.title: Common income streams
steps.body:
- **Live performance**: concerts, weddings, corporate events, cafés.
- **Teaching**: private, school, online.
- **Session work**: recording for artists, films, ads.
- **Composition**: songs, jingles, film/TV/game scores, production music libraries.
- **Royalties**: from your registered works and recordings.
- **Content and community**: videos, memberships, merchandise.

Most working musicians combine several.

steps.title: Professional habits
steps.body:
- Be **on time, prepared and easy to work with** — reputation drives referrals.
- Keep a simple **EPK** (electronic press kit): bio, photos, best 3 recordings/videos, contact details.
- Use **written agreements** for gigs: date, times, fee, advance, sound requirements, cancellation terms.
- Keep accounts, receipts and invoices; consult a tax professional about your obligations.

steps.title: Worked example: pricing a gig
steps.body:
Fee should cover: rehearsal time + travel + performance + equipment wear + your skill level.

If you need ₹30,000/month from gigs and play 6 gigs, each must average ₹5,000 **after** costs. If travel and gear cost ₹800 per gig, quote at least ₹5,800.

steps.title: Look after yourself
steps.body: Irregular income, late nights and rejection are stressful. Protect your hearing (earplugs at loud gigs), your voice and your body. If stress, anxiety or low mood persist, speak to someone you trust or a professional — in India, **Tele-MANAS: 14416**.

activity.prompt: List your current music income streams and two new ones you could add in the next six months. What first step will you take this week?
activity.hint: Example: 'Current: weekend café gigs. New: online beginner guitar lessons; registering my 6 songs with a collecting society. This week: make a one-page lesson plan and gather my song metadata.'

quiz.q: Why do many musicians combine several income streams?
options: To smooth irregular income and reduce risk
quiz.why: Combining several income streams smooths irregular earnings and reduces risk. Relying on one source is fragile.

quiz.q: An EPK is…
options: An electronic press kit for promoters and media
quiz.why: An EPK is an electronic press kit, a professional pack for promoters and media with bio, music and photos.

quiz.q: You need ₹5,000 net per gig and costs are ₹800. Minimum quote?
quiz.why: You need ₹5,000 net plus ₹800 costs, so the minimum quote is ₹5,000 + ₹800 = ₹5,800.

quiz.q: Which number is India's Tele-MANAS mental-health helpline?
quiz.why: Tele-MANAS is India's mental-health helpline at 14416. 112 is for emergencies, 100 is police and 1098 is child help.

questions.q: The 'master' is…
questions.why: The master is the sound recording, which carries its own copyright separate from the composition (melody and lyrics).

questions.q: Sync fees come from…
questions.why: Sync fees are paid when music is used with visuals, such as films, ads and videos. Gigs and teaching bring other income.

questions.q: IPRS represents…
questions.why: IPRS represents authors, composers and publishers, so it is a writers' society. Record labels and venues are not its members in that role.

questions.q: PPL India licenses…
questions.why: PPL India licenses sound recordings, the recording side of music rights. It doesn't license lyrics, instruments or sheet music.

questions.q: Performance royalties arise when music is…
questions.why: Performance royalties arise when music is publicly performed or communicated, such as on radio or at venues. Practice at home does not generate them.

questions.q: Copyright term for sound recordings in India is…
options: 60 years from the year after publication
questions.why: In India, sound recordings are protected for 60 years from the year after publication. Life plus 60 applies to musical works.

questions.q: An ISWC identifies…
questions.why: An ISWC identifies a musical work, the composition. A recording is identified by an ISRC.

questions.q: Which is a contract red flag?
options: 'All rights, worldwide, forever' with no payment
questions.why: 'All rights, worldwide, forever' with no payment is an overbroad grant and a red flag. Audit rights, fixed terms and reversion clauses protect you.

questions.q: Session musicians are commonly paid…
options: A one-time fee agreed in writing
questions.why: Session musicians are commonly paid a one-time fee agreed in writing. They usually don't get composition royalties or label shares.

questions.q: Sync licensing a released song usually requires permission from…
questions.why: Syncing a released song needs permission from both the composition owner and the master owner, because there are two copyrights.

questions.q: Royalties often go unpaid because of…
options: Wrong or missing metadata and registrations
questions.why: Royalties often go unpaid because of wrong or missing metadata and registrations. Societies can't pay what they cannot match.

questions.q: Under India's 2012 amendment, lyricists' and composers' royalty rights for certain uses…
options: Cannot be waived or assigned except to legal heirs or a copyright society
questions.why: Under India's 2012 amendment, certain royalty rights of lyricists and composers cannot be waived or assigned, except to legal heirs or a copyright society. This protects authors.

questions.q: Best first step before signing a label deal?
options: Ask the label to explain only
Get independent legal advice and negotiate key terms
questions.why: Get independent legal advice and negotiate key terms before signing. Asking the label alone to explain may favour the label.

arts-music.title: Music: sing and play
arts-music.description: Singing from breath to stage, Hindustani swaras, alankars and taal, western notes, rhythm and scales, and starter paths for guitar, keyboard, tabla and bansuri.

courses.title: Singing basics: breath, pitch and a healthy voice
courses.summary: Learn how the voice works, breathe for singing, match pitch, find your range, warm up, look after your voice and sing a song with confidence.
outcomes: Learners can use low, relaxed breathing to support sound
Learners can match pitch and recognise when they are sharp or flat
Learners can do a safe 10-minute vocal warm-up
Learners know voice-care habits and when to see a doctor
Learners can prepare and perform one song

lessons.title: How your voice works and breathing for singing

scenes.text: Aarav, 15, from Indore, wants to sing at the school annual day. In every long line, he runs out of breath and his voice cracks.
His music teacher, Mrs. D'Souza, puts his hand on his belly: “Breathe so that this moves, not your shoulders.”
They practise a slow 'sss' exhale, counting how long he can keep it steady.
Three weeks later he sings the whole verse in two breaths, steady and calm.

steps.title: The voice in three parts
steps.body:
Your voice works like an instrument with three parts:

- **Power** – air from the lungs, controlled by breathing muscles (including the diaphragm and the muscles of the ribs and belly).
- **Source** – the **vocal folds** (vocal cords) in the larynx (voice box) vibrate as air passes, making sound.
- **Resonance** – the throat, mouth and nasal spaces shape and amplify that sound into vowels and tone.

Pitch changes mainly by changing the **length and tension** of the vocal folds.

steps.title: Low, relaxed breathing
steps.body:
- Stand tall, knees soft, shoulders relaxed.
- Breathe in through the nose or mouth so that the **belly and lower ribs expand** — shoulders stay still.
- Breathe out slowly, keeping the ribs gently open for as long as is comfortable.

This gives a **steady** airflow — the base of good tone. 'Support' means managing the outflow steadily, not pushing hard.

steps.title: Worked example: the 'sss' test
steps.body:
1. Breathe in low for 4 counts.
2. Breathe out on a steady 'sss' (like a slow tyre leak), counting seconds.
3. Aim for an even, quiet hiss — no bursts.

If you manage 10–15 seconds now, practise daily; many people gradually reach 20–30 seconds. The goal is **steadiness**, not a record.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lifting the shoulders on the in-breath (creates neck tension).
- Pushing air hard to sing louder — this strains the voice.
- Holding the breath before singing; flow straight from breath into sound.
- Taking breaths in the middle of words. Mark breath spots (✓) in your lyrics at phrase ends.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do the breathing activity below for 4 rounds. Then sing 'Sa' (or 'ah') on one comfortable note for as long as the breath is steady. Open the sound-waves lab to see how a steady tone looks.

activity.label: Singer's breath: in low for 4, hold 2, steady 'sss' out for 8, rest 2

quiz.q: Which part of the voice actually vibrates to make sound?
quiz.why: The vocal folds, two small bands of tissue in the larynx, vibrate to make sound. The tongue, teeth and lungs shape or power it but don't vibrate to make the voice.

quiz.q: When you breathe in for singing, what should expand?
quiz.why: Breathe low so the belly and lower ribs expand, which keeps the neck and shoulders free. Raising shoulders creates tension.

quiz.q: 'Support' in singing means…
options: Managing a steady outflow of air
quiz.why: Support means managing a steady, controlled outflow of air. Pushing hard or holding the breath strains the voice.

quiz.q: Where should breath marks usually go?
quiz.why: Breath marks go at phrase ends, the natural breaks in the music and words. Breathing in the middle of a word breaks meaning.

quiz.q: Pitch changes mainly by…
quiz.why: Pitch changes mainly because the vocal folds change length and tension. Mouth size and head position don't set pitch.

lessons.title: Pitch: matching notes and singing in tune

scenes.text: Dhruv, 11, in Patna, was told he is 'tone-deaf' and should not sing.
A new teacher, Mr. Okafor, plays one note on a keyboard and asks Dhruv to hum it, then slide up and down until it 'locks'.
With a tuner app, Dhruv sees when he's flat (too low) or sharp (too high) and adjusts.
A month later, he sings 'Happy Birthday' in tune at his sister's party. He was never tone-deaf — just untrained.

steps.title: Pitch is frequency
steps.body: A note's **pitch** is how fast the sound wave vibrates — its **frequency**, measured in **hertz (Hz)**. Higher frequency = higher pitch. The note **A above middle C is commonly tuned to 440 Hz**. Going up one **octave doubles** the frequency (A = 880 Hz is one octave higher). Open the sound-waves lab to see and hear this.

steps.title: Matching pitch
steps.body:
1. Listen to the note; imagine it in your head first.
2. Hum it aloud. Is your note **lower** (flat) or **higher** (sharp)?
3. **Slide** slowly towards the note until the two sounds blend.
4. Then sing it on 'ah' or 'Sa'.

When two notes are close but not equal you may hear a slow 'wah-wah' wobble (called **beating**). It slows down and disappears as you get in tune — a great guide.

steps.title: Is anyone truly tone-deaf?
steps.body: True congenital amusia (a lifelong difficulty perceiving pitch) is **uncommon**. Most people who sing out of tune can improve with practice in listening, matching and feedback. Children especially improve quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Singing louder to find the note — volume doesn't fix pitch.
- Starting too high or low for your voice; pick a comfortable key.
- Not listening to the accompaniment. Singing in tune is 50% listening.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use a free tuner app or the lab. Sing 5 different notes and hold each for 3 seconds, watching the needle. Then sing a 5-note scale (Sa Re Ga Ma Pa or do re mi fa so) up and down slowly.

statements.s: Higher frequency means higher pitch.
statements.why: Pitch rises as vibrations per second increase.

statements.s: Going up one octave doubles the frequency.
statements.why: A 440 Hz → A 880 Hz.

statements.s: Singing louder helps you find the right note.
statements.why: Volume and pitch are different; listen and slide instead.

statements.s: Most people who sing out of tune can improve with practice.
statements.why: True amusia is uncommon; pitch matching is a learnable skill.

statements.s: 'Flat' means your note is higher than the target.
statements.why: Flat = too low; sharp = too high.

quiz.q: A common tuning reference for A above middle C is…
quiz.why: A above middle C (A4) is usually tuned to 440 Hz, which is the standard concert pitch.

quiz.q: Your note is lower than the target. You are…
quiz.why: If your note is lower than the target, you are flat. Sharp is too high.

quiz.q: What 'wobble' helps you tune?
quiz.why: Beating is the slow wobble between two close notes. It slows down and stops as the pitches match, so it helps you tune.

quiz.q: A note an octave above 220 Hz is…
quiz.why: An octave above doubles the frequency, so 220 Hz × 2 = 440 Hz.

quiz.q: Best first step to match a note is…
options: Listen, hum softly, slide until it locks
quiz.why: The best first step is to listen, hum softly and slide until your pitch locks with the target. Guessing or shouting does not help.

lessons.title: Range, warm-ups and voice care

scenes.text: Grace, 40, leads a church choir in Shillong. Before Christmas, half the choir loses their voice from shouting and over-practising.
An ENT doctor tells her: rest, water, no forced whispering, no harsh throat-clearing, and gentle warm-ups — not long, loud rehearsals.
Grace plans shorter rehearsals with a 10-minute warm-up and water breaks.
On Christmas Eve, every voice is healthy and the choir sounds its best ever.

steps.title: Your range and voice type
steps.body: Your **range** is the span from your lowest to highest comfortable note. Common choir voice types, from high to low: **soprano, alto, tenor, bass**, with in-between types like mezzo-soprano and baritone. Range grows with healthy practice, but don't force notes that hurt.

steps.title: A 10-minute vocal warm-up
steps.body:
- **1 min** – body: shoulder rolls, neck stretches, jaw massage, yawn-sigh.
- **2 min** – breath: 'sss' exhales, then 'sh-sh-sh' pulses.
- **2 min** – lip trills (brrr) or humming on slides, low to high and back.
- **2 min** – 5-note scales on 'ma-me-mi-mo-mu', moving up by half steps.
- **2 min** – arpeggios (Sa Ga Pa Sa' or do mi so do') on 'ah'.
- **1 min** – a few lines of your song, softly.

steps.title: Voice-care habits
steps.body:
- Drink water through the day; steam inhalation can soothe.
- Avoid **shouting** and long periods of speaking over noise.
- Avoid habitual **throat-clearing**; swallow or sip water instead.
- Forced **whispering** can strain the voice; when resting it, speak gently or stay quiet.
- Sleep well; smoking and acid reflux can irritate the voice.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See an **ENT doctor** (ideally a laryngologist or voice clinic) if hoarseness lasts more than **two weeks**, if singing hurts, if you lose range suddenly, or if you cough blood. Singers can develop problems like nodules from strain — early care helps. This is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find your range: with a tuner app or keyboard, slide down to your lowest comfortable note and up to your highest comfortable note. Write them down. Re-test every month.

activity.prompt: My daily voice-care routine
items: Did not clear my throat harshly

quiz.q: Hoarseness lasting more than about two weeks should be…
quiz.why: Hoarseness lasting more than about two weeks should be checked by an ENT doctor. Whispering or singing louder can strain the voice more.

quiz.q: Which is a good warm-up exercise?
quiz.why: Lip trills gently balance breath and voice, so they warm up the voice safely. Starting on your highest note, screaming or coughing strains cold vocal folds.

quiz.q: Instead of throat-clearing, try…
quiz.why: Throat-clearing slams the vocal folds together. Swallowing or sipping water clears mucus more gently, while shouting or coughing harder adds strain.

quiz.q: Which voice type is usually the lowest?
quiz.why: Bass is the lowest common voice type in a choir. Tenor, alto and soprano are progressively higher.

sources: General voice-care guidance from ENT/voice clinicians

lessons.title: Singing a song: diction, expression and stage nerves

scenes.text: Fatima, 21, in Hyderabad, signs up for a café open mic. Her hands shake just thinking about it.
She prepares one song carefully: marks breaths, practises tricky words, decides the feeling of each verse.
Before going on, she does slow breathing and reminds herself: nerves are energy.
She sings. A few notes wobble, but the room claps warmly. She signs up for next month.

steps.title: Diction: clear words
steps.body:
- **Vowels carry the tone** — sustain the vowel, put consonants quickly at the edges.
- Final consonants (t, d, k) need a tiny bit of extra crispness so the audience understands.
- In Hindi/Urdu songs, take care with sounds like **ड़, ज़, ख़** and nasal vowels. Speak the lyrics slowly as a poem before singing.

steps.title: Plan the expression
steps.body:
Write the song's story in one sentence. Then for each section note:

- **Feeling** (longing, joy, anger…)
- **Dynamics** (soft p, medium mf, loud f)
- **Where the climax is**

Example: verse 1 – gentle, remembering (p); chorus – hopeful (mf); last chorus – full, joyful (f), then a soft final line.

steps.title: Handling stage nerves
steps.body:
- Nerves are normal — your body is preparing to perform.
- **Prepare thoroughly**: know the song so well that nerves can't knock it out.
- Breathe slowly (long exhales calm the body).
- Pick a few friendly faces or look slightly above the audience.
- If you make a mistake, **keep going** — audiences rarely notice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Picking a song in a key that's too high when nervous — choose a comfortable key.
- Holding the mic too far away or covering the grille; keep it a few centimetres from the mouth, pointing at you.
- Apologising before singing — just start.

a.text: At the open mic, you forget the second verse's first line. The guitarist is still playing.

choices.label: Hum or sing 'la' for a moment and come back in at the chorus
choices.feedback: Professional move — keep the music flowing.

choices.label: Stop and say sorry repeatedly
choices.feedback: Stopping makes the mistake bigger.

b.text: You rejoin at the chorus. The audience is smiling.

choices.label: Finish the song with full feeling
choices.feedback: Perfect — confidence is what people remember.

c.text: The guitarist looks at you, unsure. The room is quiet.

choices.label: Smile, ask to restart from the chorus, and sing
choices.feedback: A graceful recovery.

choices.label: Walk off stage
choices.feedback: It's okay — but next time, try to keep going.

end1.text: You turned a slip into a confident performance. Most of the audience never noticed.

end2.text: Restarting gracefully is fine. Practise 'recovery' at home: start from any section.

end3.text: Many great performers had shaky first shows. Practise performing for friends and try again next month.

quiz.q: Which part of the word mainly carries the singing tone?
quiz.why: Vowels carry the sustained singing tone, while consonants are quick sounds that shape the words. So you hold the vowel and keep the consonant short.

quiz.q: You forget a lyric on stage. Best action?
options: Keep the music going and rejoin
quiz.why: If you forget a lyric, keep the music going and rejoin when you can. Stopping or leaving breaks the performance, and the audience often won't notice.

quiz.q: A long, slow exhale before performing…
quiz.why: A long, slow exhale activates the body's calming response and slows the heart rate, so it helps with performance nerves.

quiz.q: Where should a handheld mic usually be?
options: A few centimetres from the mouth, pointed at you
quiz.why: Hold a handheld mic a few centimetres from your mouth, pointed at you. Covering the grille or holding it far away causes feedback or a weak sound.

questions.q: Vocal folds are located in the…
questions.why: The vocal folds sit in the larynx, or voice box, in the throat. They are not in the nose, stomach or lungs.

questions.q: Shoulders rising when you breathe in suggests…
questions.why: Rising shoulders when you breathe in suggest shallow, tense breathing from the upper chest. Good singing breath is low and relaxed, with the belly and lower ribs expanding.

questions.q: Flat means…
questions.why: Flat means lower than the target pitch. Sharp means higher.

questions.q: An octave up from 440 Hz is…
questions.why: An octave above a note doubles its frequency, so 440 Hz × 2 = 880 Hz.

questions.q: Lip trills are…
questions.why: Lip trills are a gentle warm-up that balance breath and vocal-fold vibration. They are safe for people of all ages.

questions.q: Which habit harms the voice?
questions.why: Frequent shouting strains the vocal folds and can make the voice hoarse. Warming up, resting and drinking water protect the voice.

questions.q: Hoarseness for 3 weeks: what next?
questions.why: Hoarseness lasting more than about two weeks should be checked by an ENT doctor. Three weeks is beyond that, so don't ignore it or strain the voice more.

questions.q: Which voice types are commonly higher?
questions.why: Soprano and alto are the higher choir voices. Tenor, baritone and bass are lower.

questions.q: The 'beating' sound between two close notes tells you…
options: They are slightly out of tune
questions.why: The beating between two close notes shows they are slightly out of tune. As the pitches match, the beating slows and stops.

questions.q: Why sustain vowels and keep consonants short?
options: It's a rule only for opera
Vowels carry tone; quick consonants keep words clear
questions.why: Vowels carry the singing tone, so you sustain them, and quick consonants keep the words clear. Good diction balances both.

questions.q: Someone says they are 'tone-deaf' after one bad attempt. Most accurate reply?
options: True amusia is uncommon; most people can improve pitch with practice
questions.why: True amusia, the real inability to perceive pitch, is uncommon. Most people can improve pitch matching with practice, so one bad attempt doesn't mean tone-deaf.

questions.q: Which breath plan suits a long phrase?
options: Breathe in the middle of words
Plan breaths at phrase ends and manage a steady outflow
Push all air out at once
questions.why: For a long phrase, plan your breaths at phrase ends and manage a steady outflow of air. Holding the breath or pushing all the air out at once makes it harder.

questions.q: Before a performance, the most reliable help for nerves is…
questions.why: Thorough preparation builds confidence, and slow breathing calms the body, so together they help nerves most reliably. Skipping practice or too much caffeine makes it worse.

courses.title: Hindustani music: swaras, alankars and taal
courses.summary: Learn the seven swaras, shuddha/komal/tivra notes, the three saptaks, essential alankars, the ten thaats and basic taals — the foundation of Hindustani singing and instruments.
outcomes: Learners can name and sing the seven swaras and their full names
Learners can identify komal and tivra swaras and the 12 notes
Learners can sing 6 basic alankars with a tanpura or drone
Learners can name the ten thaats and relate some to western scales
Learners can clap teentaal, dadra and keherwa

lessons.title: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni: the seven swaras

scenes.text: Pooja, 10, in Varanasi, starts lessons with Pandit-ji next door. He tunes a tanpura and asks her to sing 'Sa'.
Her Sa is a little low. He tells her: “Your Sa is your home — every other note is measured from it.”
They climb the 'ladder' Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa', slowly, one note per breath.
By the end of the month, she can sing the sargam up and down in tune with the tanpura.

steps.title: The seven swaras
steps.body:
Hindustani music uses seven main notes (**swaras**). Short names and full names:

- **Sa** – Shadja
- **Re** – Rishabh
- **Ga** – Gandhar
- **Ma** – Madhyam
- **Pa** – Pancham
- **Dha** – Dhaivat
- **Ni** – Nishad

Together they are the **sargam** (from Sa-Re-Ga-Ma).

steps.title: Sa is movable
steps.body: Unlike western fixed note names, **Sa can be any pitch** — the singer or instrumentalist chooses a comfortable Sa (for example on C, C♯, D…). All other notes are measured relative to Sa. **Sa and Pa are 'achal' (fixed)**: they have only one form. The tanpura usually plays Sa and Pa (or Ma/Ni in some ragas) as a constant drone.

steps.title: Three saptaks (octaves)
steps.body:
- **Mandra saptak** – lower octave (written with a dot **below**, e.g. Ṇ, Ḍ)
- **Madhya saptak** – middle octave (no dot)
- **Taar saptak** – upper octave (written with a dot **above**, e.g. Ṡ, or as Sa')

Taar Sa has double the frequency of madhya Sa.

steps.title: Worked example: Sa on C
steps.body:
If Sa = C on a harmonium/keyboard, the **shuddha** (natural) swaras fall on the white keys:

Sa = C, Re = D, Ga = E, Ma = F, Pa = G, Dha = A, Ni = B, Sa' = C (higher).

This is the same pattern as the western **major scale** — and as **Bilawal thaat**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a Sa that's too high, then straining in taar saptak. Pick a Sa where you can comfortably sing well below and above it.
- Singing Ga and Ni slightly flat — check with a tuner or drone.
- Rushing: hold each swara steady for a full breath before moving on.

activity.prompt: Match each swara to its full name.

quiz.q: Which two swaras are achal (never altered)?
quiz.why: Sa and Pa are achal swaras, which means fixed; they never have komal or tivra versions. The other swaras can be altered.

quiz.q: Taar saptak is the…
quiz.why: Taar saptak is the upper octave. Mandra is the lower and madhya is the middle octave.

quiz.q: If Sa = C, then Pa = …
quiz.why: If Sa is C, the swaras go Re D, Ga E, Ma F and Pa G. So Pa is G, a perfect fifth above Sa.

quiz.q: In Hindustani music, Sa is…
quiz.why: In Hindustani music, Sa is movable, so the performer picks the pitch that suits their voice. It is not fixed at C or 440 Hz.

quiz.q: The full name of Dha is…
quiz.why: The full name of the swara Dha is Dhaivat. Dhun, Dhrut and Dhrupad are other words.

lessons.title: Komal and tivra: the twelve swaras and ten thaats

scenes.text: Imran, 34, in Aligarh, plays harmonium by ear. His teacher says, “Raag Bhairavi uses komal swaras — find them.”
He discovers that the black keys between the white keys give the komal (flat) notes, and one gives tivra Ma.
His teacher shows him a chart of ten thaats — parent scales — and Imran recognises songs he already plays.
Suddenly he understands why some melodies feel bright and others feel serious or tender.

steps.title: Shuddha, komal and tivra
steps.body:
- **Shuddha** = natural.
- **Komal** = flat (lower by a semitone). Possible for **Re, Ga, Dha, Ni**.
- **Tivra** = sharp (higher by a semitone). Only for **Ma**.
- **Sa and Pa** have only one form.

So: 7 shuddha + 4 komal + 1 tivra = **12 swaras** in an octave (the same 12 semitones as western music). In Bhatkhande notation, komal is shown with a line below the note and tivra Ma with a vertical line above; in Roman shorthand many teachers write komal as small letters (r, g, d, n) and tivra Ma as capital M.

steps.title: With Sa = C
steps.body: Sa C · komal Re C♯ · Re D · komal Ga D♯ · Ga E · Ma F · tivra Ma F♯ · Pa G · komal Dha G♯ · Dha A · komal Ni A♯ · Ni B · Sa' C.

steps.title: The ten thaats (Bhatkhande system)
steps.body:
Pandit V. N. Bhatkhande classified ragas under **ten thaats** (parent scales of 7 notes):

- **Bilawal** – all shuddha (like the major scale)
- **Kalyan** – tivra Ma
- **Khamaj** – komal Ni
- **Kafi** – komal Ga, Ni
- **Asavari** – komal Ga, Dha, Ni
- **Bhairavi** – komal Re, Ga, Dha, Ni
- **Bhairav** – komal Re, Dha
- **Poorvi** – komal Re, Dha; tivra Ma
- **Marwa** – komal Re; tivra Ma
- **Todi** – komal Re, Ga, Dha; tivra Ma

steps.title: Bridges to western modes
steps.body: Some thaats share notes with western modes: Bilawal ≈ Ionian (major), Kalyan ≈ Lydian, Khamaj ≈ Mixolydian, Kafi ≈ Dorian, Asavari ≈ Aeolian (natural minor), Bhairavi ≈ Phrygian. A raga is much more than its scale, though — it also has characteristic phrases, emphasis and mood.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a thaat is the same as a raga. A thaat is a scale category; ragas live inside them with their own rules.
- Mixing komal and shuddha versions of the same note carelessly — the mood changes completely.

activity.prompt: Sort the swaras: which forms can they take besides shuddha?

quiz.q: Tivra applies to which swara?
quiz.why: Only Ma has a tivra (sharp) form. Re, Ga, Dha and Ni have komal forms, and Sa and Pa are fixed.

quiz.q: How many swaras in total in an octave?
quiz.why: There are 12 swaras in an octave: 7 shuddha, 4 komal (Re, Ga, Dha, Ni) and 1 tivra (Ma). The 22 figure refers to shrutis instead.

quiz.q: Kalyan thaat is Bilawal with…
quiz.why: Kalyan thaat is Bilawal with tivra Ma, which is like the Lydian mode. Bilawal has all shuddha swaras.

quiz.q: Which thaat uses komal Re, Ga, Dha and Ni?
quiz.why: Bhairavi thaat uses komal Re, Ga, Dha and Ni, all four komal swaras. Kafi has only komal Ga and Ni.

quiz.q: Who classified ragas into ten thaats?
quiz.why: Pandit V. N. Bhatkhande classified ragas into ten thaats. Bharata wrote the Natyashastra, and Tansen was a court musician.

lessons.title: Alankars: daily exercises for voice and fingers

scenes.text: Riya, 17, in Ahmedabad, wants to sing film songs with clean taans (fast runs).
Her guru gives her a riyaz chart: six alankars, each at three speeds, with a tanpura app every morning.
She practises 20 minutes daily before school.
After two months her fast phrases are clear and in tune — and her friends notice at the college fest.

steps.title: What alankars are
steps.body: **Alankars** (also called *paltas*) are **patterns of swaras** sung or played up (aaroh) and down (avroh). They train pitch accuracy, voice agility, breath and memory — like scales and exercises in western music. Traditionally they are practised daily with a tanpura drone.

steps.title: Six essential alankars (shuddha swaras)
steps.body:
1. **Straight**: Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Dha Ni Sa' | Sa' Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa
2. **Pairs**: SaSa ReRe GaGa MaMa… (each note twice)
3. **Groups of 2**: SaRe ReGa GaMa MaPa PaDha DhaNi NiSa' | down: Sa'Ni NiDha DhaPa PaMa MaGa GaRe ReSa
4. **Groups of 3**: SaReGa ReGaMa GaMaPa MaPaDha PaDhaNi DhaNiSa' | down: Sa'NiDha NiDhaPa DhaPaMa PaMaGa MaGaRe GaReSa
5. **Groups of 4**: SaReGaMa ReGaMaPa GaMaPaDha… up to PaDhaNiSa'
6. **Skip pattern**: SaGa ReMa GaPa MaDha PaNi DhaSa' | down: Sa'Dha NiPa DhaMa PaGa MaRe GaSa

steps.title: Three speeds (laya)
steps.body:
- **Vilambit** – slow
- **Madhya** – medium
- **Drut** – fast

Practise each alankar first at one note per beat, then two notes per beat (**dugun**), then four (**chaugun**), using a metronome or tabla app. Only speed up when the slower speed is perfectly in tune.

steps.title: How to sing them well
steps.body:
- Use 'aa' (**akaar**) as well as sargam names — akaar trains a clean, open voice.
- Keep the volume even across notes.
- Record and listen back; check Ga and Ni especially.
- For instruments (harmonium, flute, sitar), play the same patterns for finger dexterity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Racing ahead to drut before vilambit is accurate.
- Letting the voice get breathy on high notes — reduce volume, keep support.
- Practising without a drone — you lose the sense of Sa.

activity.prompt: Complete the groups-of-3 alankar (aaroh).

quiz.q: Alankars mainly train…
quiz.why: Alankars are exercises that train pitch accuracy, agility and breath control. They are core technical practice, not only memory or rhythm.

quiz.q: Drut laya means…
quiz.why: Drut laya means fast tempo. Vilambit is slow, and madhya is medium.

quiz.q: In the skip pattern, after SaGa comes…
quiz.why: In the skip pattern, the pairs go SaGa, ReMa, GaPa and so on, each pair starting one note higher. After SaGa comes ReMa.

quiz.q: When should you increase speed?
options: Only when the slower speed is in tune and even
quiz.why: Increase speed only when the slower speed is in tune and even. Accuracy comes first, then speed.

quiz.q: Akaar means singing on…
quiz.why: Akaar means singing on the open 'aa' vowel. It is a good vowel for steady tone and relaxed jaw.

lessons.title: Taal basics: teentaal, dadra and keherwa

scenes.text: Anil, 63, a retired teacher in Nagpur, joins a bhajan group. He can sing but loses the beat.
The tabla player shows the 'clap and wave' (tali and khali) system for keherwa and dadra.
Anil counts 1 to 8 for keherwa and 1 to 6 for dadra, clapping on the right beats.
Now he always comes back in on sam with the group.

steps.title: What a taal is
steps.body:
A **taal** is a repeating rhythmic cycle of a fixed number of beats (**matras**), divided into sections (**vibhags**). Key words:

- **Sam** – beat 1, the strongest; marked **X**, shown with a clap.
- **Tali** – other clapped sections, marked 2, 3…
- **Khali** – 'empty' section, marked **0**, shown with a wave.
- **Theka** – the basic tabla bol pattern for the taal.
- **Laya** – tempo.

steps.title: Three common taals
steps.body:
- **Dadra** – 6 beats (3+3): Dha Dhi Na | Dha Ti Na. Clap on 1 (X), wave on 4 (0). Common in light classical and film songs.
- **Keherwa** – 8 beats (4+4): Dha Ge Na Ti | Na Ka Dhi Na. Clap on 1 (X), wave on 5 (0). Very common in bhajans, folk and film music.
- **Teentaal** – 16 beats (4+4+4+4): Dha Dhin Dhin Dha | Dha Dhin Dhin Dha | Dha Tin Tin Ta | Ta Dhin Dhin Dha. Claps on 1 (X), 5 (2), 13 (3); wave on 9 (0).

Bol spellings vary slightly between teachers.

steps.title: Clap-and-count practice
steps.body: Say the beat numbers aloud while showing the hand signs. For keherwa: **clap** 2 3 4 **wave** 6 7 8. For dadra: **clap** 2 3 **wave** 5 6. Then recite the theka bols while doing the hand signs. Try the rhythm game to test your steadiness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clapping on khali — it's a wave, to show the 'empty' part.
- Losing sam during long phrases. Keep a silent count or watch the tabla player.
- Confusing number of beats with tempo; a taal can be slow or fast.

activity.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

quiz.q: Keherwa has how many beats?
quiz.why: Keherwa has 8 beats, in two groups of four. It is a common light-music taal.

quiz.q: Khali in dadra falls on beat…
quiz.why: Dadra has 6 beats in two groups of 3, and khali falls on beat 4, where the wave is shown. Sam is beat 1.

quiz.q: Sam is marked…
quiz.why: Sam, the first beat of the cycle, is marked X. Khali is marked 0.

quiz.q: The basic tabla bol pattern of a taal is the…
quiz.why: The theka is the basic tabla bol pattern that defines a taal. A thaat is a scale classification, and a tihai is a thrice-repeated phrase.

questions.q: The first swara is…
questions.why: Sa, short for Shadja, is the first swara. It's the tonic and the reference for all other notes.

questions.q: Komal means…
questions.why: Komal means flat, a semitone lower than the shuddha swara. It is not about speed or loudness.

questions.q: Teentaal has…
questions.why: Teentaal has 16 beats, grouped 4+4+4+4. Keherwa has 8 and dadra has 6.

questions.q: Which swaras can be komal?
questions.why: Only Re, Ga, Dha and Ni can be komal. Sa and Pa are fixed, and Ma can be tivra instead.

questions.q: If Sa = C, komal Ga is…
questions.why: If Sa is C, shuddha Ga is E, so komal Ga is a semitone lower: E♭ (also written D♯).

questions.q: Mandra saptak notes are written with…
questions.why: Notes in mandra saptak, the lower octave, are written with a dot below. Taar saptak notes have a dot above.

questions.q: Which thaat matches the western major scale's notes?
questions.why: Bilawal thaat uses all shuddha swaras, so it matches the western major scale. Kafi, Todi and Bhairavi have komal notes.

questions.q: Khamaj thaat has…
questions.why: Khamaj thaat has komal Ni with the other swaras shuddha, so it matches the Mixolydian mode.

questions.q: Keherwa khali is on beat…
questions.why: Keherwa has 8 beats in two groups of four (4+4), and the khali is on beat 5, the start of the second group.

questions.q: Which statement about thaat and raga is correct?
options: A thaat is a parent scale; a raga has its own phrases and rules
questions.why: A thaat is a parent scale used to classify ragas, and a raga has its own phrases and rules. They are not the same, and thaats are not rhythms.

questions.q: Todi thaat contains…
options: Komal Re and tivra Ma only
Komal Re, Ga, Dha and tivra Ma
questions.why: Todi thaat has komal Re, Ga and Dha and tivra Ma, written r g M d. Its other swaras are shuddha.

questions.q: The groups-of-2 alankar descending starts…
questions.why: The descending groups-of-2 alankar starts from the upper Sa: Sa'Ni NiDha DhaPa and so on, each pair stepping one note down.

questions.q: Kafi thaat is closest to which western mode?
questions.why: Kafi thaat has komal Ga and komal Ni, which matches the Dorian mode in Western music. Lydian has a raised 4th instead.

courses.title: Western music basics: notes, rhythm, scales and chords
courses.summary: Read notes on the staff, count rhythms, build major and minor scales from their formulas, understand intervals and key signatures, and build the main chords of any key.
outcomes: Learners can name notes on treble and bass clef
Learners can count note values and rests in 4/4, 3/4 and 6/8
Learners can build any major scale with W-W-H-W-W-W-H
Learners can build natural and harmonic minor scales
Learners can name intervals and build I, IV and V chords

lessons.title: Notes on the keyboard and the staff

scenes.text: Sofia, 12, in Goa, gets a piano book from her grandmother. The black dots on five lines look like a secret code.
Her teacher, Mr. Fernandes, shows her the keyboard pattern: groups of two and three black keys. C is just left of the two black keys.
Then he teaches two sentences to remember the treble-clef lines and spaces.
By the weekend, Sofia plays 'Ode to Joy' from the page.

steps.title: The musical alphabet
steps.body:
Western music uses seven letter names: **A B C D E F G**, then it repeats. Between most neighbouring letters is a black key (**sharp ♯** or **flat ♭**), except between **E–F** and **B–C**, which are only a **half step (semitone)** apart.

On a keyboard, **C** is the white key immediately to the left of each group of **two black keys**. The C nearest the middle of a piano is **middle C**.

steps.title: The staff and clefs
steps.body:
Music is written on a **staff** of 5 lines and 4 spaces. Higher on the staff = higher pitch.

- **Treble clef** (G clef) – for higher notes (piano right hand, voice, flute, violin, guitar*). Lines bottom to top: **E G B D F** ('Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit'); spaces: **F A C E**.
- **Bass clef** (F clef) – for lower notes (piano left hand, cello, bass). Lines: **G B D F A** ('Good Boys Do Fine Always'); spaces: **A C E G** ('All Cows Eat Grass').
- **Middle C** sits on a small **ledger line** just below the treble staff, or just above the bass staff.

*Guitar music is written in treble clef but sounds an octave lower.

steps.title: Worked example: reading a phrase
steps.body:
A treble-clef melody has notes on: bottom line, second space, third line, third line.

- Bottom line = **E**
- Second space = **A**
- Third line = **B**

So the melody is **E – A – B – B**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading bass clef with treble-clef names (everything comes out wrong).
- Forgetting that E–F and B–C have no black key between them.
- Counting lines from the top. Always count from the **bottom** line.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write the treble-clef lines and spaces on a card. Each day, read 10 random notes in under 30 seconds. Then do the same for bass clef.

cards.back: E G B D F — Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit
G B D F A — Good Boys Do Fine Always
A C E G — All Cows Eat Grass

cards.front: Where is C on a keyboard?
cards.back: The white key just left of a group of two black keys.

cards.front: Which letter pairs are a half step apart with no black key between?

quiz.q: What is the treble clef's bottom line?
quiz.why: The treble clef's lines from the bottom are E G B D F, so the bottom line is E.

quiz.q: Which pair has no black key between them?
quiz.why: E and F (and B and C) have no black key between them because they are only a semitone apart. The other neighbouring white keys have a black key between them.

quiz.q: Bass clef spaces spell…
quiz.why: Bass clef spaces from the bottom spell A C E G, remembered as 'All Cows Eat Grass'. FACE is for treble spaces.

quiz.q: Middle C in treble clef sits…
options: On a ledger line below the staff
quiz.why: Middle C in treble clef sits on a ledger line below the staff. It is the first note below the bottom line E.

quiz.q: Higher position on the staff means…
quiz.why: Higher position on the staff means higher pitch. Loudness, speed and length are shown by other symbols.

lessons.title: Rhythm: beats, note values and time signatures

scenes.text: Kwame, 14, a Ghanaian-Indian drummer in Bengaluru, can groove but can't read rhythms.
His teacher sets a metronome at 60 BPM — one click per second — and has him clap whole, half, quarter and eighth notes.
Kwame realises rhythm notation is just maths: fractions of a bar.
He reads and plays his first written drum groove the next day.

steps.title: Note values (in 4/4)
steps.body:
- **Whole note** (semibreve) = 4 beats
- **Half note** (minim) = 2 beats
- **Quarter note** (crotchet) = 1 beat
- **Eighth note** (quaver) = ½ beat
- **Sixteenth note** (semiquaver) = ¼ beat

Each has a matching **rest** (silence) of the same length. A **dot** after a note adds **half its value**: a dotted half note = 2 + 1 = **3 beats**.

steps.title: Time signatures
steps.body:
The two numbers at the start of music:

- **Top** = how many beats per bar.
- **Bottom** = which note value gets one beat (4 = quarter note, 8 = eighth note).

Examples: **4/4** (common time, 4 quarter-note beats), **3/4** (waltz, 3 beats), **6/8** (six eighth notes grouped in two sets of three — feels like 2 big beats).

steps.title: Worked example: does this bar add up?
steps.body:
In 4/4, a bar has: half note + quarter note + two eighth notes.

2 + 1 + ½ + ½ = **4 beats** ✓

In 3/4: dotted half note = 3 beats ✓ (fills the bar).

steps.title: Counting aloud
steps.body: Count quarter notes '1 2 3 4'. Eighth notes: '1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &'. Sixteenths: '1 e & a 2 e & a…'. Always count with a metronome at a slow tempo first. The rhythm game is a fun way to test yourself.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cutting long notes short (holding a half note for only 1 beat).
- Ignoring rests — silence is part of the rhythm.
- Speeding up on easy bars. Use a metronome.

activity.prompt: In 4/4 time, add up: one dotted half note + one quarter note + two eighth notes. How many beats is that? (Does it fit in one bar?)

quiz.q: A dotted half note lasts…
quiz.why: A dot adds half the note's value. A half note is 2 beats, so the dotted half note is 2 + 1 = 3 beats.

quiz.q: In 3/4, how many quarter-note beats per bar?
quiz.why: In 3/4 the top number is 3, so there are three beats per bar, and the bottom 4 means they are quarter notes.

quiz.q: Eighth notes are counted…
quiz.why: Eighth notes divide the beat into two, so they are counted '1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &'. Each '&' is the second eighth of the beat.

quiz.q: A metronome at 60 BPM clicks…
quiz.why: 60 BPM means 60 beats per minute, which is one beat per second.

quiz.q: 6/8 usually feels like…
options: 2 big beats of 3 eighth notes each
quiz.why: 6/8 usually feels like two big beats, each made of three eighth notes. It is not six slow beats.

lessons.title: Major and minor scales from formulas

scenes.text: Tara, 19, studies music in Mumbai and keeps getting confused by key signatures.
Her lecturer, Dr. Menon, writes one formula on the board: W W H W W W H.
Starting from any note, Tara builds G major, D major and F major on paper — and finds the sharps and flats appear by themselves.
Key signatures stop being magic and become logic.

steps.title: Whole and half steps
steps.body:
- **Half step (semitone, H)** = the very next key on the keyboard (white or black).
- **Whole step (tone, W)** = two half steps.

The **major scale formula** is: **W W H W W W H**.

steps.title: Worked example: G major
steps.body:
Start on G and apply W W H W W W H:

G → (W) A → (W) B → (H) C → (W) D → (W) E → (W) **F♯** → (H) G

So G major = **G A B C D E F♯ G** — one sharp (F♯), which is G major's key signature. Each letter appears once.

steps.title: Worked example: F major
steps.body:
F → (W) G → (W) A → (H) **B♭** → (W) C → (W) D → (W) E → (H) F

F major = **F G A B♭ C D E F** — one flat. We write **B♭**, not A♯, because each letter must appear exactly once.

steps.title: Minor scales
steps.body:
- **Natural minor** formula: **W H W W H W W**. A natural minor = A B C D E F G A (all white keys). It shares its key signature with **C major** — A minor is C's **relative minor** (it starts on the 6th note of the major scale).
- **Harmonic minor**: natural minor with a **raised 7th** — A B C D E F G♯ A. This creates a strong pull back to the tonic.
- **Melodic minor** (classical): raised 6th and 7th going up (A B C D E F♯ G♯ A), natural minor coming down.

steps.title: The circle of fifths
steps.body:
Going up a **perfect fifth** each time adds one sharp: C (0) → G (1♯) → D (2♯) → A (3♯) → E (4♯) → B (5♯)…
Going down a fifth adds one flat: C → F (1♭) → B♭ (2♭) → E♭ (3♭) → A♭ (4♭)…
Order of sharps: **F C G D A E B**. Order of flats: **B E A D G C F**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping or repeating a letter (writing A♯ instead of B♭ in F major).
- Forgetting the half steps fall between notes 3–4 and 7–8 in major.
- Thinking minor always means 'sad'. Mood depends on tempo, rhythm and style too.

activity.prompt: Build D major using W W H W W W H. Fill in the two sharp notes (type F# or F♯).
activity.text: D  E  ___  G  A  B  ___  D

quiz.q: The major scale formula is…
options: W W W H W W H
W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
H W W H W W W
quiz.why: The major scale pattern is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H). This puts half steps between notes 3–4 and 7–8.

quiz.q: How many sharps does G major have?
quiz.why: G major has one sharp, F♯. The scale is G A B C D E F♯ G.

quiz.q: The relative minor of C major is…
quiz.why: The relative minor starts on the 6th note of the major scale. In C major, the 6th note is A, so the relative minor is A minor.

quiz.q: Harmonic minor raises which degree?
quiz.why: Harmonic minor is natural minor with a raised 7th degree. This creates a leading tone for a stronger resolution.

quiz.q: In F major we write B♭, not A♯, because…
options: Each letter name must appear once
quiz.why: A scale uses each letter name once, so F major's fourth note is written B♭, not A♯. A♯ would repeat the letter A and skip B.

lessons.title: Intervals and the chords that play a thousand songs

scenes.text: Jordan, 28, an Australian working in Gurugram, wants to accompany friends' singing on guitar.
His colleague Simran shows him that many songs use just three chords: I, IV and V.
In G major these are G, C and D. Jordan learns them and suddenly plays dozens of songs.
At the office picnic, everyone sings along.

steps.title: Intervals
steps.body:
An **interval** is the distance between two notes. Count it in semitones:

- Minor 2nd = 1 · Major 2nd = 2
- Minor 3rd = 3 · Major 3rd = 4
- Perfect 4th = 5 · Tritone = 6
- Perfect 5th = 7 · Minor 6th = 8 · Major 6th = 9
- Minor 7th = 10 · Major 7th = 11 · Octave = 12

The interval *number* counts letter names including both ends: C to E is a 3rd (C-D-E).

steps.title: Triads
steps.body:
A **triad** is three notes stacked in thirds: **root, third, fifth**.

- **Major** = root + major 3rd (4) + perfect 5th (7). C major = C E G.
- **Minor** = root + minor 3rd (3) + perfect 5th (7). A minor = A C E.
- **Diminished** = root + minor 3rd (3) + diminished 5th (6). B dim = B D F.

steps.title: I, IV and V in any key
steps.body:
Number the notes of the major scale 1–7. Build a triad on 1, 4 and 5:

- **C major**: I = C, IV = F, V = G
- **G major**: I = G, IV = C, V = D
- **D major**: I = D, IV = G, V = A

Add **vi** (the relative minor: Am in C, Em in G) and you have the famous **I–V–vi–IV** progression used in a huge number of pop songs.

steps.title: Use your ear
steps.body: **V** wants to resolve to **I** (it feels like a question → answer). Play C → G in C major and stop on G — notice the 'unfinished' feeling. Then play C. That pull is called tension and resolution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing chord numbers with frets or fingers.
- Forgetting chords on 2, 3 and 6 are **minor** in a major key (ii, iii, vi), and 7 is diminished (vii°).

activity.prompt: Match each interval to its number of semitones.

quiz.q: C major triad is…
quiz.why: A C major triad stacks a root (C), major third (E) and perfect fifth (G), giving C E G.

quiz.q: In G major, the IV chord is…
quiz.why: In G major the scale is G A B C D E F♯, so the IV chord is built on the 4th note, C.

quiz.q: A minor triad has a ___ third.
quiz.why: A minor triad has a minor third, 3 semitones above the root, and a perfect fifth. A major triad has a major third.

quiz.q: How many semitones in a perfect fifth?
quiz.why: A perfect fifth spans 7 semitones, such as C to G.

quiz.q: The chord on degree vi in a major key is…
quiz.why: In a major key, ii, iii and vi are minor chords. I, IV and V are major, and vii° is diminished.

questions.q: C is the white key just left of…
questions.why: C is the white key just left of the group of two black keys. The group of three black keys is next to F, G, A and B.

questions.q: A quarter note in 4/4 lasts…
questions.why: In 4/4 the bottom 4 means a quarter note gets one beat, so a quarter note lasts 1 beat.

questions.q: Treble clef spaces spell…
questions.why: The treble clef spaces from the bottom spell F A C E. The lines spell E G B D F.

questions.q: A dot after a note…
questions.why: A dot after a note adds half of its value, so a dotted quarter lasts 1½ beats.

questions.q: Major scale formula?
options: W H W W H W W
H H W W W W H
W W H W W W H
W W W W H H W
questions.why: The major scale formula is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H).

questions.q: How many semitones in a major third?
questions.why: A major third spans 4 semitones, for example C to E. A minor third is 3 semitones.

questions.q: D major's key signature has…
questions.why: D major has two sharps, F♯ and C♯, since the scale is D E F♯ G A B C♯.

questions.q: Relative minor of G major is…
questions.why: The relative minor starts on the 6th note of the major scale. In G major the 6th note is E, so it is E minor.

questions.q: In C major, the V chord is…
questions.why: The V chord is built on the 5th note of the scale. In C major that's G, so the V chord is G.

questions.q: A harmonic minor scale on A is…
options: A B C D E F G♯ A
